side_cards/side_cards_seed_v1.json.title: Where are lists commonly used?
side_cards/side_cards_seed_v1.json.body: Lists are frequently used to handle multiple values in order. Most data sets consisting of multiple items—such as lists of students, scores, files, search results, or cards—can be represented as lists.
side_cards/side_cards_seed_v1.json.detail: With lists, you can process items one by one using a `for` loop, add new values with `append`, or count the number of items with `len`. When reading code and encountering a list, you should check the order in which the values are stored and how they are used in loops. Lists are frequently used when collecting and processing multiple values in order.

side_cards/side_cards_seed_v1.json.title: The foundation of code reading is the movement of values
side_cards/side_cards_seed_v1.json.body: The key to understanding code is to follow the flow of values. Variables act like labels that point to values, and assignment statements redefine the value that the label points to.
side_cards/side_cards_seed_v1.json.detail: For example, if you encounter `x = 3` followed by `x = x + 1`, you should interpret it as first reading the previous value of `x` (3) from the right side, adding 1 to it, and then storing the result (4) back into `x`. Even as the code gets longer, writing down how the values change line by line helps stabilize your understanding of the flow. The foundation of code reading is observing the flow of values.

side_cards/side_cards_seed_v1.json.title: Dict and JSON are often used together
side_cards/side_cards_seed_v1.json.body: You’ll encounter `dict` and JSON very frequently in real-world Python programming. A dict is a data type that stores key-value pairs, while JSON is a string format frequently used to exchange data with servers or files.
side_cards/side_cards_seed_v1.json.when_to_show: When reviewing dict, json, key, value
side_cards/side_cards_seed_v1.json.detail: At first glance, both use curly braces, but a Python dict is already a data structure, whereas JSON typically arrives as a string and must be converted using `json.load`. When reading code, you must first determine whether a given value is a string or a dict. This card is not just for memorizing definitions; it serves as a supplementary explanation to help you understand how these concepts relate to variables, data types, functions, files, and API flows in actual Python code.

side_cards/side_cards_seed_v1.json.title: The difference between row["key"] and row.get("key")
side_cards/side_cards_seed_v1.json.body: Bracket access raises KeyError when a key is absent, which is useful for validating a required field. get returns None or a chosen default, which is convenient for optional fields. Using get everywhere can hide invalid data, so first decide whether the field is required or optional.

side_cards/side_cards_seed_v1.json.title: Filtering Patterns
side_cards/side_cards_seed_v1.json.body: A filtering pattern is a process of retaining only the values that meet certain conditions from a larger set. In Python, this is typically done by iterating through the values one by one using a `for` loop and appending them to a new list only if the `if` condition is `True`. For example, code that keeps only scores of 60 or higher from a list of scores, or code that finds only cards with short body lengths from a list of cards, is an example of filtering.
side_cards/side_cards_seed_v1.json.when_to_show: When reviewing for, if, append, filter
side_cards/side_cards_seed_v1.json.detail: A filtering pattern is a process that retains only the values from the original list that meet a certain condition. It uses a `for` loop to iterate through the candidates one by one, an `if` statement to determine whether they meet the condition, and either `append` or a comprehension to build the result. When reading the code, separating the four elements—the original list, the current value, the condition, and the destination—makes it easier to see whether the condition is too broad or too narrow.

side_cards/side_cards_seed_v1.json.title: Normalization is the starting point for deduplication
side_cards/side_cards_seed_v1.json.body: Normalization applies a defined rule for whitespace, case, or representation before comparison. Because it can merge distinct originals, define domain rules first and preserve the source value. casefold may suit human-language case matching better than lower, while URLs, names, and identifiers need different rules.

side_cards/side_cards_seed_v1.json.title: json.loads converts a string into a data structure
side_cards/side_cards_seed_v1.json.body: `json.loads` is a function that converts a JSON string into a Python data structure. For example, a string like `'{"name":"A"}'` is simply a sequence of characters on its own, but when passed through `json.loads`, it becomes a dictionary from which you can retrieve values using keys, such as `row['name']`. Conversely, `json.dumps` converts a Python dictionary or list into a JSON string.
side_cards/side_cards_seed_v1.json.detail: `json.loads` converts a JSON string into a Python dictionary or list, and `json.dumps` converts a Python data structure into a JSON string. JSON files often consist of a single structure, whereas JSONL stores an independent JSON object on each line. When reading the code, you must distinguish between reading the entire file at once and iterating line by line.

side_cards/side_cards_seed_v1.json.title: JSONL is widely used in LLM datasets.
side_cards/side_cards_seed_v1.json.body: JSONL stores one independent JSON value per line and supports sequential processing of large datasets. A loop can parse each line with json.loads(), but a malformed record is not repaired automatically: record its line number and decide whether to skip or stop. Also define blank-line and encoding rules.

side_cards/side_cards_seed_v1.json.title: Most batch scripts follow an input-processing-output structure.
side_cards/side_cards_seed_v1.json.body: Most batch scripts follow an input-processing-output structure. First, they read data from a file or folder; then, they transform or validate the data; and finally, they write the results to a new file or report. In Python code, a common workflow involves creating a path using `Path`, reading data with `json.loads`, processing it with `for` and `if` statements, and saving it with `write_text`.
side_cards/side_cards_seed_v1.json.when_to_show: When reviewing pipeline, input, output, main
side_cards/side_cards_seed_v1.json.detail: Most batch scripts can be analyzed in terms of input, processing, and output. First, identify which files or folders are being read; then, determine what transformations, filtering, or validation are performed during processing; and finally, identify where the final result is saved. If an error occurs, identify which stage—input path, processing rules, or output permissions—is causing the problem.

side_cards/side_cards_seed_v1.json.title: You can guess the purpose just by looking at the `import` statement.
side_cards/side_cards_seed_v1.json.body: Just by looking at the `import` statements, you can make a reasonable guess about the purpose of the code. If `json` is imported, it’s likely that the code will handle JSON files or strings; if `Path` from `pathlib` is imported, it’s likely that the code will handle file paths. If you see `collections.Counter`, the code may be counting something.
side_cards/side_cards_seed_v1.json.when_to_show: When reviewing import, argparse, pathlib, json
side_cards/side_cards_seed_v1.json.detail: The list of imports is the first clue that helps you predict the purpose of the code. JSON is likely related to data conversion, pathlib to path handling, CSV to spreadsheet files, and `collections.Counter` to counting. By looking at the `import` statements and then tracing where the actual functions are used, you can grasp the overall purpose of a long file more quickly.

side_cards/side_cards_seed_v1.json.title: Breaking Down Features into Components
side_cards/side_cards_seed_v1.json.body: Breaking down functionality into smaller components makes the code easier to read. Even large programs are ultimately a collection of small functions that receive input, modify values, evaluate conditions, and store or output results. For example, a validation tool can be broken down into small tasks such as reading files, parsing JSON, checking required fields, and outputting errors.
side_cards/side_cards_seed_v1.json.detail: Breaking down functionality into individual components makes even large codebases easier to read. Functions such as login, authentication, and card creation can be broken down into smaller steps like receiving input, validating it, converting it, saving it, and updating the screen. By connecting function names, input values, and return values, you can see the responsibilities of each component and where to make changes.

side_cards/side_cards_seed_v1.json.title: Common Risks to Look for in Code Reviews
side_cards/side_cards_seed_v1.json.body: During code reviews, we don’t just check whether the code runs; we also assess the risk of future issues. For example, we verify that there are no duplicate IDs, that `answer` is within `choices`, that file paths actually exist, and that the code safely halts in the event of an exception. This review perspective is important even at the beginner level.
side_cards/side_cards_seed_v1.json.when_to_show: When reviewing risk, code_review, encoding, api_key
side_cards/side_cards_seed_v1.json.detail: During code reviews, we look not only at whether the code runs, but also at the risk of future problems. We check for issues such as duplicate IDs, missing fields, incorrect paths, insufficient exception handling, exposed API keys, meaningless names, and functions that are too large. By reading the code from a review perspective, we can determine whether code that works now will remain safe after future modifications.

side_cards/language_cards_v1.json.title: Python: Indentation defines code blocks
side_cards/language_cards_v1.json.body: Python uses indentation, the spaces at the start of a line, to show which lines belong inside an if, loop, or function. Lines at the same depth belong to the same block.
side_cards/language_cards_v1.json.when_to_show: if, for, def, Python Syntax Problems
side_cards/language_cards_v1.json.detail: After a colon in if, for, while, def, or class, the following block is indented. When the indentation returns to the earlier depth, that block has ended.

side_cards/language_cards_v1.json.title: C: A language close to memory
side_cards/language_cards_v1.json.body: C works with memory addresses and array sizes more directly than Python. This gives fine control and speed, but pointer or bounds mistakes can cause serious errors.
side_cards/language_cards_v1.json.when_to_show: When reviewing c, pointer, memory, overflow
side_cards/language_cards_v1.json.detail: C is a language that deals with memory addresses, array sizes, and pointers in a relatively direct way. While this allows you to create fast, low-level programs, out-of-bounds access and memory deallocation errors can be dangerous. When studying Python, it’s helpful to understand terms like “byte,” “stack,” “heap,” and “pointer” by relating them to the C-style memory model.

side_cards/language_cards_v1.json.title: Java: Class-Based Structure
side_cards/language_cards_v1.json.body: Java often organizes code around classes. A class is a blueprint that groups data and behavior.
side_cards/language_cards_v1.json.when_to_show: Class, Object-Oriented Programming, Type Comparison Problems
side_cards/language_cards_v1.json.detail: Java defines data and methods inside classes and creates objects from those classes. The broad idea is similar to Python classes, although Java has stricter syntax and type rules.

side_cards/language_cards_v1.json.title: JavaScript: The Web Browser's Default Language
side_cards/language_cards_v1.json.body: JavaScript makes web pages react to clicks, update the screen, and load data. Think of it as a language that drives browser behavior.
side_cards/language_cards_v1.json.when_to_show: When reviewing javascript, web, browser, nodejs
side_cards/language_cards_v1.json.detail: HTML gives a web page structure and CSS gives it appearance; JavaScript handles behavior such as clicks, screen updates, and loading data. fetch() is commonly used to request data from a server.

side_cards/language_cards_v1.json.title: SQL: Structured Query Language
side_cards/language_cards_v1.json.body: SQL is used to find or change data stored in database tables. SELECT reads data and WHERE adds a condition.
side_cards/language_cards_v1.json.when_to_show: When reviewing sql, database, select, join
side_cards/language_cards_v1.json.detail: SELECT name FROM users reads the name column from the users table. Adding WHERE age >= 20 keeps only rows that match the condition. Read SQL as: which table, which columns, and which condition?

side_cards/language_cards_v1.json.title: Cypher: Neo4j Graph Database Query Language
side_cards/language_cards_v1.json.body: Cypher is a query language for finding patterns of nodes and relationships in graph databases such as Neo4j. For example, `(student)-[:STRUGGLES_WITH]->(concept)` describes a path from a student node to a concept node through a `STRUGGLES_WITH` relationship. Parentheses `()` represent nodes, square brackets `[]` hold relationship information, and the arrow shows direction.
side_cards/language_cards_v1.json.when_to_show: Graph, node, edge, and knowledge-graph questions
side_cards/language_cards_v1.json.detail: Cypher is a query language used to find nodes and relationship patterns in graph databases such as Neo4j. Parentheses often denote nodes, while square brackets or arrows typically represent relationships and their directions. When reading the code, you must identify the starting node, determine how many steps to follow along a relationship, and distinguish whether the returned value is a node or a path.

side_cards/language_cards_v1.json.title: Rust: Striving for Both Safety and Performance
side_cards/language_cards_v1.json.body: Rust aims for C- or C++-like performance while using strict rules to reduce memory mistakes. As a first step, think of ownership as a rule that controls where and how a value may be used.
side_cards/language_cards_v1.json.detail: Rust is a language designed to enforce strict memory safety while maintaining performance. Although its ownership and borrowing rules may seem strict at first, they have the advantage of catching many errors before execution. When reading code, it is important to consider who owns a value, how long a reference remains in memory, and whether it is a mutable reference.

side_cards/language_cards_v1.json.title: Go: A language well-suited for servers and cloud tools
side_cards/language_cards_v1.json.body: Go is a language widely used for servers and cloud tools. Its syntax is relatively simple, it’s easy to build executable files with it, and it excels at handling multiple tasks simultaneously.
side_cards/language_cards_v1.json.when_to_show: When reviewing go, server, cloud, infra
side_cards/language_cards_v1.json.detail: There are also many tools built with Go in cloud ecosystems such as Docker and Kubernetes. As a Python learner, you don’t need to have an in-depth understanding of Go code right away, but it’s good to keep in mind that you’ll likely come across the name “Go” frequently when reading documentation on server tools or infrastructure.

side_cards/language_cards_v1.json.title: PowerShell: Windows Automation Shell
side_cards/language_cards_v1.json.body: PowerShell is a widely used automation shell on Windows. It allows you to perform tasks such as navigating folders, deleting files, running scripts, executing Git commands, and running Python code using commands.
side_cards/language_cards_v1.json.when_to_show: File Automation, Windows Paths, Script Issues
side_cards/language_cards_v1.json.detail: PowerShell often uses backticks for line continuation, and the default path notation follows the Windows convention. In development work, even for the same Python code, the command syntax may differ depending on whether it is executed in PowerShell or Bash. Therefore, you should check your current shell before pasting commands.

side_cards/language_cards_v1.json.title: Bash: The default shell for Linux/Ubuntu
side_cards/language_cards_v1.json.body: Bash is the default shell commonly used in Linux and Ubuntu environments. Like PowerShell, you can use commands to navigate folders, view files, and run programs.
side_cards/language_cards_v1.json.detail: When running Python projects on a server, you’ll frequently encounter Bash commands. For example, you’ll use commands like `cd`, `ls`, `cat`, `grep`, and `python`. When reading code, a Bash script isn’t Python code itself, but it can serve as an operational procedure that specifies the order in which Python is executed.

side_cards/language_cards_v1.json.title: A function is a small task box
side_cards/language_cards_v1.json.summary: You can think of a function as a small box of code that takes an input, performs a specific task, and returns a result.
side_cards/language_cards_v1.json.detail: The names inside the parentheses of a function definition are parameters. The actual values supplied in a call such as `add(2, 3)` are arguments. Trace which argument is bound to each parameter, execute the body, and then follow any `return` value back to the call site. A function with no `return` statement returns `None` by default.
examples: def add(a, b): return a + b
Input: a, b / Output: return value
side_cards/language_cards_v1.json.body: A function is a named block of code. Calling `len('Python')` supplies a string and returns the length 6. `result = len(items)` stores a return value in `result`, while `print(result)` displays that stored value on the screen. Returning and printing are not the same action. Read a function by tracing ① where it is called, ② which arguments are supplied, ③ how the body changes the values, and ④ what it returns.

side_cards/cs_fundamentals_v1.json.title: Binary: Computers use 0s and 1s.
side_cards/cs_fundamentals_v1.json.body: Binary uses only 0 and 1 to represent values. Computers store many kinds of information as patterns of these two digits.
side_cards/cs_fundamentals_v1.json.detail: For example, decimal 2 is binary 10. As a beginner, focus on the idea that computers represent values with patterns of 0 and 1 rather than memorizing conversion formulas first.

side_cards/cs_fundamentals_v1.json.title: bit and byte
side_cards/cs_fundamentals_v1.json.body: A bit is one 0-or-1 value, and a byte usually groups eight bits. You often see bytes when reading file or memory sizes.
side_cards/cs_fundamentals_v1.json.when_to_show: File Size, Memory, and Data Representation Issues
side_cards/cs_fundamentals_v1.json.detail: Eight bits usually make one byte. KB, MB, and GB group bytes into larger units, so this idea connects directly to file and memory sizes.

side_cards/cs_fundamentals_v1.json.title: Integer: A number without a decimal point
side_cards/cs_fundamentals_v1.json.body: An integer (int) is a whole number such as 1, 2, or 100. The text '10' is a string, not the number 10, so the two behave differently.
side_cards/cs_fundamentals_v1.json.detail: Python uses int for whole numbers. int('3') converts the string '3' into the number 3. Check quotation marks and int() conversions when a value looks numeric.

side_cards/cs_fundamentals_v1.json.title: Integer Overflow
side_cards/cs_fundamentals_v1.json.body: An integer overflow is a problem that occurs when a number exceeds the range in which it can be stored. In some languages, the size of integers is fixed, so calculating values that are too large may result in unexpected values or cause errors. While Python’s `int` type handles large numbers relatively flexibly, you must consider range limitations when exchanging data with other languages or systems.
side_cards/cs_fundamentals_v1.json.when_to_show: Problems with int, numpy, tensor, and dtype
side_cards/cs_fundamentals_v1.json.detail: While Python’s `int` type handles large numbers with relative flexibility, this is not the case in all environments. When working with NumPy dtypes, tensors, C extensions, or external APIs, there may be restrictions on the integer range. When reading code, if it involves calculations with large numbers or data type conversions, check the maximum and minimum values as well as the dtype.

side_cards/cs_fundamentals_v1.json.title: Floating-point error
side_cards/cs_fundamentals_v1.json.body: Floating-point error is a small discrepancy that occurs because computers cannot accurately represent decimal values. For example, a number like 0.1 may seem simple to humans, but it may not be stored exactly as intended in a computer’s internal binary representation. As a result, the outcome of decimal calculations may differ very slightly from what is expected.
side_cards/cs_fundamentals_v1.json.when_to_show: float, numerical calculations, data analysis problems
side_cards/cs_fundamentals_v1.json.detail: Since `float` stores numbers as approximations, calculations like `0.1 + 0.2` may differ very slightly from what a person would expect. When reading code, be careful when comparing floating-point numbers directly using the `==` operator. For values where accuracy is critical—such as monetary amounts—check whether `Decimal`, rounding, or tolerance criteria are needed.

side_cards/cs_fundamentals_v1.json.title: Character Encoding and UTF-8
side_cards/cs_fundamentals_v1.json.body: Encoding is the rule used to turn text into stored bytes and back into text. UTF-8 is a common encoding for Korean, English, and many other characters.
side_cards/cs_fundamentals_v1.json.when_to_show: open, reading files, Korean character display issues
side_cards/cs_fundamentals_v1.json.detail: A file should be read with the same encoding used to save it. When you see open(..., encoding='utf-8') or read_text(encoding='utf-8'), read it as 'interpret the file text as UTF-8.'

side_cards/cs_fundamentals_v1.json.title: Stacks and Heaps
side_cards/cs_fundamentals_v1.json.body: Stacks and heaps are concepts that come up when explaining how programs use memory. While you don’t need to understand them in great depth at the beginner level, they are helpful for understanding where function calls, local variables, and objects are stored. In Python, you rarely have to manage memory directly, but understanding how objects like lists and dictionaries are associated with variable names makes concepts like shallow copies and mutability easier to grasp.
side_cards/cs_fundamentals_v1.json.detail: Stacks and heaps are fundamental concepts that explain memory structure. In beginner-level Python, it is sufficient to relate them to understanding function calls, local variables, and object references, rather than delving into deep internal implementations. Understanding that assigning a list or dictionary to another variable can cause both to point to the same object makes it easier to grasp the concepts of mutability and copying.

side_cards/cs_fundamentals_v1.json.title: Compiled Languages and Interpreted Languages
side_cards/cs_fundamentals_v1.json.body: Compilation changes code into a form that is easier to execute, while interpretation processes code as it runs. Python implementations can use more than one of these steps.
side_cards/cs_fundamentals_v1.json.when_to_show: When reviewing compile, interpreter, python, c
side_cards/cs_fundamentals_v1.json.detail: CPython first changes Python source into an intermediate form called bytecode. The Python virtual machine then executes that bytecode. For a beginner, the key idea is simply that Python also has a conversion step before execution.

side_cards/cs_fundamentals_v1.json.title: Type System
side_cards/cs_fundamentals_v1.json.body: A type tells you what kind of value something is. For example, 3 is an int while '3' is a string, so they can behave differently even if they look similar.
side_cards/cs_fundamentals_v1.json.when_to_show: Type, Java Comparison, Python Variable Problem
side_cards/cs_fundamentals_v1.json.detail: The same + symbol adds numbers for int values but joins text for str values. When reading code, check quotation marks and conversions such as int(), str(), and type() instead of judging only by how a value looks.

side_cards/cs_fundamentals_v1.json.title: Hash Table: Fast Lookup by Key
side_cards/cs_fundamentals_v1.json.body: A hash table is a data structure designed to quickly find values using keys. Python dictionaries are also related to the concept of hash tables. While finding a value in a list may require checking from the beginning sequentially, a dictionary is more like a method that uses a key to find a value immediately.
side_cards/cs_fundamentals_v1.json.detail: A hash table is a data structure that uses keys to quickly find values, and it forms the foundation for understanding Python dictionaries. When reading code that uses a dictionary, check which values serve as keys, and determine whether the `get` method is used when a key is missing or if an exception is raised. They frequently appear in code related to caching, counting, removing duplicates, and creating indexes.

side_cards/cs_fundamentals_v1.json.title: Graph: Nodes and Edges
side_cards/cs_fundamentals_v1.json.body: A graph is a structure composed of nodes and relationships. A node represents a single entity—such as a concept, person, document, or place—while a relationship shows how those entities are connected.
side_cards/cs_fundamentals_v1.json.detail: For example, if “Python,” “list,” and “append” are each a node, “append” can be used to connect them via the relationship that “append adds values to a list.” When reading code, the graph perspective helps you understand the connections between functions and data, files and results, and concepts and examples. This card is not intended merely for memorizing word definitions; rather, it serves as a supplementary explanation to help you identify how specific variables, data types, functions, files, and API flows are connected in actual Python code.

side_cards/cs_fundamentals_v1.json.title: JSON and JSONL
side_cards/cs_fundamentals_v1.json.body: JSON and JSONL are formats frequently used for storing and exchanging data. JSON represents object or list structures as strings, while JSONL places a single JSON object on a single line.
side_cards/cs_fundamentals_v1.json.detail: A single JSON file is sufficient for small configuration files, but JSONL can be more convenient for large training datasets or logs. In Python, you can use `json.loads` to convert a string into a dictionary or list, and `json.dumps` to convert it back into a string. When reading code, you must distinguish whether the entire file is a single JSON object or if each line contains a separate JSON object.

side_cards/cs_fundamentals_v1.json.title: APIs and REST
side_cards/cs_fundamentals_v1.json.body: An API is an interface for exchanging requests and responses. REST is an architectural style that commonly uses HTTP resources, methods, and status codes.
side_cards/cs_fundamentals_v1.json.detail: GET often retrieves and POST often submits or creates, but the actual contract defines their meaning; read the endpoint documentation, authentication, input schema, failures, and response format.

side_cards/cs_fundamentals_v1.json.title: batch and shard
side_cards/cs_fundamentals_v1.json.body: “Batch” and “shard” are terms frequently used when dividing large tasks into smaller parts for processing. A “batch” is a unit consisting of multiple items processed at once, while a “shard” is a large dataset or scope of work divided into multiple pieces. For example, instead of validating 1,000 cards all at once, it is easier to manage them by processing them in batches of 100.
side_cards/cs_fundamentals_v1.json.when_to_show: Batch Processing, LLM Pipelines, and Retry Mechanisms
side_cards/cs_fundamentals_v1.json.detail: A "batch" is a unit that groups multiple tasks for processing, while a "shard" is a range created by dividing a large task into multiple pieces. In bulk data processing and LLM pipelines, restart capabilities, duplicate prevention, and completion logging are critical. When reading the code, check how the current shard number, the total range, and the items already processed are stored.

side_cards/cs_fundamentals_v1.json.title: mutable / immutable
side_cards/cs_fundamentals_v1.json.summary: A mutable value is one whose content can change after it is created, while an immutable value is one whose content does not change after it is created.
examples: When two variables share the same list
side_cards/cs_fundamentals_v1.json.body: Lists, dictionaries, and sets are mutable, so a change is visible through every name referencing the same object. Strings, integers, and tuples themselves are immutable, but a tuple can contain a mutable object whose contents still change. Distinguish rebinding a name from mutating an existing object.

side_cards/cs_fundamentals_v1.json.title: shallow copy / deep copy
side_cards/cs_fundamentals_v1.json.summary: A shallow copy copies only the outer container, while a deep copy copies the inner objects as well.
side_cards/cs_fundamentals_v1.json.body: A shallow copy creates a new outer container but shares references to nested objects. copy.deepcopy() recursively copies nested objects, yet custom copy behavior and non-copyable resources mean it is not an unconditional promise that every resource becomes independent. Choose based on the object graph and intended mutations.

side_cards/cs_fundamentals_v1.json.title: Matrices and Vectors Code
side_cards/cs_fundamentals_v1.json.summary: A matrix is a structure in which numbers are arranged in rows and columns, while a vector is a sequence of numbers arranged in a single direction.
side_cards/cs_fundamentals_v1.json.detail: Matrix and vector code is an exercise in understanding how multiple numbers are organized into a specific structure. A vector can be viewed as a single row of values, while a matrix can be viewed as a table with rows and columns. In NumPy, the @ operator is used for matrix multiplication and frequently appears in code involving coordinate transformations, embeddings, and Kalman filters. Start by confirming the dimensions and the meanings of rows and columns.
side_cards/cs_fundamentals_v1.json.body: Matrices and vectors are basic structures for organizing and working with multiple numbers. You can think of a vector as a line of numbers, and a matrix as a table where numbers are arranged in rows and columns. In introductory Python courses, lists are introduced first, but later on, in data analysis or AI code, lists are often used in ways similar to vectors or matrices.

side_cards/ai_cards_v1.json.title: The Differences Between AI, ML, and DL
side_cards/ai_cards_v1.json.body: AI, ML, and DL are often used interchangeably, but their scopes differ. AI is a broad field that enables computers to perform tasks that humans do intelligently.
side_cards/ai_cards_v1.json.when_to_show: When reviewing ai, ml, deep_learning, model
side_cards/ai_cards_v1.json.detail: ML is a method of learning rules from data, and DL is one of the machine learning methods that uses multi-layer neural networks. LLMs are also deep learning-based models. When you come across the term “AI” while reading code, you should check the context to determine whether it actually refers to a rule-based program, a machine learning model, or a deep learning model.

side_cards/ai_cards_v1.json.title: LLM: Large Language Model
side_cards/ai_cards_v1.json.body: LLM stands for Large Language Model.
side_cards/ai_cards_v1.json.detail: These models are trained on vast amounts of text to understand and generate sentences, and are used for tasks such as question-answering, summarization, translation, and code generation. However, since LLMs do not always guarantee factual accuracy, it may be necessary to search for and verify sources. When reading code, LLM calls must be understood in the context of prompt construction, input tokens, output processing, cost, and error handling.

side_cards/ai_cards_v1.json.title: MLM: Masked Language Model
side_cards/ai_cards_v1.json.body: MLM stands for Masked Language Model, a training method in which parts of a sentence are masked and the model is trained to fill in the blanks. For example, the model can be asked to predict the blank in the sentence “Python is a [MASK] language.” It has been widely used in BERT-family models and is closely related to sentence understanding and representation learning.
side_cards/ai_cards_v1.json.detail: MLM can be understood as a learning method where part of a sentence is masked and the user must fill in the blank. It differs in approach and purpose from conversational generative models, which continue writing the next sentence. When reading the code, you should verify whether the model is being used for blank prediction, sentence classification, embedding generation, or free generation. In particular, it is helpful to distinguish between the BERT family and generative LLMs.

side_cards/ai_cards_v1.json.title: Token: A segment read by the model
side_cards/ai_cards_v1.json.body: A token is the basic unit that a model uses to read and process text.
side_cards/ai_cards_v1.json.detail: Even if something looks like a single word to a human, it can be split into multiple tokens internally by the model, and Korean characters or special characters can also affect the number of tokens. Since the model has a limit on the number of tokens it can process at once, long documents or conversations must be split into smaller chunks. When reading code, settings such as `token limit`, `context window`, and `max_tokens` are linked to computational cost, response length, and the likelihood of failure.

side_cards/ai_cards_v1.json.title: Embedding: Converting Meaning into Numeric Vectors
side_cards/ai_cards_v1.json.body: Embedding is a method of converting the meaning of sentences or words into numerical vectors.
side_cards/ai_cards_v1.json.when_to_show: When reviewing embedding, vector, rag, search
side_cards/ai_cards_v1.json.detail: Since computers cannot directly understand the meaning of text, they transform it so that sentences with similar meanings are positioned close to each other in the numerical space. The vectors created in this way can be used for search, recommendation, clustering, and duplicate detection. In RAG, the question and document fragments are embedded, and then the closest match is found.

side_cards/ai_cards_v1.json.title: Vector DB: A database for embedding search
side_cards/ai_cards_v1.json.body: A vector database is a database designed for embedding-based search. It converts documents or sentences into numerical vectors for storage, and after converting the user’s query into a vector as well, it finds document fragments with similar meanings. While traditional keyword search requires exact matches to find results, vector search can find results even if the phrasing differs slightly, as long as the meaning is similar.
side_cards/ai_cards_v1.json.when_to_show: When reviewing vector_db, embedding, rag, search
side_cards/ai_cards_v1.json.detail: A vector database can be viewed as a storage system for search that stores embeddings and finds nearby vectors. When reviewing the code, verify that the document storage phase and the query search phase are separated. The top-k count, filter conditions, similarity criteria, and source metadata directly affect answer quality. You should also check whether the search results are verified rather than simply accepted at face value.

side_cards/ai_cards_v1.json.title: RAG: Search and Answer
side_cards/ai_cards_v1.json.body: RAG stands for Retrieval-Augmented Generation, a method of generating answers based on retrieved evidence.
side_cards/ai_cards_v1.json.when_to_show: When reviewing rag, retrieval, embedding, llm
side_cards/ai_cards_v1.json.detail: Rather than answering solely from memory, the model first locates relevant document fragments and then references that content to formulate its response. As such, it is linked to stages such as document retrieval, chunking, embedding, prompting, and citation. When reading RAG code, you should check how the question is converted into a search query, which documents are selected, and how the selected evidence is incorporated into the response.

side_cards/ai_cards_v1.json.title: AI Agent: AI That Uses Tools to Achieve Its Goals
side_cards/ai_cards_v1.json.body: An AI agent refers to an AI architecture that selects tools and performs multiple steps to achieve a goal. While a simple chatbot focuses on answering questions directly, an agent can use tools such as searching, reading files, performing calculations, and executing code to carry out tasks. However, using tools isn’t always safe, so planning, execution, verification, and constraints are necessary.
side_cards/ai_cards_v1.json.when_to_show: Code Agent, Automation, and Tool Usage Issues
side_cards/ai_cards_v1.json.detail: An AI Agent is a framework in which a model selects tools and executes a series of steps to achieve a goal. When reviewing the code, don’t just look at the model’s responses; examine the entire workflow—including planning, invoking tools, verifying results, retrying, and handling failures. Using tools doesn’t always guarantee safety, so permission restrictions and verification steps are also necessary.

side_cards/ai_cards_v1.json.title: Tool Calling: How the Model Calls Tools
side_cards/ai_cards_v1.json.body: Tool Calling is a method in which a model calls upon necessary tools to continue its work. Rather than generating all answers on its own, the model can utilize external functions such as search tools, calculation tools, file-reading tools, and code-execution tools. For example, if a user asks for the latest information, the model uses a search tool; if numerical calculations are needed, it uses a calculation tool.
side_cards/ai_cards_v1.json.when_to_show: When reviewing tool_calling, agent, api, workflow
side_cards/ai_cards_v1.json.detail: Tool Calling is a method by which a model invokes an external function in a specified format. When reading the code, check the tool name, input schema, invocation conditions, handling of return values, and the fallback flow in case of failure. You must distinguish whether the content is the model’s direct response or reflects the results of a search or computational tool.

side_cards/ai_cards_v1.json.title: Labeling and Annotation
side_cards/ai_cards_v1.json.body: Labeling and annotation involve attaching correct answers or descriptive tags to data.
side_cards/ai_cards_v1.json.when_to_show: When reviewing labeling, annotation, dataset, training
side_cards/ai_cards_v1.json.detail: For example, indicating whether a sentence is positive or negative, marking the location of objects in an image, or assigning difficulty levels and concepts to problem cards are all forms of labeling. AI models are trained or evaluated based on these labels. In code, they may appear as fields such as `label`, `annotation`, `target`, or `answer`.

side_cards/ai_cards_v1.json.title: Evaluation Sets and Benchmarks
side_cards/ai_cards_v1.json.body: Evaluation datasets and benchmarks are reference data used to compare the performance of AI systems or programs. Just because a model produces plausible answers doesn’t necessarily mean it’s good; its performance must be verified against defined problems, correct answers, or evaluation criteria. Even in learning apps, verification criteria such as the number of cards, whether correct answers are included, missing fields, and difficulty distribution are necessary.
side_cards/ai_cards_v1.json.when_to_show: When reviewing eval, benchmark, dataset, quality
side_cards/ai_cards_v1.json.detail: Evaluation sets and benchmarks serve as criteria for verifying whether a model or rule actually works well. When reading code, I look at the input data, the ground truth, how scores are calculated, and whether failure cases are recorded. A high score alone isn’t enough; I also need to verify that the evaluation data aligns with the context in which I intend to use it.

side_cards/ai_cards_v1.json.title: Understanding LLM/API Costs
side_cards/ai_cards_v1.json.summary: The cost of the LLM API increases based on the number of requests, input length, output length, and the number of retries.
side_cards/ai_cards_v1.json.detail: In batch jobs or AI API calls, the number of requests, input length, output length, and number of retries are all tied to costs. Therefore, you should skip results that have already been processed, use caching, set timeouts and retry limits, and log request and response sizes. During code reviews, we first look for infinite loops, duplicate calls, exposed API keys, and excessive retry attempts following failures.
side_cards/ai_cards_v1.json.body: An understanding of LLM/API costs is essential basic knowledge when turning code into a service. While Python tutorials typically start with `print` statements and functions, real-world AI apps can incur costs with every model call. If an external API is called every time a user asks a question, the cost increases based on the number of requests, the number of characters in the input, and the number of characters in the output.

side_cards/ai_cards_v1.json.title: Retrieval
side_cards/ai_cards_v1.json.summary: Retrieval is the stage in which documents or chunk candidates relevant to the query are first identified.
side_cards/ai_cards_v1.json.detail: In RAG, the model does not provide an answer immediately; instead, it first searches for relevant evidence. Searches can be performed using keywords, BM25, embedding/vector search, hybrid search, and other methods. During the code review, we examine the workflow involving query input, index search, top_k, score, and reranking.
side_cards/ai_cards_v1.json.body: Retrieval is the process by which the system first locates the necessary data before the model generates an answer. When a user asks a question, instead of reading the entire document, the system searches for relevant excerpts and passes them to the model. This allows the model to respond based on actual data rather than relying solely on its memory.

side_cards/ai_cards_v1.json.title: State estimation
side_cards/ai_cards_v1.json.summary: State estimation is the process of using observations to estimate unobservable states such as position, velocity, and attitude.
side_cards/ai_cards_v1.json.detail: In robotics, autonomous driving, and UAM, it is difficult to determine the current state immediately because sensor measurements are noisy. Methods such as the Kalman Filter combine predicted values and measured values to produce more stable state estimates. During a code review, look for the `state`, `predict`, `update`, and `noise` variables first.
side_cards/ai_cards_v1.json.body: State estimation is the process of estimating the current state of a system. A state is a value that indicates the current condition of a program or device, such as position, velocity, direction, remaining battery life, or progress stage. Since sensor readings are not always perfect, the system calculates the current state by combining the previous state with new observations.

side_cards/ai_cards_v1.json.title: Sensor fusion
side_cards/ai_cards_v1.json.summary: Sensor fusion is the process of combining data from multiple sensors to achieve more reliable recognition.
side_cards/ai_cards_v1.json.detail: For example, LiDAR, radar, cameras, and GNSS/IMU each have their own strengths and weaknesses. Sensor fusion code aligns measurement values with a common state or coordinate system and uses both predicted and observed values together. During a code review, we examine the measurement, timestamp, calibration, and update step.
side_cards/ai_cards_v1.json.body: Sensor fusion is a method of combining information from multiple sensors to make more reliable decisions. In robots and autonomous driving systems, cameras, LiDAR, radar, and location sensors each provide different types of information. Cameras are good at detecting color and shape, while radar is effective at providing distance and speed information.

side_cards/platform_cards_v1.json.title: Endpoint: The address that receives requests
side_cards/platform_cards_v1.json.body: An endpoint is an address that receives requests. In a web service, when a user sends a request to a specific URL, the server executes the code associated with that endpoint.
side_cards/platform_cards_v1.json.when_to_show: When reviewing endpoint, api, server, http
side_cards/platform_cards_v1.json.detail: For example, URLs such as /api/home, /login, and /search can serve as endpoints. When reading Python or JavaScript code, an endpoint is the entry point where input is received. It’s easier to understand the service flow by checking which methods are accepted, which parameters are read, and what JSON is returned.

side_cards/platform_cards_v1.json.title: CLI: A command-line tool used in the terminal
side_cards/platform_cards_v1.json.body: CLI stands for Command Line Interface, which is a way of using programs via commands in a terminal. Unlike a GUI, where you click buttons, the CLI performs tasks by entering commands and options.
side_cards/platform_cards_v1.json.detail: Commands such as `git status`, `python script.py`, and `npm install` are examples of CLI usage. The CLI is well-suited for automating repetitive tasks and is widely used in server environments. When reading code, you should check what input options CLI tools accept and what output or files they generate.

side_cards/platform_cards_v1.json.title: sudo: Run as administrator
side_cards/platform_cards_v1.json.body: "sudo" is a term used in Linux and Ubuntu to run commands with administrative privileges.
side_cards/platform_cards_v1.json.detail: Since regular users cannot freely modify system-wide settings or specific folders, they use "sudo" to run commands with higher privileges when necessary. However, because these privileges are so powerful, a single mistake could corrupt system files. When you see `sudo` while running code or installing a package, you should verify whether the task truly requires administrative privileges and what files or settings it will modify.

side_cards/platform_cards_v1.json.title: Environment Variables: Settings Outside the Code
side_cards/platform_cards_v1.json.body: Environment variables are configuration values supplied from outside the source code at runtime.
side_cards/platform_cards_v1.json.detail: The same code can use different API endpoints or modes on a development PC and a server, and API keys do not have to be written directly in the source. Python reads them by name with calls such as `os.getenv('NAME')` or `os.environ['NAME']`. Environment-variable values are strings by default, so numbers and booleans need conversion and validation.

side_cards/platform_cards_v1.json.title: Cron: Runs at a specified time
side_cards/platform_cards_v1.json.body: Cron is a mechanism for running tasks at scheduled times. It allows you to automatically perform tasks—such as collecting data every morning or generating reports every night—without having to manually press a button each time. In a Python project, you can create a script and have it run periodically in a production environment.
side_cards/platform_cards_v1.json.when_to_show: When reviewing cron, schedule, automation, batch
side_cards/platform_cards_v1.json.detail: Cron is a system that automatically executes commands at specified intervals. When reviewing the code, you should consider not only the script’s contents but also its execution cycle, time zone, working directory, log location, and whether it retries in case of failure. This is particularly important for recurring tasks—such as daily data collection or periodic backups—that run automatically without requiring manual intervention.

side_cards/platform_cards_v1.json.title: Harvest: The data collection phase
side_cards/platform_cards_v1.json.body: Harvest is the data collection phase. It retrieves raw data from sources such as web pages, APIs, files, and RSS feeds, and either stores it or passes it on to the next processing stage. Since URLs may change, responses may fail, or duplicate data may be received during the collection stage, logging and validation are crucial.
side_cards/platform_cards_v1.json.when_to_show: Collection, Pipeline, and Data Processing Issues
side_cards/platform_cards_v1.json.detail: Harvest is the first step in retrieving data from external sources. By reading web pages, APIs, RSS feeds, and files, and logging the source ID, URL, collection time, and status code, it becomes easy to track the data later. When reading the code, we assess the pipeline’s stability by verifying the collection targets, duplicate prevention, retry mechanisms for failures, and storage locations.

side_cards/platform_cards_v1.json.title: Curation: The process of selecting what is important
side_cards/platform_cards_v1.json.body: Curation is the process of selecting what is important from a large number of candidates. Once data is collected, not every item is equally useful. Duplicate items, outdated items, low-quality items, and items that do not fit the topic must be filtered out.
side_cards/platform_cards_v1.json.when_to_show: When reviewing curation, ranking, dedup, quality
side_cards/platform_cards_v1.json.detail: Curation is the process of selecting items that meet specific criteria from a large pool of candidates. It involves more than just sorting by recency; it also takes into account duplicates, quality, topic relevance, priority, and exclusion rules. When reading the code, check where score calculations, filter conditions, sorting criteria, and the selection of the top N items take place.

side_cards/platform_cards_v1.json.title: Pipeline: Step-by-Step Processing Flow
side_cards/platform_cards_v1.json.body: A pipeline is a workflow that divides tasks into multiple stages and processes them sequentially.
side_cards/platform_cards_v1.json.when_to_show: When reviewing pipeline, etl, batch, workflow
side_cards/platform_cards_v1.json.detail: As with data collection, cleaning, validation, storage, and report generation, each stage receives the results from the previous stage and passes them on to the next. Most Python batch scripts follow a pipeline structure. When reading the code, don’t just look at it line by line; instead, try to identify whether the current stage is reading input, transforming data, or storing results—this will help you see the overall flow more clearly.

side_cards/platform_cards_v1.json.title: DB Types at a Glance
side_cards/platform_cards_v1.json.body: Storage choice depends on consistency, query patterns, update frequency, scale, and operating constraints—not only data shape. A system may use several stores.
side_cards/platform_cards_v1.json.when_to_show: When reviewing database, rdb, nosql, graphdb
side_cards/platform_cards_v1.json.detail: Compare the actual read/write and recovery requirements before choosing an RDB, document store, vector store, graph database, or object storage.

side_cards/platform_cards_v1.json.title: GraphDB: A Database That Puts Relationships First
side_cards/platform_cards_v1.json.body: GraphDB is a database that prioritizes relationships. It is well-suited for data where connections are crucial—such as which concept is a prerequisite for another, which document explains a particular topic, or which student is stuck on a specific problem. In learning services, it can be used to create personalized recommendations by connecting concept nodes, problem nodes, and hint nodes.
side_cards/platform_cards_v1.json.when_to_show: Graph DB, KG, and Cypher Issues
side_cards/platform_cards_v1.json.detail: GraphDB is a database that retrieves data by traversing connections between nodes and edges. In learning services, it is useful for exploring relationships between concepts, problems, hints, and documents. When reading the code, check which elements are nodes and which relationships are edges, whether the edges are directed, and how many steps the traversal goes through.

side_cards/platform_cards_v1.json.title: Object Storage: Storage for Large Files
side_cards/platform_cards_v1.json.body: Object storage keeps objects such as images, PDFs, backups, and model artifacts under keys with metadata. It is not limited to large files, but its query, consistency, and permission model differs from a file system or relational table. Check bucket/key naming, access, retention, versioning, integrity, and links to database metadata.
side_cards/platform_cards_v1.json.when_to_show: File Storage, Original Text, and Large Data Issues

side_cards/platform_cards_v1.json.title: Cache: Temporarily stores frequently used results
side_cards/platform_cards_v1.json.body: Caching is a method of temporarily storing frequently used results. Recalculating the same request from scratch or re-making the API call every time takes a long time and increases costs. Therefore, previous results are stored so that when the same request is received, it can be returned quickly.
side_cards/platform_cards_v1.json.when_to_show: When reviewing cache, performance, api, server
side_cards/platform_cards_v1.json.detail: Caching is a method of temporarily storing frequently used results to reduce processing time and costs. When reviewing code, check what the cache key is, when values are stored and when they are recalculated, and whether there are expiration times or conditions for forced refresh. You must also consider the risk of outdated values remaining after a fast response. For API responses and browser caches, the criteria for updating are particularly important.

side_cards/web_app_cards_v1.json.title: Front End and Back End
side_cards/web_app_cards_v1.json.body: "Frontend" and "Backend" are terms that describe the division of roles in a web application.
side_cards/web_app_cards_v1.json.when_to_show: When reviewing frontend, backend, api, web
side_cards/web_app_cards_v1.json.detail: The frontend consists of the user interface—including screens, buttons, and input fields—while the backend handles tasks on the server, such as data storage, login, API processing, and validation. Although Python is primarily used for backend development, there are also structures—such as learning apps—where static JSON is read directly on the screen. When reviewing code, it becomes easier to understand if you can distinguish whether a file is intended for the user interface or for server-side processing.

side_cards/web_app_cards_v1.json.title: HTML, CSS, JavaScript
side_cards/web_app_cards_v1.json.body: HTML, CSS, and JavaScript are the three fundamental elements used to create web pages.
side_cards/web_app_cards_v1.json.when_to_show: When reviewing html, css, javascript, web
side_cards/web_app_cards_v1.json.detail: HTML defines the structure of the page, CSS determines its appearance—such as colors and sizes—and JavaScript handles actions like button clicks and data loading. In the Python learning app, data is stored in JSON format, and JavaScript reads that data on the screen to display it as cards. When reading web code, you must distinguish between structure, style, and behavior.

side_cards/web_app_cards_v1.json.title: PWA: Using the Web Like an App
side_cards/web_app_cards_v1.json.body: PWA stands for Progressive Web App, which is a way to make a website function like an app. Although it opens in a browser just like a regular web page, it can be added to the home screen, use an offline cache, and provide an app-like experience. In a learning app, for example, it receives a lesson JSON file and displays it on the screen, while a service worker can cache certain files.
side_cards/web_app_cards_v1.json.when_to_show: Mobile Web App, GitHub Pages Issue
side_cards/web_app_cards_v1.json.detail: A PWA is a method that allows users to install and use a website just like an app. It combines standard HTML, CSS, and JavaScript with a manifest, service workers, and a caching strategy to enable features such as adding the app to the home screen and offline usage. When reviewing the code, you should examine the app version, the files targeted for caching, and the update process following a new deployment.

side_cards/web_app_cards_v1.json.title: GitHub Pages: Deploying a Static Site
side_cards/web_app_cards_v1.json.body: GitHub Pages is a GitHub feature that allows you to deploy static websites.
side_cards/web_app_cards_v1.json.detail: You can publish files—such as HTML, CSS, JavaScript, images, and JSON—that can be read directly in a browser without server-side code via a web address. If your Python learning app has a static PWA structure, you can deploy it on a platform like GitHub Pages. When reading code, you must distinguish whether it involves server-side processing or a structure where the browser reads pre-generated files.

side_cards/web_app_cards_v1.json.title: localStorage: Browser Storage
side_cards/web_app_cards_v1.json.body: localStorage is a feature that stores small amounts of data within the browser. Even without a server, it allows you to save values such as user settings, the last card viewed, and simple progress status in the browser.
side_cards/web_app_cards_v1.json.when_to_show: When reviewing localStorage, browser, memo, progress
side_cards/web_app_cards_v1.json.detail: Since values are typically stored as strings, you must convert objects or lists to strings using `JSON.stringify` to store them, and then restore them using `JSON.parse` when reading them back. When reading the code, it’s important to distinguish that localStorage is a storage mechanism within the user’s browser, not a server database.

side_cards/web_app_cards_v1.json.title: CORS: Browser permission for cross-origin responses
side_cards/web_app_cards_v1.json.body: An origin is the combination of scheme, host, and port; a difference in any one makes it a different origin in the browser. For front-end JavaScript to use an API response across origins, the server must authorize the relevant origin, HTTP method, and request headers through CORS response headers. For some requests the browser first sends an OPTIONS preflight, while a simple request may reach the server but still be unreadable to JavaScript when the required response header is absent.
side_cards/web_app_cards_v1.json.when_to_show: When connecting a browser front end to an API on a different origin
side_cards/web_app_cards_v1.json.detail: Compare the schemes, hosts, and ports of the front-end and request URLs, then inspect the server's allowed origins, methods, headers, and actual CORS response headers. Distinguish a preflight failure from an API failure, and do not mistake CORS for authentication or access control.

side_cards/web_app_cards_v1.json.title: Routing: Linking Addresses to Screens/Functions
side_cards/web_app_cards_v1.json.body: Routing is a structure that links addresses to screens or functions. For example, when a user navigates to /home, the home screen is displayed, and when a request is made to /api/items, data is returned. Front-end routing changes the screen based on the URL, while back-end routing executes server functions based on the URL.
side_cards/web_app_cards_v1.json.when_to_show: When reviewing routing, url, endpoint, spa
side_cards/web_app_cards_v1.json.detail: Routing is a set of rules that maps URLs to screens or server functions. Front-end routing changes the screen state based on the URL, while back-end routing selects the function to execute based on the URL and HTTP method. When reading code, you should check the URL the user entered, the matching route, how unrecognized URLs are handled, and how API endpoints are distinguished.

side_cards/web_app_cards_v1.json.title: Certification and Authorization
side_cards/web_app_cards_v1.json.body: Authentication and authorization are common concepts in web service security. Authentication is the process of verifying a user’s identity, while authorization is the process of determining which features that user is permitted to use. Logging in is similar to authentication, whereas restricting access to a specific page to administrators only is similar to authorization.
side_cards/web_app_cards_v1.json.when_to_show: When reviewing auth, oauth, jwt, session
side_cards/web_app_cards_v1.json.detail: Authentication is the process of verifying a user’s identity, while authorization is the process of determining what that user is permitted to do. A successful login does not automatically grant all permissions. When reading code, you should distinguish between the parts that validate tokens or sessions and those that check roles, permissions, and administrator status.

side_cards/web_app_cards_v1.json.title: API Request
side_cards/web_app_cards_v1.json.summary: An API request is an action in which client or server code calls a function on another server.
side_cards/web_app_cards_v1.json.detail: An API request is an agreed-upon channel through which clients and servers exchange data. During code reviews, we examine everything from the URL, method, headers, query parameters, body payload, timeout, and status code to the handling of `response.json` and error handling. It’s important not only to verify whether the request was successful but also to see how failure responses and network exceptions are handled.
side_cards/web_app_cards_v1.json.body: An API request is a request sent by a program to another program or server to obtain necessary information. Just as a person clicks a button in a web browser, Python code can also send requests to a server’s address and receive responses. For example, a weather app sends location information to a weather server, and the server returns data such as temperature and forecasts.

side_cards/ai_architecture_cards_v1.json.title: An AI system is not just a single model
side_cards/ai_architecture_cards_v1.json.body: An AI system isn’t made up of just a single model.
side_cards/ai_architecture_cards_v1.json.when_to_show: AI Services, RAG, and Agent Issues
side_cards/ai_architecture_cards_v1.json.detail: Actual services involve multiple stages, such as input preparation, searching, evidence selection, prompt generation, model invocation, output validation, log storage, and cost management. The model is merely the core component responsible for generating answers or making decisions. When reading code, don’t just look at the line that calls the model; to understand the overall structure, you must also examine what data is prepared beforehand and what validation is performed afterward.

side_cards/ai_architecture_cards_v1.json.title: Prompt: Instructions for the model
side_cards/ai_architecture_cards_v1.json.body: A prompt is a set of instructions given to the model.
side_cards/ai_architecture_cards_v1.json.when_to_show: When reviewing prompt, llm, instruction, output_format
side_cards/ai_architecture_cards_v1.json.detail: While it can consist solely of a user’s question, in actual services, it often includes the model’s role, response format, prohibited actions, reference materials, and examples. A good prompt clearly tells the model what it should and should not do. When reading code, if the prompt is a long string, it should be treated as a critical setting for adjusting output quality.

side_cards/ai_architecture_cards_v1.json.title: Context Window: The range the model can see at one time
side_cards/ai_architecture_cards_v1.json.body: A context window is the amount of information a model can reference in one request. The limit is measured in tokens rather than characters, and system instructions, the user request, prior conversation, and retrieved documents all share that space. If the input is too large, an API may reject it or the application may need to remove content, leaving less room for the answer.
side_cards/ai_architecture_cards_v1.json.when_to_show: Chunks, RAG, and the Challenge of Processing Long Documents
side_cards/ai_architecture_cards_v1.json.detail: The context window is the maximum amount of input a model can process at one time. Since it cannot accommodate entire long documents or lengthy conversations, it is necessary to perform searches, summarization, chunk selection, and prioritization. When reading code, ensure that the prompt length, the number of search results, and the maximum token setting do not conflict with one another.

side_cards/ai_architecture_cards_v1.json.title: Chunking: Breaking Down Long Documents
side_cards/ai_architecture_cards_v1.json.body: Chunking is the process of dividing a long document into smaller pieces. Since models and search systems have difficulty handling documents that are too long all at once, they split them into paragraphs or sections and store and search them in that format. In RAG, chunks relevant to the query are identified and passed to the model.
side_cards/ai_architecture_cards_v1.json.when_to_show: JSONL, RAG, and Document Processing Problems
side_cards/ai_architecture_cards_v1.json.detail: Chunking is the process of dividing a long document into searchable units. If the chunks are too large, irrelevant content may be included; if they are too small, necessary context may be lost. When reading the code, you must examine the chunk size, overlap, metadata on the original text’s location, and whether the title is preserved to understand the search quality.

side_cards/ai_architecture_cards_v1.json.title: Fine-tuning: Changing the Model's Behavior
side_cards/ai_architecture_cards_v1.json.body: Fine-tuning uses additional training data to adapt output format, tone, decision patterns, or task ability. It may teach some facts, but it is not a guaranteed way to retrieve current knowledge; changing facts are better handled with retrieval or tools. Check the train/evaluation split, base model, checkpoint, and model actually loaded for inference.
side_cards/ai_architecture_cards_v1.json.when_to_show: Training Data, LoRA, and Model Improvement Issues

side_cards/ai_architecture_cards_v1.json.title: LoRA: How to Perform Lightweight Fine-Tuning
side_cards/ai_architecture_cards_v1.json.body: LoRA is a method for tailoring a large model to a specific format or task by training only a small set of additional weights, without having to retrain the entire model. Training the entire model is costly and time-consuming, but LoRA allows for relatively lightweight experimentation. However, LoRA does not provide all the necessary knowledge from scratch, so data quality and the target format are crucial.
side_cards/ai_architecture_cards_v1.json.when_to_show: When reviewing lora, finetuning, adapter, gpu
side_cards/ai_architecture_cards_v1.json.detail: It’s easier to understand LoRA as a method that involves training the model with small adapter weights rather than modifying the entire large model directly. In the code, the base model path and the adapter path are often defined separately. Checking whether the adapter is used separately or combined with the base model during inference can help you better understand the execution structure.

side_cards/ai_architecture_cards_v1.json.title: Inference: The step of generating answers using the trained model
side_cards/ai_architecture_cards_v1.json.body: Inference is the process of using a trained model to generate actual answers or predictions.
side_cards/ai_architecture_cards_v1.json.when_to_show: Issues with model calls, APIs, and server costs
side_cards/ai_architecture_cards_v1.json.detail: If training is the process of teaching the model, then inference is the process of feeding input into the trained model and receiving the results. When a chatbot answers a question or an image model classifies an image, that is also inference. When reading code, inference involves model loading, input preprocessing, prediction execution, and output postprocessing.

side_cards/ai_architecture_cards_v1.json.title: Latency: The time it takes to receive a response
side_cards/ai_architecture_cards_v1.json.body: Latency is the time it takes for a response to be returned after a request is sent. In AI apps, model calls, searches, database queries, and network round-trip times all affect latency. If the response takes too long, users may feel as though the service has stopped working.
side_cards/ai_architecture_cards_v1.json.when_to_show: When reviewing latency, performance, api, rag
side_cards/ai_architecture_cards_v1.json.detail: Latency is directly linked to the wait time experienced by the user. In AI apps, searches, database queries, model calls, post-processing, and network round trips all contribute to latency. When reviewing the code, it’s easy to identify bottlenecks by checking for repetitive calls, caching, timeouts, and streaming processing.

side_cards/ai_architecture_cards_v1.json.title: Hallucination: A Plausible Wrong Answer
side_cards/ai_architecture_cards_v1.json.body: Hallucination is fluent output that is unsupported or false. Retrieval, citations, validators, and abstention rules can reduce risk but do not guarantee accuracy. Verify that citations support the claims and use trusted tools or rules for consequential facts.
side_cards/ai_architecture_cards_v1.json.when_to_show: When reviewing hallucination, rag, evidence, evaluation

side_cards/ai_architecture_cards_v1.json.title: Guardrail: A Safety Mechanism for AI Outputs
side_cards/ai_architecture_cards_v1.json.body: Guardrail is a safety mechanism for AI outputs. Since models can generate incorrect, dangerous, or unformatted answers, services implement safeguards such as prohibition rules, output validation, justification checks, and handling of follow-up questions. For example, in a learning app, rules can be set to restrict terminology that exceeds a student’s level or to provide hints rather than immediately revealing the correct answer.
side_cards/ai_architecture_cards_v1.json.when_to_show: When reviewing guardrail, safety, policy, validation
side_cards/ai_architecture_cards_v1.json.detail: A guardrail is a safety mechanism applied before and after model output. It may include rules such as blocking prohibited topics, removing personal information, limiting the model to student-level responses, validating the output format, and withholding answers when there is insufficient evidence. When reading the code, distinguish whether the guardrail filters the input before the model is called or checks the results after the call.

side_cards/data_system_cards_v1.json.title: RDB: Relational Database
side_cards/data_system_cards_v1.json.body: An RDB is a relational database that stores data in tabular form. Data is typically organized into a structure consisting of tables, rows, and columns.
side_cards/data_system_cards_v1.json.when_to_show: When reviewing database, rdb, sql, table
side_cards/data_system_cards_v1.json.detail: For example, you can create a student table, a problem table, and a solution record table, and link them together using IDs. RDBs have a clear structure and excel at conditional searches, sorting, and aggregation. However, changing the data structure may require a schema change.

side_cards/data_system_cards_v1.json.title: NoSQL: A Database with a Flexible Structure
side_cards/data_system_cards_v1.json.body: NoSQL refers to a method of storing data in various structures, not just traditional tabular databases.
side_cards/data_system_cards_v1.json.when_to_show: When reviewing nosql, database, document_db, key_value
side_cards/data_system_cards_v1.json.detail: Document-based databases can store data in document units similar to JSON, while key-value stores are well-suited for quickly retrieving values using keys. While NoSQL offers the advantage of flexible structure, it can become difficult to manage if data conventions become unclear. Therefore, you must consider the schema and validation rules together.

side_cards/data_system_cards_v1.json.title: Document DB: Stored as JSON
side_cards/data_system_cards_v1.json.body: Document DB is a database that stores data in document units resembling JSON.
side_cards/data_system_cards_v1.json.when_to_show: JSON, NoSQL, and Document Storage Issues
side_cards/data_system_cards_v1.json.detail: While relational databases are centered around rows and columns in a table format, Document DB is more akin to a structure where multiple fields are contained within a single object. It is well-suited for data whose structure may vary slightly, such as study cards, user settings, and logs. However, just because the structure is flexible doesn’t mean you can store data haphazardly—doing so will make searching and validating data difficult later on, so it’s important to establish a schema and field conventions.

side_cards/data_system_cards_v1.json.title: GraphDB: Focused on Relationship Exploration
side_cards/data_system_cards_v1.json.body: A GraphDB is a database designed to store and retrieve data with a focus on exploring relationships. While traditional tables are row- and column-oriented, graph databases are node- and edge-oriented. For example, you can treat students, concepts, problems, and hints as nodes and connect them with relationships to show which students are struggling with which concepts.
side_cards/data_system_cards_v1.json.detail: GraphDB views data as nodes and edges and excels at traversing relationships. When you encounter GraphDB in code, first identify which objects are nodes and which connections are edges. By examining the direction of the relationships, the starting nodes, the traversal depth, and the result constraints, it becomes easier to understand recommendation systems and knowledge graph workflows.

side_cards/data_system_cards_v1.json.title: VectorDB: Semantic Search
side_cards/data_system_cards_v1.json.body: A vector database stores embeddings and metadata for sentences or document chunks, then finds items close to a query vector. An embedding is a numeric representation of text features, and similarity search compares the distance or similarity between those arrays. This can retrieve relevant text even when the wording differs, but it does not perfectly understand meaning or guarantee a correct answer.
side_cards/data_system_cards_v1.json.detail: VectorDB is used to store text or documents as embedding vectors and to find items with similar meanings. When reading the code, break down the process into distinct steps: dividing the source text into chunks, generating embeddings, storing them, performing a top-k search, and feeding the search results into the prompt. You should also verify the source and score of the search results.

side_cards/data_system_cards_v1.json.title: Index: An index for quick reference
side_cards/data_system_cards_v1.json.body: An index is a tool for quickly finding data. Just like the index at the back of a book, it helps you jump directly to the information you need without having to search through the entire book from start to finish.
side_cards/data_system_cards_v1.json.when_to_show: When reviewing index, database, search, performance
side_cards/data_system_cards_v1.json.detail: In a database, creating an index on a specific field can speed up searches. However, indexes also require storage space and incur management costs. When reading code and encountering the term “index,” you must use context to distinguish whether it refers to a list index number or an index used to improve search performance.

side_cards/data_system_cards_v1.json.title: Schema: The Promise of Data
side_cards/data_system_cards_v1.json.body: A schema is a set of conventions for data. It can be viewed as a set of rules that define which fields must be present, whether each field is a string, a number, or a list, and whether it is required or optional.
side_cards/data_system_cards_v1.json.when_to_show: When reviewing schema, json, validation, database
side_cards/data_system_cards_v1.json.detail: For example, if a “lesson” card must include “id,” “title,” “code,” “choices,” and “answer,” this is also part of the schema. When reading code, knowing the schema allows you to predict which keys are valid and what errors will occur if any are missing. This card is not just for memorizing word definitions; it serves as a supplementary explanation to help you understand how variables, data types, functions, files, and API flows are connected in actual Python code.

side_cards/data_system_cards_v1.json.title: ETL: Extract, Transform, Load
side_cards/data_system_cards_v1.json.body: ETL stands for Extract, Transform, Load, and refers to the process of retrieving, transforming, and storing data. Extract is the step of reading data from source files or APIs; Transform is the step of adjusting the format or selecting only the necessary fields; and Load is the step of storing the results in a database or file. Most Python batch scripts follow an ETL structure.
side_cards/data_system_cards_v1.json.when_to_show: When reviewing etl, harvest, transform, load
side_cards/data_system_cards_v1.json.detail: ETL is a process that reads data from its source, transforms it into the required format, and stores it in a database or file. When reviewing long batch code, it becomes easier to understand if you break it down into its individual stages: Extract, Transform, and Load. You should verify the inputs and outputs of each stage, as well as failure handling, duplicate prevention, and re-execution safety.

side_cards/data_system_cards_v1.json.title: Dedup: Duplicate Removal
side_cards/data_system_cards_v1.json.body: "Dedup" refers to deduplication. If the same data is entered multiple times, statistics may be skewed, or users may see the same card repeatedly. To identify duplicates, criteria such as matching IDs, matching titles, matching normalized strings, or nearly identical content are required.
side_cards/data_system_cards_v1.json.when_to_show: When reviewing dedup, set, hash, curation
side_cards/data_system_cards_v1.json.detail: Deduplication is the process of reducing duplicate data. You must first define comparison criteria, such as the same URL, the same ID, normalized titles, or content hashes. When reviewing the code, check whether it removes only completely identical entries, groups similar entries together, and which entry is retained as the representative after determining duplicates. In some cases, selecting a representative item and documenting the rationale are more important than simply deleting data.

side_cards/data_system_cards_v1.json.title: Metadata: Data that describes data
side_cards/data_system_cards_v1.json.body: Metadata is data that describes other data.
side_cards/data_system_cards_v1.json.when_to_show: When reviewing metadata, source, tag, filter
side_cards/data_system_cards_v1.json.detail: For example, values such as the date a photo was taken, the source of a document, the difficulty level of a card, or the level of a lesson are not the original content itself, but rather information that describes that data. In a Python project, properly attaching metadata makes it easier to search, filter, sort, and validate the data later on. When reading code, you should distinguish metadata from the actual body of the code and verify what each value describes and where it is used.

side_cards/dev_environment_cards_v1.json.title: Terminal: A window for controlling the computer using commands
side_cards/dev_environment_cards_v1.json.body: The Terminal is a window for controlling your computer using commands.
side_cards/dev_environment_cards_v1.json.when_to_show: When reviewing terminal, cli, shell, command
