side_cards/dev_environment_cards_v1.json.detail: Instead of opening folders and running programs with the mouse, you change directories using commands like `cd` or `Set-Location` and run scripts with the `python` command. Developers use the Terminal to repeatedly test, verify, check Git status, and install packages. Beginners often find the error messages displayed on the screen intimidating, but Terminal output provides important clues about where the code went wrong.

side_cards/dev_environment_cards_v1.json.title: Shell: A program that interprets commands
side_cards/dev_environment_cards_v1.json.body: A shell is a program that interprets user commands and passes them to the operating system. Examples of shells include PowerShell, Bash, and zsh.
side_cards/dev_environment_cards_v1.json.detail: Developers use shells to navigate folders, check files, run Python, execute Git commands, and install packages. Even for the same command, line breaks and path notation may differ depending on the shell. When running code, you must verify whether you are using PowerShell or Bash, and you must also distinguish whether an error message is due to a shell syntax issue or a Python issue.

side_cards/dev_environment_cards_v1.json.title: Package Manager: A tool for managing installations
side_cards/dev_environment_cards_v1.json.body: A package manager is a tool that manages the installation of necessary libraries. In Python, pip is the most common example, while in JavaScript, tools like npm and pnpm are frequently used.
side_cards/dev_environment_cards_v1.json.when_to_show: When reviewing pip, npm, apt, package
side_cards/dev_environment_cards_v1.json.detail: Since projects typically depend on multiple external libraries, you must document which packages need to be installed for the code to run. If an `import` fails while reading the code, it may be because the package isn’t installed or the virtual environment is different. You should also check files like `requirements.txt`.

side_cards/dev_environment_cards_v1.json.title: venv: Python virtual environment
side_cards/dev_environment_cards_v1.json.body: venv isolates a project's Python path and package installation location. Activation only changes the current shell's PATH for convenience; code can instead invoke the environment's interpreter explicitly.
side_cards/dev_environment_cards_v1.json.when_to_show: Issues with the Python environment and package installation
side_cards/dev_environment_cards_v1.json.detail: Verify that installation and execution use the same interpreter with sys.executable and python -m pip.

side_cards/dev_environment_cards_v1.json.title: Git: Change History Management
side_cards/dev_environment_cards_v1.json.body: Git is a tool for managing change history. When you modify a file and create a commit, you can record the changes made at that point in time, allowing you to track later on which files were changed and why.
side_cards/dev_environment_cards_v1.json.when_to_show: When reviewing git, commit, branch, push
side_cards/dev_environment_cards_v1.json.detail: Tags are used to assign names to specific commits and establish fixed reference points. If a problem arises during development, use `git status` to check the current state of changes and `git log` to review the previous workflow. When fixing code, it’s important to get into the habit of making small changes, verifying them, and then committing.

side_cards/dev_environment_cards_v1.json.title: GitHub: A platform for hosting Git repositories
side_cards/dev_environment_cards_v1.json.body: GitHub is a platform for hosting and sharing Git repositories. While Git manages the history of changes on your computer, GitHub stores that history remotely and enables you to collaborate with others.
side_cards/dev_environment_cards_v1.json.when_to_show: When reviewing github, git, pages, repo
side_cards/dev_environment_cards_v1.json.detail: A commit is a group of changes, and a tag is a label assigned to a specific point in time. When reading or modifying code, understanding GitHub and Git allows you to track what changed in each version. This card is not just for memorizing definitions; it serves as a reference to help you identify how these concepts relate to variables, data types, functions, files, and API flows in actual Python code.

side_cards/dev_environment_cards_v1.json.title: API Key: A secret key used to call the service
side_cards/dev_environment_cards_v1.json.body: An API key is a secret key used when calling external services. The server uses this key to determine who made the request, whether they have permission, and which account to charge for the costs.
side_cards/dev_environment_cards_v1.json.when_to_show: When reviewing api_key, env, security, secret
side_cards/dev_environment_cards_v1.json.detail: Therefore, it is risky to hardcode an API key directly into your code and upload it to a public repository. Typically, it is stored in a .env file or as an environment variable and is not exposed on the client-side interface. When reading code, you should verify where the API Key is fetched from and ensure it isn’t logged.

side_cards/dev_environment_cards_v1.json.title: .env: Secret configuration file
side_cards/dev_environment_cards_v1.json.body: A .env file commonly stores local configuration as NAME=value, not only secrets, and Python does not read it automatically. A loader such as python-dotenv is required.
side_cards/dev_environment_cards_v1.json.when_to_show: Environment Variables, API Keys, GitHub Issues
side_cards/dev_environment_cards_v1.json.detail: Exclude files containing secrets from Git; .gitignore does not remove an already tracked file, and any exposed key must be rotated.

side_cards/dev_environment_cards_v1.json.title: Logging: Recording Execution History
side_cards/dev_environment_cards_v1.json.body: Logging records stages, timing, counts, and failures at useful severity levels. Check destination, retention, and exception traces, but never record API keys, tokens, or personal data—even at DEBUG. Keep user-facing results separate from diagnostic records.
side_cards/dev_environment_cards_v1.json.when_to_show: When reviewing logging, debug, batch, server

side_cards/dev_environment_cards_v1.json.title: Debugging: Identifying the Cause of a Problem
side_cards/dev_environment_cards_v1.json.body: Debugging is the process of finding the cause of why code isn’t behaving as intended.
side_cards/dev_environment_cards_v1.json.when_to_show: When reviewing debugging, error, traceback, log
side_cards/dev_environment_cards_v1.json.detail: It involves reading error messages, checking which line caused the failure, and verifying whether variable values differ from expectations. Beginners often assume that if an error occurs, the entire code is wrong, but in reality, the issue is often a small typo, a path problem, a data type mix-up, or a problem with the flow of a conditional statement. When debugging, it’s important to get into the habit of narrowing down the problem by examining the input, intermediate values, and output in that order.

side_cards/dev_environment_cards_v1.json.title: API Keys and Security
side_cards/dev_environment_cards_v1.json.summary: By default, API keys should not be hard-coded but should be read from environment variables or a secure secret store.
side_cards/dev_environment_cards_v1.json.detail: If you hardcode an API key directly into your code, it could be exposed through GitHub pushes, logs, screen sharing, and other means. Generally, os.environ, .env, secret managers, or server-side storage are used. During code reviews, check whether the key is read from a secure source, whether it appears in logs, and whether it is exposed to the client.
side_cards/dev_environment_cards_v1.json.body: API keys and security are topics that require careful attention from the very beginning of development. An API key is similar to a secret key that allows you to use external services. If you hardcode this value directly into your code and upload it to GitHub, others could use the service through your account or incur charges.

reference_side_cards/python_development_.title: Development flow: before coding through after release
reference_side_cards/python_development_.body: Development is more than the moment you write code. Before coding, confirm the goal and current state; during coding, make small changes; afterward, validate, record, and release.
reference_side_cards/python_development_.detail: Splitting work into before coding → during coding → validation and review → release and operation makes the next check easier to remember. Even in a small personal project, this flow makes causes easier to trace and changes easier to undo.
reference_side_cards/python_development_.when_to_show: When reviewing the overall development workflow

reference_side_cards/python_development_.title: Before coding: define what success means
reference_side_cards/python_development_.body: Before changing code, write down what should change and what must stay the same. This gives you concrete results to use when deciding whether the change succeeded.
reference_side_cards/python_development_.detail: For example, 'the button saves' may not be enough. Include the saved format, error behavior, and whether existing data is preserved so the later test criteria are clear.
reference_side_cards/python_development_.when_to_show: Before adding a feature or fixing a bug

reference_side_cards/python_development_.title: Before coding: reproduce the current problem
reference_side_cards/python_development_.body: Before fixing a bug, check whether the same input and steps make it happen again. Reproduction lets you compare before and after under the same conditions.
reference_side_cards/python_development_.detail: Record the input, execution steps, error message, and relevant version. If you change many things before you can reproduce the problem, it becomes harder to know what the original cause was.

reference_side_cards/python_development_.title: Before coding: preserve a baseline
reference_side_cards/python_development_.body: A baseline is the known state before a change. Record something you can compare later, such as test results, sample output, or processed record counts.
reference_side_cards/python_development_.detail: Without a baseline, a changed number can be hard to classify as improvement or breakage. Keep the same input and measurement conditions so the comparison remains meaningful.
reference_side_cards/python_development_.when_to_show: Before changing performance, output, or behavior

reference_side_cards/python_development_.title: Before coding: inspect the impact area
reference_side_cards/python_development_.body: One changed line can affect several functions or screens that use its value. Check not only the file being edited but also where its input comes from and where its result is used.
reference_side_cards/python_development_.detail: Shared functions, data formats, and storage keys can have wide impact even when the diff is small. Searching uses and call relationships helps decide what regression testing is needed.
reference_side_cards/python_development_.when_to_show: Before changing shared functions or data formats

reference_side_cards/python_development_.title: During coding: isolate the work
reference_side_cards/python_development_.body: For a larger change, work in a separate workspace or Git branch instead of mixing it directly into the known-good version. This preserves a stable reference until validation is complete.
reference_side_cards/python_development_.detail: A branch creates a boundary for experiments; it does not guarantee safety by itself. Check the current branch and changed files, then test and review the diff before integration.
reference_side_cards/python_development_.when_to_show: When changing several files or experimenting

reference_side_cards/python_development_.title: During coding: change one small thing at a time
reference_side_cards/python_development_.body: When possible, make a small change around one cause or one feature. If the result changes, it is then easier to trace which edit caused the difference.
reference_side_cards/python_development_.detail: Changing several unrelated problems at once makes a later test failure harder to localize. Repeating small change → check → next change narrows failures faster.
reference_side_cards/python_development_.when_to_show: During feature work and bug fixing

reference_side_cards/python_development_.title: During coding: reproduce → hypothesize → inspect → change
reference_side_cards/python_development_.body: Debugging is not changing random lines. Reproduce the problem, form a cause hypothesis, inspect logs or values, make a small change, and verify again with the same method.
reference_side_cards/python_development_.detail: A disproved hypothesis is still useful information. Checking input, intermediate values, and output in order usually narrows the cause better than changing several pieces without observation.

reference_side_cards/python_development_.title: During coding: idempotence and rerun safety
reference_side_cards/python_development_.body: Idempotence means that repeating the same operation under the same conditions does not keep changing the final state unnecessarily. It is useful for safe reruns in automation and data processing.
reference_side_cards/python_development_.detail: Examples include creating an existing directory without failure or avoiding appending the same row on every rerun. Not every function must be idempotent; it matters especially when an operation may be retried.
reference_side_cards/python_development_.when_to_show: When building file, batch, or automation work

reference_side_cards/python_development_.title: Validation: unit, integration, and smoke tests
reference_side_cards/python_development_.body: A unit test checks a small behavior, an integration test checks connected parts, and a smoke test quickly checks that an application's essential path works at all.
reference_side_cards/python_development_.detail: One test type rarely finds every problem. Checking the changed function, its connection to other modules, and the real screen or execution path at different scopes reduces missed errors.
reference_side_cards/python_development_.when_to_show: When deciding which tests are needed after a change

reference_side_cards/python_development_.title: Validation: regression testing
reference_side_cards/python_development_.body: Regression testing checks whether a new change broke behavior that used to work. Its direction is different from testing only the newly added feature.
reference_side_cards/python_development_.detail: After changing a shared function or data format, recheck existing paths that depend on it instead of looking only at the edited screen. Keeping a test for a previously found bug also helps prevent recurrence.
reference_side_cards/python_development_.when_to_show: After bug fixes and behavior changes

reference_side_cards/python_development_.title: Validation: review the actual diff
reference_side_cards/python_development_.body: A diff shows the lines that actually changed between before and after. Before committing, check that only intended files changed and that code was not accidentally deleted or left behind.
reference_side_cards/python_development_.detail: A small number of changed lines does not always mean small impact. Shared functions, conditions, and storage formats can change execution paths, so inspect their surrounding code and tests too.
reference_side_cards/python_development_.when_to_show: Before a commit or pull request

reference_side_cards/python_development_.title: Validation: CI quality gates
reference_side_cards/python_development_.body: CI can automatically run selected tests and checks when code is pushed. If a required check fails, the normal rule is to understand the cause before proceeding to release.
reference_side_cards/python_development_.detail: Do not delete a failing test simply because it is old. First distinguish a code defect from a justified change to the test expectation. Automation reduces the chance of forgetting the same manual check repeatedly.
reference_side_cards/python_development_.when_to_show: When using GitHub Actions or other automated validation

reference_side_cards/python_development_.title: Before release: leave reproducible evidence
reference_side_cards/python_development_.body: For a release, keep enough information to identify which code and input passed which validation. A version or commit SHA and the key test results are common pieces of evidence.
reference_side_cards/python_development_.detail: If a problem appears later, a precise code point and validation condition are more useful than remembering that it once passed. Record input versions or environment details when they can change the result.

reference_side_cards/python_development_.title: Release: prepare a rollback point
reference_side_cards/python_development_.body: Rollback means returning to the previous known-good state when a new version has a serious problem. Before release, know the last good version and how to restore it.
reference_side_cards/python_development_.detail: Returning only the code may not be enough if the new release already changed a data format. Check whether the release changes code, configuration, data, or several of them together.

reference_side_cards/python_development_.title: After release: verify real behavior
reference_side_cards/python_development_.body: Do not stop at a successful deployment message. Check that an actual user path works, and briefly inspect error logs and a key screen or API result.
reference_side_cards/python_development_.detail: A development environment can pass while deployment settings or caches cause a production problem. A short post-release check finds issues early and makes rollback possible before the impact grows.

side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.title: Terminal commands are interpreted as consisting of a command, options, arguments, and output.
side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.body: A terminal is a window where developers issue text-based commands to a computer. What matters is not the black window itself, but the ability to understand the structure of the commands.
side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.when_to_show: When reading terminal commands, the CLI, and execution logs
side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.detail: For example, a command like `python script.py --check data.json` can be broken down into the program to be executed, the file being passed, the options, and the output. The command specifies what to run, the options modify how it runs, and the arguments pass target files or values. Just like reading code, commands are read from left to right.

side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.title: Shell is a set of rules for interpreting commands, and PowerShell and Bash have different syntaxes.
side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.body: A shell is a program that interprets commands entered by the user and passes them to the operating system. PowerShell, Bash, and zsh are all shells, but they differ in syntax and basic tools.
side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.when_to_show: When Looking at Differences Between PowerShell and Bash Commands, Line Breaks, and Path Notation Issues
side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.detail: PowerShell is commonly used on Windows, while Bash is frequently used on Ubuntu or Linux servers. Even within the same Python project, the line-breaking conventions, environment variable notation, path separators, and script activation commands vary depending on which shell is used to execute the commands. When reading PowerShell commands, look for verbs such as Set-Location, Get-Content, Test-Path, and Remove-Item.

side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.title: Ubuntu and Linux are the foundation for server development commands.
side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.body: Linux is a family of operating systems, and Ubuntu is a distribution that packages Linux in a user-friendly way.
side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.when_to_show: When reading about Ubuntu/Linux server commands, WSL, and GPU server setup
side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.detail: Even if developers work on a local Windows machine, they frequently encounter Ubuntu commands on servers, in Docker, on GitHub Actions, and on GPU workstations. Learning Ubuntu does not mean delving deeply into every operating system; rather, it means mastering the basic workflow of finding files on a server, installing packages, checking permissions, and running Python. When reading Ubuntu documentation, you’ll encounter terms such as bash commands, apt installation, sudo permissions, home directories, root directories, and file permissions.

side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.title: When dealing with path issues, you need to consider both the current working directory and the absolute/relative paths.
side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.body: A path is an address that specifies the location of a file or folder. In a development environment, many errors are caused by differences in the execution location rather than by the code itself.
side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.when_to_show: When encountering FileNotFoundError, relative paths, and Set-Location issues
side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.detail: An absolute path specifies the full location starting from the drive or root, while a relative path is determined relative to the current working directory. A path like `.\data\file.json` can point to different files depending on where PowerShell is currently located. When reading a command, first check the current working directory.

side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.title: Although `sudo` runs commands with administrative privileges, using it out of habit can be dangerous.
side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.body: sudo is a tool in Ubuntu/Linux that allows you to run commands with administrative privileges. Since regular users cannot freely modify system-wide settings or protected folders, sudo is used only for necessary tasks.
side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.when_to_show: When you see "sudo," "Permission denied," or commands requiring administrator privileges
side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.detail: For example, installing system packages, restarting services, or modifying specific protected paths may require sudo. However, because of its powerful capabilities, using it incorrectly can corrupt system files or cause ownership issues in project folders. When you run a `sudo` command, it first asks why administrator privileges are needed.

side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.title: apt and pip are used for different types of installations.
side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.body: Although apt and pip both appear to be installation tools, they serve different purposes. apt is a tool for installing Ubuntu system packages, while pip is a tool for installing Python packages.
side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.when_to_show: When comparing `apt install` and `pip install`
side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.detail: For example, if `import requests` fails in your Python code, you may need to run `pip install requests`. Conversely, if external executable tools such as `pdfimages`, `tesseract`, or `poppler` are missing, you may need to install system packages using `apt install`. When reading a command, first determine whether you are trying to install a Python import target or an operating system executable.

side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.title: chmod and file permissions determine who can read and execute a file
side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.body: chmod is a command used to change file permissions in Linux/Ubuntu. File permissions determine who can read, write, or execute a file.
side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.when_to_show: When you see "chmod +x," "execution permission," or "Permission denied"
side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.detail: If you have a script file and receive a “Permission denied” error when trying to run it, you may not have execute permissions. In such cases, you can add execute permissions using a command like `chmod +x script.sh`. Since file permissions represent a balance between security and convenience, granting them indiscriminately can be risky.

side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.title: venv is a Python toolbox used separately for each project.
side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.body: venv does not copy the operating system; it isolates a project-specific Python path and site-packages. Activation is a PATH convenience, and an explicit environment interpreter works without it.
side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.when_to_show: When reviewing venv, virtual_environment, python, dependency
side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.detail: Pins and tests are also needed for stronger reproducibility.

side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.title: "activate" and "deactivate" change which Python environment the current terminal is using.
side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.body: Activation changes the current shell's PATH so the environment's Python is preferred; deactivation reverses that change. Activation is optional because the environment interpreter can be invoked directly.
side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.when_to_show: When looking at the commands to activate/deactivate a venv
side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.detail: Verify the real path with sys.executable and python -m pip --version rather than trusting only the prompt label.

side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.title: `python -m pip` ensures that the pip currently associated with Python is used.
side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.body: "python -m pip" means to run the pip module using the currently running Python. If you simply use "pip install," which version of pip is used may depend on the PATH settings in your shell.
side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.when_to_show: When imports fail due to differences between the pip and Python environments
side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.detail: In particular, if you have multiple Python installations on Windows, or if you repeatedly activate and deactivate venv, pip and Python may point to different environments. In this case, using a command like `python -m pip install requests` ensures that pip from the same environment as the current Python is used. When interpreting the command, the installation location is checked before the target to be installed.

side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.title: requirements.txt is a list of packages needed to reproduce the new environment.
side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.body: requirements.txt supplies package requirements to pip. Version ranges, a different Python or OS, and changing transitive dependencies can produce different environments, so the file alone is not a perfect lock.
side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.when_to_show: When looking at the requirements, pip freeze, and the reproducible environment
side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.detail: Install into a clean environment, document runtime constraints, and run real tests.

side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.title: When encountering a `ModuleNotFoundError`, you should first suspect a mismatch in the current environment rather than whether the module is installed.
side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.body: ModuleNotFoundError means Python could not resolve an import name. Causes include an environment mismatch, a typo, launch location, package structure, or a local file shadowing another module.
side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.when_to_show: When you encounter import errors or package installation issues
side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.detail: Check sys.executable, python -m pip show, the import path, and filenames in order.

side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.title: Git manages the working directory, staging area, commits, and remote repositories separately.
side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.body: Git is a tool for managing the history of file changes.
side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.when_to_show: When looking at the overall Git workflow and the relationship between status, add, commit, and push
side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.detail: Beginners often think of Git as something like a "Save" button, but in reality, it consists of distinct components: the working directory, the staging area, commits, and remote repositories. The working directory contains the current state of the files you’re editing, while the staging area is where you select changes to include in your next commit. A commit is the action of saving the selected changes as a single record, and “remote” refers to a remote repository like GitHub.

side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.title: "status," "diff," "add," and "commit" are the basic steps for safely creating a commit.
side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.body: `status`, `diff`, `add`, and `commit` are Git’s most basic workflows. `git status` shows which files have changed, and `git diff` shows exactly which lines have been added or deleted.
side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.when_to_show: When reviewing git_status, git_diff, git_add, git_commit
side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.detail: `git add` selects the changes to include in the next commit, and `git commit` saves that set of changes as a commit. Following this sequence helps minimize the risk of accidentally committing temporary files or unintended changes. After modifying the code, first run a validation command, then use `git status --short` to view the list of modified files.

side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.title: "tag," "push," and "pull" are commands used to synchronize the local repository with a remote reference.
side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.body: A tag is a label attached to a specific commit. If you apply a tag when a feature has stabilized or at a deployment milestone, it makes it easy to revisit that state later.
side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.when_to_show: When viewing tag creation, the origin/main branch, and the push/pull workflow
side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.detail: `push` is a command that sends local commits or tags to a remote repository, while `pull` is a command that fetches remote changes and merges them into the local repository. `origin` is typically the default remote repository name, and `origin/main` refers to the state of the remote `main` branch. When reading commands, you must distinguish whether a commit exists only locally or has also been pushed to the remote repository.

side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.title: "branch," "conflict," and "restore" are ways to split and revert changes.
side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.body: A branch is a Git feature that creates a separate workflow from the main branch. Major experiments or risky changes can be carried out on a new branch and merged into the main branch after validation.
side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.when_to_show: When viewing branches, merge conflicts, and undo commands
side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.detail: A merge is the action of combining changes from another branch into the current branch. If different people have made conflicting changes to the same part of the same file, a conflict occurs. Since Git cannot automatically resolve this, a user must review the conflict indicators and choose which changes to keep.

side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.title: Environment variables and .env files inject configurations and secrets from outside the code.
side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.body: Environment variables are configuration values injected from outside the code.
side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.when_to_show: When viewing API keys, .env, os.getenv, and environment settings
side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.detail: It is safer not to hardcode values that vary by environment—such as API keys, database addresses, execution modes, and model paths—directly into the code. A .env file is used to store these values separately during local development, and Python code can read them using `os.getenv` or the `dotenv` library. It is crucial not to upload actual sensitive values to public repositories.

side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.title: GPU, NVIDIA driver, CUDA, and PyTorch CUDA build are different layers.
side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.body: Separate GPU hardware, the NVIDIA driver, the PyTorch build in the selected environment, and its compatible CUDA runtime.
side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.when_to_show: When looking at CUDA installation, GPU servers, and the PyTorch runtime environment
side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.detail: PyTorch wheels can bundle required runtime components, so a system CUDA toolkit is not always required. Compare nvidia-smi, torch.cuda.is_available(), torch.version.cuda, and sys.executable.

side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.title: `torch.cuda.is_available` checks whether PyTorch can actually use the GPU.
side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.body: `torch.cuda.is_available()` is a function that checks whether PyTorch in the current Python environment can use a CUDA GPU.
side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.when_to_show: When looking at the code for checking PyTorch CUDA and selecting a device
side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.detail: If this value is `True`, it means that PyTorch can use a CUDA device; if it is `False`, the code will run on the CPU, or you will need to review your environment settings. In AI code, it is common to use a pattern like `device = 'cuda' if torch.cuda.is_available() else 'cpu'` to use the GPU if available, and fall back to the CPU if not. When reading code, verify that the model and tensors are on the same device.

side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.title: nvidia-smi is a basic diagnostic tool for checking GPU usage and VRAM status.
side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.body: `nvidia-smi` is the primary command for checking the status of an NVIDIA GPU. This command displays the GPU name, driver version, CUDA compatibility information, GPU utilization, VRAM usage, and running processes.
side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.when_to_show: When you see "GPU usage," "VRAM shortage," or "CUDA out of memory"
side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.detail: When AI tasks are running slowly, you can quickly check whether the GPU is actually being used, if memory is already full, or if another process is monopolizing the GPU. When reviewing the output, look at the “GPU util” and “memory usage” metrics. A low “GPU util” value does not necessarily mean the GPU is performing poorly.

side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.title: A virtual environment is a project-specific Python toolbox.
side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.body: A virtual environment is not a way to install Python anew, but rather a method for isolating the package space used by a single project. For example, Project A can use NumPy 1.x, while Project B can use NumPy 2.x. If you mix the two in a single global environment, it becomes confusing later on to determine which project depends on which version.
side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.detail: It’s easy to think of a virtual environment as a project-specific Python toolbox. Rather than changing the Python installation on the entire computer, it isolates a separate space for the packages used by a specific project. This helps reduce conflicts when multiple projects require different library versions and makes it easy to recreate the same environment later.

side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.title: The reason for using a virtual environment is to reduce conflicts and ensure reproducibility.
side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.body: The main reason for using a virtual environment is to minimize package conflicts, since the required libraries and versions can vary from project to project. Another reason is reproducibility. If you save the environment you’ve created in a `requirements.txt` file, you can recreate a similar environment later on another PC or server. As a beginner, you might wonder, “Why make things so complicated?” but as soon as you have two or more projects, a virtual environment becomes a safety net that helps reduce mistakes.
side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.detail: The reason for using a virtual environment is to minimize package conflicts and ensure a reproducible runtime environment. While this may seem like a hassle when you’re working on a single project, as the number of projects increases, it becomes difficult to trace which global installation caused a code failure. When used in conjunction with `requirements.txt`, it makes it easy to recreate the environment on a new PC or server.

side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.title: You must use pip after running `activate` for the installation to take effect in that environment.
side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.body: Activation makes python prefer the environment interpreter, which is convenient for installation and execution. It is not required; the environment's Python can be invoked directly. Use python -m pip and sys.executable to confirm that installation and execution target the same interpreter.

side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.title: requirements.txt is a notepad for recreating the installation list.
side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.body: requirements.txt is a list of packages required for a project. Typically, you can generate it by running `pip freeze > requirements.txt` to save the list of installed packages in the current environment, or you can manually list only the essential packages. On another computer, you can recreate a similar environment by running `python -m pip install -r requirements.txt`.
side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.detail: requirements.txt is a file that lists the packages required to run the project. Although it is not code itself, it serves as a checklist for setting up the environment to run the code, so it is often included in the repository. In a new environment, run `python -m pip install -r requirements.txt` to install the packages. Don’t just check for a successful installation message; you must also verify that the code actually runs.

side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.title: Ubuntu and WSL can serve as a way to practice Linux commands.
side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.body: Ubuntu is a Linux distribution that frequently appears in documentation on server development and AI development. WSL is a feature that allows you to run a Linux environment within Windows. In Windows, you often use PowerShell commands, while in Ubuntu/WSL, you typically use bash commands.
side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.detail: Ubuntu is a Linux distribution frequently mentioned in server development documentation, and WSL is a feature that allows you to practice using a Linux environment within Windows. Since PowerShell and Bash have different command syntaxes, you must verify which environment a copied command is intended for. It’s important to get into the habit of checking your current shell and path notation first.

side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.title: sudo requests administrator privileges, but it is not a one-size-fits-all solution.
side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.body: In Linux, `sudo` means to run a command with administrative privileges. It may be necessary when installing system packages, such as with `apt install`. However, it’s risky to always use `sudo` just because you get a “Permission denied” error.
side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.detail: "sudo" means running a command with administrative privileges; it is not a magic button that fixes every error. If you see a "Permission denied" error, you should first check the file location, execution permissions, ownership, and any issues with the virtual environment. In particular, be careful when using `sudo pip install`, as it can mess up your system Python.

side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.title: To troubleshoot CUDA issues, check the GPU, drivers, and PyTorch build separately
side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.body: When a GPU isn’t detected during AI development, don’t focus on just one possible cause. First, use `nvidia-smi` to verify that the GPU and drivers are recognized. Next, check in PyTorch to see if `torch.cuda.is_available()` returns `True`.
side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.detail: If you encounter a CUDA issue, you should check the GPU hardware, NVIDIA driver, CUDA runtime, and PyTorch CUDA build separately. While `nvidia-smi` displays the hardware and driver status, you must use `torch.cuda.is_available` to verify whether your Python code is actually using the GPU. An OOM error is more likely caused by insufficient VRAM than by an installation issue.

side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.title: Start by learning the Git workflow: status → add → commit → push
side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.body: When you’re first learning Git, you don’t need to memorize all the commands at once. Start by using `git status` to check your current changes, then use `git add` to select the files you want to include in the commit, and finally use `git commit` to create a local commit. To push changes to a remote repository like GitHub, use `git push`.
side_cards/python_dev_environment_founda.detail: The basic Git workflow involves checking the status to review changes, using `add` to select files to commit, creating a local commit with `commit`, and then pushing the changes to the remote repository with `push`. Modifying files, saving changes, and pushing them to the remote repository are distinct steps. Checking the diff before committing can help minimize unintended changes.

side_cards/python_foundation_side_cards_.title: print() displays the current value on the screen
side_cards/python_foundation_side_cards_.when_to_show: When predicting the output of `print()` or following the execution order of multi-line code
side_cards/python_foundation_side_cards_.body: print() is a function that displays the value inside the parentheses on the screen. When reading code, it serves as a reference point for checking what the calculated value is up to the current line.
side_cards/python_foundation_side_cards_.detail: Python code executes line by line from top to bottom, unless there are special conditional statements or loops. Therefore, if a variable’s value has changed before `print()` is called, the output will reflect the updated value. If there are quotation marks, as in `print("name")`, the string “name” is printed exactly as written; if there are no quotation marks, as in `print(name)`, the value stored in the variable `name` is retrieved and printed.

side_cards/python_foundation_side_cards_.title: Output prediction follows all lines preceding the `print` statement.
side_cards/python_foundation_side_cards_.when_to_show: When tracking changes in variable values in a problem involving selecting output results
side_cards/python_foundation_side_cards_.body: It’s easy to get the output prediction problem wrong if you solve it by looking only at the last `print` line.
side_cards/python_foundation_side_cards_.detail: `print` doesn’t suddenly generate a value on that line; rather, it displays on the screen values that have already been stored and calculated in previous lines. Therefore, you must first check what values have been assigned to the variables and then trace the flow to see if those values are copied to other variables or recalculated. If a value is assigned to the same variable multiple times, the value stored last is used in subsequent lines.

side_cards/python_foundation_side_cards_.title: A variable is a label used to track a value.
side_cards/python_foundation_side_cards_.when_to_show: When reading code in which a value is stored in a variable or the value of the same variable is changed again
side_cards/python_foundation_side_cards_.body: A variable is a name assigned to a value so that it can be referenced later. “x = 3” means that the name “x” now refers to the value 3.
side_cards/python_foundation_side_cards_.detail: If you assign a new value to the same variable—such as “x = 5”—the code will use the new value, 5, from that point on. Therefore, when reading a problem involving variables, it’s safest to write down the variable’s current value on each line. A common mistake beginners make is confusing the variable name itself with the value it holds.

side_cards/python_foundation_side_cards_.title: In college entrance exams, you calculate the right side and then store the result on the left.
side_cards/python_foundation_side_cards_.when_to_show: When reading code that updates the value of the same variable, such as `x = x + 1`,
side_cards/python_foundation_side_cards_.body: In assignment, the right-hand side is evaluated first, and the result is then stored in the variable on the left.
side_cards/python_foundation_side_cards_.detail: For example, `x = x + 1` might seem strange, but the expression first reads the previous value of `x` from the right-hand side, adds 1 to it, and then stores the result back into `x`. Therefore, the value of a variable can change over time. When reading code, if the same variable name appears multiple times, you shouldn’t just remember the initial value; you must continuously update your understanding of what the new value is after each line is executed.

side_cards/python_foundation_side_cards_.title: If there are quotation marks, read it literally
side_cards/python_foundation_side_cards_.when_to_show: When distinguishing between strings and variable names that look similar
side_cards/python_foundation_side_cards_.body: In Python, a value enclosed in quotes is a string. Since a string is a literal value, "name" is a four-character string, not code that searches for the variable `name`.
side_cards/python_foundation_side_cards_.detail: Conversely, "name" without quotes is interpreted as a variable name. If you write `print(name)` after `name = "Python"`, "Python" is printed, but if you write `print("name")`, the word "name" is printed. This distinction is a very common source of errors in beginner-level output prediction problems.

side_cards/python_foundation_side_cards_.title: String numbers and actual numbers are different.
side_cards/python_foundation_side_cards_.when_to_show: When distinguishing between the results of calculations involving numbers with quotation marks and those without
side_cards/python_foundation_side_cards_.body: Even though they look similar on the screen, '3' and 3 are different values. '3' is a string, and 3 is a number.
side_cards/python_foundation_side_cards_.detail: When you add two strings together, it’s concatenation, not arithmetic, so '3' + '4' becomes '34'. When you add two numbers together, it’s arithmetic, so 3 + 4 equals 7. A common mistake beginners make is assuming that two values are the same just because they look the same on the screen.

side_cards/python_foundation_side_cards_.title: Basic errors often occur with names, quotation marks, and indentation.
side_cards/python_foundation_side_cards_.when_to_show: When reading about common runtime errors and syntax errors in beginner-level code
side_cards/python_foundation_side_cards_.body: Beginners often make mistakes in basic syntax rather than with complex algorithms. If you use a variable like `print(name)` before declaring it, you may get a `NameError`.
side_cards/python_foundation_side_cards_.detail: Failing to close the quotation marks around a string can result in a SyntaxError. If the indentation is incorrect in code following a colon—such as in `if` or `for` statements—an IndentationError may occur. Error messages may look intimidating, but they usually contain hints about the line where the problem occurred or its cause.

side_cards/python_foundation_side_cards_.title: Basic grammar is the backbone of real-world code.
side_cards/python_foundation_side_cards_.when_to_show: When explaining how the beginner-level grammar cards relate to actual project code,
side_cards/python_foundation_side_cards_.body: Basic syntax elements—such as print, variables, strings, and numbers—aren’t just used in small examples.
side_cards/python_foundation_side_cards_.detail: Real-world project code ultimately follows the same flow: storing values, calculating necessary values, and outputting the results to the screen or a file. Code that reads data files must distinguish between strings and numbers, and web app code also processes user-entered values as variables. Therefore, even though the beginner-level cards may seem like simple problems, they form the foundation for reading real-world code.

side_cards/python_foundation_side_cards_.title: String numbers and actual numbers behave differently.
side_cards/python_foundation_side_cards_.when_to_show: When distinguishing between the results of calculations involving numbers with quotation marks and those without
side_cards/python_foundation_side_cards_.body: type() shows that '3' is a str while 3 is an int. Values can look similar on screen but behave differently when their types differ.
side_cards/python_foundation_side_cards_.detail: type('3') reports str and type(3) reports int. This card focuses on checking the actual type rather than judging by appearance. With +, strings join text while integers add numbers, so quotation marks and type() results matter when reading code.

side_cards/python_foundation_side_cards_.title: int(), float(), and str() convert the type of a value
side_cards/python_foundation_side_cards_.when_to_show: When using string representations of numbers in calculations or when outputting numbers combined with text
side_cards/python_foundation_side_cards_.body: int() converts a string that looks like a number into an integer, and float() converts a string containing a decimal number into a floating-point number. Conversely, str() is used to convert a number into a string.
side_cards/python_foundation_side_cards_.detail: Values received via `input()` are initially strings, even if the user enters them as numbers, so a conversion like `int(input())` is required for calculations. When reading code, you should first check whether a value is a string or a number, and then follow where that value is stored in a variable. Beginners often make judgments based solely on what they see on the screen, but Python operates based on data types and execution order.

side_cards/python_foundation_side_cards_.title: The `type()` function checks the data type of a value.
side_cards/python_foundation_side_cards_.when_to_show: When reading code where it's unclear whether a value is a string or a number
side_cards/python_foundation_side_cards_.body: `type()` is a function that checks the data type of a value. Each value has its own type: the number 3 is an `int`, the string '3' is a `str`, and the list [1, 2] is a `list`.
side_cards/python_foundation_side_cards_.detail: Knowing the data type allows you to predict what operations are possible. For example, adding two strings concatenates them, while adding two numbers performs arithmetic. When reading code as a beginner, you can reduce errors by checking the actual data type rather than just looking at what the value appears to be.

side_cards/python_foundation_side_cards_.title: `input()` accepts input values as strings.
side_cards/python_foundation_side_cards_.when_to_show: When reading code in which user-entered values are stored in variables and reused,
side_cards/python_foundation_side_cards_.body: The `input()` function reads the value entered by the user as a string.
side_cards/python_foundation_side_cards_.detail: Even if you enter 3—which looks like a number—Python first treats it as the string "3." Therefore, you must convert it to an int or float using int() or float() to use it in calculations. When reading code, just think of it this way: whenever you encounter a line with `input`, the program pauses briefly to wait for the user's input. To understand the flow, you need to follow what happens on the next line—whether the input is printed as-is, compared to a condition, or converted to a number.

side_cards/python_foundation_side_cards_.title: To calculate the input value, it must be converted to a number.
side_cards/python_foundation_side_cards_.when_to_show: When reading code that adds or compares values received via `input()`
side_cards/python_foundation_side_cards_.body: To perform calculations on input values, you must convert them to numbers. Since `input()` always returns a string, even if the user enters 10, the initial value is '10'.
side_cards/python_foundation_side_cards_.detail: To use this value in numerical calculations, you must convert it using `int('10')` or `float('10')`. If you add the value without converting it, the operation will result in string concatenation rather than arithmetic, or it may cause an error. When reading code, it’s important to get into the habit of checking whether a conversion like `int` or `float` follows `input`.

side_cards/python_foundation_side_cards_.title: len() counts the length of strings and lists
side_cards/python_foundation_side_cards_.when_to_show: When checking the number of characters in a string or the number of elements in a list
side_cards/python_foundation_side_cards_.body: len() is a function that returns the number of elements in a value whose length can be counted, such as a string or a list.
side_cards/python_foundation_side_cards_.detail: When applied to a string, it counts the number of characters; when applied to a list, it counts the number of elements. len("abc") is 3, and len(["a", "b"]) is 2. It is important to note that len is not a mutable function; rather, it is a function that returns an integer representing the length.

side_cards/python_foundation_side_cards_.title: Be careful with uppercase and lowercase letters and spaces when comparing input values.
side_cards/python_foundation_side_cards_.when_to_show: When comparing user input to reference strings such as "yes" or "no,"
side_cards/python_foundation_side_cards_.body: When comparing input values, you must be careful about case sensitivity and whitespace. Values received via `input()` are always strings, and users may add leading or trailing spaces or enter text with different case.
side_cards/python_foundation_side_cards_.detail: For example, 'yes', 'YES', and ' yes ' may look similar to a human, but a computer may treat them differently. Therefore, it is common to remove whitespace using `strip()` or convert the case using `lower()` before performing a comparison. When reading code, you should check what kind of preprocessing was performed before the comparison.

side_cards/python_foundation_side_cards_.title: `split()` splits a string into a list.
side_cards/python_foundation_side_cards_.when_to_show: When reading code that splits an input string delimited by commas or spaces,
side_cards/python_foundation_side_cards_.body: `split()` is a basic tool that splits an input string into multiple pieces and returns them as a list.
side_cards/python_foundation_side_cards_.detail: For example, if a user enters "red blue," using `text.split()` will split the string based on spaces, resulting in `["red", "blue"]`. For comma-separated values, you can specify the delimiter, such as `text.split(",")`. The key point here is that the result is a list, not a single string.

side_cards/python_foundation_level2_side.title: The `if` statement executes the code inside it only when the condition is True.
side_cards/python_foundation_level2_side.when_to_show: When determining which line is executed in an `if` statement
side_cards/python_foundation_level2_side.body: An `if` statement executes the indented code inside it only when the result of the conditional expression is `True`.
side_cards/python_foundation_level2_side.detail: A comparison expression such as `score >= 60` evaluates to either `True` or `False`, and that result determines the flow of execution. If the condition is `False`, the indented block following the `if` statement is skipped. Therefore, when reading an `if` problem, you must first check the variable values and use those values to determine whether the conditional expression is true or false.

side_cards/python_foundation_level2_side.title: The `else` clause is the alternative path that is executed when the `if` condition is false.
side_cards/python_foundation_level2_side.when_to_show: When choosing which of the two branches of an if/else statement to execute
side_cards/python_foundation_level2_side.body: The `else` block is an alternative path that executes when the `if` condition is `False`. If the `if` condition is `True`, the `if` block is executed and the `else` block is skipped.
side_cards/python_foundation_level2_side.detail: Conversely, if the `if` condition is `False`, the `if` block is not executed and the `else` block is executed. When reading code, you must not assume that both blocks will be executed. You should interpret the structure as one where only one path is chosen based on the condition’s value.

side_cards/python_foundation_level2_side.title: Comparison operators return True or False.
side_cards/python_foundation_level2_side.when_to_show: When reading the meanings of comparison operators such as ==, !=, >, and >=
side_cards/python_foundation_level2_side.body: Comparison operators compare two values to return True or False. == checks if the values are equal, and != checks if they are not equal.
side_cards/python_foundation_level2_side.detail: >= checks if the value on the left is greater than or equal to the value on the right. Since = is an assignment operator that stores a value, and == is a comparison operator that compares values, it is essential to distinguish between the two. In conditional statements, the result of these comparisons determines whether the code is executed.

side_cards/python_foundation_level2_side.title: An empty string and an empty list are treated as "False" in conditional statements.
side_cards/python_foundation_level2_side.when_to_show: When reading code that uses values themselves as conditions, such as `if text` or `if items`,
side_cards/python_foundation_level2_side.body: A condition evaluates an object's truth value. None, False, numeric zero, empty strings, and empty containers are false; most non-empty containers are true.
side_cards/python_foundation_level2_side.detail: A custom object can change the rule with __bool__ or __len__, so do not generalize this as 'anything with a value is true.'

side_cards/python_foundation_level2_side.title: List indices start at 0.
side_cards/python_foundation_level2_side.when_to_show: When reading code that retrieves values by index, such as `items[0]` and `items[1]`
side_cards/python_foundation_level2_side.body: A list index is a way to retrieve values from a list by their position, and in Python, it starts at 0. If `items = ["A", "B", "C"]`, then `items[0]` is "A", `items[1]` is "B", and `items[2]` is "C".
side_cards/python_foundation_level2_side.detail: The most important point is that the first value is at index 0, not 1. `len(items)` returns the number of elements in the list. If the length is 3, the valid positive indices are 0, 1, and 2.

side_cards/python_foundation_level2_side.title: append() adds a value to the end of a list
side_cards/python_foundation_level2_side.when_to_show: When tracking how the state changes after a value is added to the list
side_cards/python_foundation_level2_side.body: `append()` is a method that adds a single value to the end of a list. If you execute `items.append('A')` after `items = []`, `items` becomes `['A']`.
side_cards/python_foundation_level2_side.detail: If `append` is called multiple times, the values are appended in the order they were called. When solving output problems, it’s safest to write down the current state of the list each time you encounter an `append` line. When reading this concept, rather than just focusing on getting the correct answer, you should check step by step which lines set values and which lines evaluate conditions or determine positions.

side_cards/python_foundation_level2_side.title: len() counts the number of elements in a list
side_cards/python_foundation_level2_side.when_to_show: When checking the length of a list after an `append` operation or determining whether a list is empty
side_cards/python_foundation_level2_side.body: len() is a function that counts the number of values in a list and returns an integer. The length of an empty list [] is 0, and the length of ["A", "B"] is 2.
side_cards/python_foundation_level2_side.detail: len(items) does not print the list itself; instead, it returns the number of elements. Therefore, it is frequently used in comparisons, loops, and conditional expressions. Since lists are mutable, the result of `len` may change if operations such as `append`, `pop`, `remove`, or index assignment are executed beforehand.

side_cards/python_foundation_level2_side.title: A list allows you to change the value at a specific position.
side_cards/python_foundation_level2_side.when_to_show: When reading code that modifies values within a list, such as `items[0] = 'Z'`
side_cards/python_foundation_level2_side.body: A list is a mutable data type, meaning its internal values can be changed even after it has been created.
side_cards/python_foundation_level2_side.detail: `items[0] = "Z"` does not create a new variable named `items`; instead, it changes the value at index 0 of the list that `items` points to. Therefore, when you print `items` on the next line, you will see the updated value. When reading a list modification problem, you must check both which position has changed and what element was actually at that position.

side_cards/python_foundation_level2_side.title: The `for` loop iterates through multiple values one by one in order and executes them.
side_cards/python_foundation_level2_side.when_to_show: When determining the output order or the number of iterations in a for loop
side_cards/python_foundation_level2_side.body: A `for` loop iterates through a collection of values—such as a list or a range—executing the same block of code repeatedly.
side_cards/python_foundation_level2_side.detail: When you write `for item in items:`, the values in `items` are assigned to the `item` variable one by one. The `print` statement inside the loop may be executed as many times as there are values. When studying this concept, you should check, in order, how many times the loop runs, the sequence in which the loop variable’s value changes, and whether string methods create new values or modify existing ones.

side_cards/python_foundation_level2_side.title: The `range()` function creates a sequence of numbers to iterate over.
side_cards/python_foundation_level2_side.when_to_show: When reading iteration ranges such as `range(3)` and `range(1, 4)`
side_cards/python_foundation_level2_side.body: The `range()` function generates a sequence of numbers commonly used in `for` loops. `range(3)` generates 0, 1, and 2 in sequence.
side_cards/python_foundation_level2_side.detail: `range(1, 4)` generates numbers starting from 1 up to but not including 4 (ending at 3). It is important to note that the end value is not included. When understanding this concept, you should check, in order: how many times the loop runs, the order in which the loop variable’s value changes, and whether a string method creates a new value or modifies an existing one.

side_cards/python_foundation_level2_side.title: During iteration, `append()` adds values to the list one by one.
side_cards/python_foundation_level2_side.when_to_show: When reading code that adds values to a list inside a `for` loop
side_cards/python_foundation_level2_side.body: When you use `append()` inside a `for` loop, a value is added to the list one at a time as the loop iterates.
side_cards/python_foundation_level2_side.detail: If you start with an empty list and write down what value is added in each iteration, you can predict the final list. Since `append` adds a value to the end of the list, the order is important. When studying this concept, you should check, in order: how many times the loop runs, the sequence in which the loop variable changes, and whether the string method creates a new value or modifies an existing one.

side_cards/python_foundation_level2_side.title: During iteration, the cumulative value reuses the previous value.
side_cards/python_foundation_level2_side.when_to_show: When reading cumulative calculations such as `total = total + n`
side_cards/python_foundation_level2_side.body: An accumulator variable generates a new value based on the previous value each time the loop iterates.
side_cards/python_foundation_level2_side.detail: The code `total = total + n` adds the previous `total` (on the right) to the current `n` and stores the result back in `total`. If you write down the `total` values for the first, second, and third iterations in order, you can see the final result. When studying this concept, you should check, in order: how many times the loop runs, the sequence in which the loop variable’s value changes, and whether the string method creates a new value or modifies an existing one.

side_cards/python_foundation_level2_side.title: `split()` splits a string into a list.
side_cards/python_foundation_level2_side.when_to_show: When reading code that converts a string separated by commas or spaces into a list
side_cards/python_foundation_level2_side.body: `split()` is a string method that splits a string into multiple pieces based on a specified delimiter and returns a list.
side_cards/python_foundation_level2_side.detail: `text.split(",")` splits the string at commas, while `text.split()` splits it at consecutive spaces by default. Since the result is a list rather than a string, subsequent code can utilize list-related constructs such as indices, `for` loops, `len`, and `append`. This method does not directly modify the original string.

side_cards/python_foundation_level2_side.title: strip() creates a new string with leading and trailing whitespace removed
side_cards/python_foundation_level2_side.when_to_show: When reading code that removes leading and trailing spaces from input values
side_cards/python_foundation_level2_side.body: The `strip()` function creates a new string by removing leading and trailing whitespace. It does not remove whitespace in the middle of the string.
side_cards/python_foundation_level2_side.detail: Since the value passed as `input` may contain accidental leading or trailing whitespace added by the user, `strip()` is often used before performing comparisons. When studying this concept, you should check, in order: how many times the loop runs, the order in which the loop variable’s value changes, and whether the string method creates a new value or modifies the existing one. Beginners often focus only on getting the final output correct and end up overlooking intermediate states.

side_cards/python_foundation_level2_side.title: The `replace()` method creates a new value by replacing a specific string with another string.
side_cards/python_foundation_level2_side.when_to_show: When reading code that replaces some characters in a string
side_cards/python_foundation_level2_side.body: `replace(old, new)` creates a new string by finding `old` within the original string and replacing it with `new`. For example, `'a-b'.replace('-', '')` replaces the hyphens with an empty string, resulting in `'ab'`.
side_cards/python_foundation_level2_side.detail: The original string itself is not automatically modified; you must store the result in a variable to use it later. When studying this concept, you should systematically verify how many times the loop runs, the order in which the loop variable’s value changes, and whether the string method creates a new value or modifies the existing one. Beginners often focus only on getting the final output correct and tend to overlook intermediate states.

side_cards/python_foundation_level2_side.title: The `lower()` and `upper()` functions convert text to lowercase or uppercase.
side_cards/python_foundation_level2_side.when_to_show: When reading code that checks for case sensitivity before comparing user input or strings,
side_cards/python_foundation_level2_side.body: The `lower()` function creates a new string with all characters in lowercase, and the `upper()` function creates a new string with all characters in uppercase.
side_cards/python_foundation_level2_side.detail: Since user input can come in various forms—such as “Yes,” “YES,” or “yes”—it is common to use `lower()` to standardize the input before comparison. When studying this concept, you should check, in order: how many times the loop runs, the order in which the loop variable’s value changes, and whether the string method creates a new value or modifies the existing one. Beginners often focus only on getting the final output correct and tend to overlook intermediate states.

side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.title: "def" creates a function, which is executed when called.
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.when_to_show: When distinguishing between function definitions and function calls
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.body: "def" is a keyword used to define a function. Defining a function means creating a named block of code.
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.detail: It’s important to note that just because you encounter a `def` line doesn’t mean the code inside the function is executed immediately. The code inside a function is executed when the function is called by adding parentheses after the function name. For example, even if there is a `print('hi')` line below `def hello()`, nothing will be printed to the screen unless you call `hello()`.

side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.title: The `return` statement returns a value to the outside of the function.
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.when_to_show: When the result of a function is stored in a variable or used in another calculation
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.body: "return" is a keyword that returns the result calculated by a function to the outside of the function.
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.detail: While "print" displays a value on the screen, "return" sends the value back to the point where the function was called. For example, in `result = add(2, 3)`, when the `add` function executes `return 5`, the entire call `add(2, 3)` is replaced with `5`, and that value is stored in `result`. You can store the return value in a variable, compare it, or reuse it as input for another function.

side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.title: A "parameter" is a placeholder, while an "argument" is the actual value entered.
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.when_to_show: When distinguishing between the name inside the function parentheses and the value passed when calling the function
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.body: "Parameter" and "argument" are terms that are often confused in the context of functions.
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.detail: A parameter is the name written inside the parentheses when defining a function, while an argument is the value actually passed when calling the function. For example, in `def greet(name):`, `name` is the parameter, and in `greet('Mina')`, `'Mina'` is the argument. When a function is executed, the argument value is used within the function as if it were assigned to the parameter name.

side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.title: "print" and "return" handle results in different ways.
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.when_to_show: When distinguishing whether a function only outputs something or returns a value
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.body: Although `print` and `return` both deal with values that appear to be results, they serve different purposes.
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.detail: `print` is a function that displays the current value on the screen, while `return` is a keyword that returns the function’s result to the point where it was called. If you execute `print('hi')` inside a function, “hi” will appear on the screen, but that does not necessarily mean the function returned a value. If you store the result of a function call that lacks a `return` statement in a variable, it usually contains `None`.

side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.title: Variables inside a function are temporary labels used during the function's execution.
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.when_to_show: When checking how far a variable created within a function is used
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.body: Variables inside a function can be thought of as temporary labels used during the function’s execution.
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.detail: Since this card serves as a reference for explaining the structure of local variables, it provides a basic model that should be the first thing to come to mind when solving scope-related problems. For example, if you define `total = a + b` inside `def add(a, b):`, `total` is a name that makes the calculation within the function easier to read. While there may be a variable named `total` outside the function, the `total` that is newly assigned inside the function does not always modify the `total` outside the function.

side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.title: Functions allow you to reuse the same rule for multiple values.
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.when_to_show: When reading a flow where the same function is called multiple times
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.body: A major advantage of functions is that the same rule can be reused for multiple values. Once you define a rule using `def`, you can call it multiple times with different arguments.
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.detail: For example, `double(3)` returns 6, and `double(5)` returns 10. Although the code inside the function is the same, the result changes because the values passed as parameters are different. When reading code, if the same function name appears multiple times, it’s a good idea to write down the argument values for each call separately.

side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.title: When a `return` statement is encountered, the function execution ends at that point.
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.when_to_show: When determining whether the code following the `return` statement is executed
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.body: The `return` statement returns a value and also terminates the execution of the function.
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.detail: When a `return` statement is encountered within a function, any code that remains in the same indented block below it is not executed. For example, even if there is a `print('after')` on the line following `return 'ok'`, `after` will not be printed if the `return` statement is executed first. When a `return` statement appears inside a conditional statement, you must verify under what conditions the function terminates early.

side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.title: A function is defined by its input, processing, and output.
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.when_to_show: When you need to quickly understand the overall purpose of a function
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.body: Functions are easier to understand if you think of them as a set of conventions regarding input, processing, and output.
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.detail: Input consists of parameters and arguments; processing is the block of code inside the function; and output is either a return value or screen output. Function names are usually chosen to briefly describe this agreement. For example, `count_items` is likely a function that counts items, and `normalize_name` is likely a function that formats names.

side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.title: A dictionary is a data structure that uses keys to look up values.
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.when_to_show: When reviewing dict, key, value
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.body: A `dict` is a data structure that stores keys and values as pairs. Since this card serves as the foundational card for defining dictionaries, it establishes the structure itself before other review cards do.
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.detail: While a list looks up values by their positions (such as 0 or 1), a `dict` looks up values using keys, which act like labels. For example, in `user = {'name': 'Mina', 'age': 13}`, `user['name']` is an expression that retrieves 'Mina'. Here, 'name' is the name being searched for, and 'Mina' is the value associated with that name.

side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.title: `get` can safely handle keys that don't exist
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.when_to_show: When retrieving a value using `dict.get()`
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.body: get returns None or a chosen default when a key is absent. This suits optional fields, but it can hide invalid input when the key is required.
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.detail: Use bracket access or explicit validation for required fields, and confirm that the default is meaningful in the domain.

side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.title: "keys," "values," and "items" are three ways of looking at a dictionary.
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.when_to_show: When checking the keys, values, and pairs in a dictionary
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.body: Use `dict.keys()` to view the keys, `dict.values()` to view the values, and `dict.items()` to view key-value pairs.
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.detail: For example, if you only need the names from a score dictionary, use `keys`; if you only need the scores, use `values`; and if you want to print both names and scores together, `items` is the appropriate choice. Items are frequently used in loops, as in `for name, score in scores.items()`. When reading code, you must distinguish what exactly is being iterated over.

side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.title: You can add or change values in a dictionary.
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.when_to_show: When adding a new key to a dictionary or changing an existing value
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.body: You can use keys to add or change values in a dictionary.
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.detail: If you assign a value to an existing key—such as `user['age'] = 14`—the value is updated; if you assign a value to a key that doesn’t exist—such as `user['city'] = 'Seoul'`—a new entry is added. When reading code, you should distinguish between the state of the dict before and after an assignment. It’s also important to note that if you assign a value to the same key multiple times, only the last value remains.

side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.title: A tuple is an ordered collection whose elements are typically not modified.
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.when_to_show: When returning a value enclosed in parentheses or multiple values at once
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.body: A tuple is ordered and its slots cannot be reassigned. A tuple can still contain a mutable list or dictionary whose contents change.
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.detail: Track both the positional meaning of returned values and the mutability of nested objects.
