side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.title: Unpacking splits a bound value among multiple variables.
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.when_to_show: When reading code like `a, b = pair`,
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.body: Unpacking is a method of breaking down a group of values—such as a tuple or list—into multiple variables. For example, if you write `point = (3, 4)` and then `x, y = point`, `x` becomes 3 and `y` becomes 4.
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.detail: When iterating over `dict.items()`, receiving the key and value separately—as in `for key, value in data.items()`—is also related to unpacking. When reading code, you must verify that the number of variables on the left matches the number of values on the right. This card is not just for memorizing definitions; it serves as a supplementary explanation to help you understand how data structures store and retrieve values in actual Python code.

side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.title: A set is a collection of unique values.
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.when_to_show: When checking for duplicates or determining whether to include an item
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.body: A set is a collection of values that does not allow duplicates. Even if a list contains the same value multiple times, converting it to a set will leave only one instance.
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.detail: For example, `set(['a', 'a', 'b'])` can be thought of as `{'a', 'b'}`. Sets are useful when the presence or absence of a value is more important than its order. When reading code, you should check whether a set is being used to reduce the number of elements, to remove duplicates, or to quickly verify if a value is present.

side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.title: Set operations are used to find similarities and differences.
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.when_to_show: When finding the common value or the combined value of two sets
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.body: Sets are useful for examining the relationships between two sets of values. You can use `a | b` for the union, `a & b` for the intersection, and `a - b` for the difference.
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.detail: For example, by comparing the set of concepts you’ve already learned with the set of concepts you mastered today, you can identify common concepts or areas where you still need improvement. When reading code, you must verify that the symbols represent relationships between sets rather than calculations. This card is not intended merely for memorizing word definitions; it serves as a supplementary explanation to help you understand how data structures store and retrieve values in actual Python code.

side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.title: The `while` loop repeats as long as the condition is True.
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.when_to_show: When determining the number of iterations and the termination condition for a `while` loop
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.body: A `while` loop repeatedly executes the same block of code as long as the condition is `True`.
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.detail: Whereas a `for` loop iterates through a fixed list in order, the number of iterations in a `while` loop is determined by when the condition becomes `False`. When reading `while` code, you should check the initial variable value, the condition, and how the values affecting the condition change within the loop. This card serves as a supplementary guide to help you understand how loop flow and loop constructs work in actual code.

side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.title: In a `while` loop, the `update` line that changes the condition is important.
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.when_to_show: When you see a line like `i = i + 1` inside a `while` loop
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.body: In a `while` loop, an update statement like `i = i + 1` is essential for terminating the loop.
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.detail: If `i` starts at 0 and the condition is `i < 3`, `i` must be incremented within the loop so that the condition eventually evaluates to `False`. The execution result may vary depending on whether the update statement is inside or outside the loop. This card serves as a supplementary explanation to help you understand how loop flow and loop constructs work in actual code.

side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.title: "break" stops the loop, and "continue" skips to the next iteration.
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.when_to_show: When a `break` or `continue` is encountered inside a loop
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.body: `break` and `continue` are keywords that alter the flow within a loop. `break` immediately terminates the entire loop, while `continue` skips the remaining lines of the current iteration and moves on to the next one.
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.detail: Since both are frequently used within `if` statements, you must verify under what conditions they operate. This card serves as a supplementary explanation to help you understand how loop flow and loop constructs are executed in actual code. When solving problems, clearly identify the loop’s starting value, the condition, the current value of the loop variable, the `update` line, and the conditions for `break` and `continue`.

side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.title: `sorted` creates a new, sorted result
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.when_to_show: When distinguishing between the sorted result and the original list
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.body: `sorted` is a function that returns a new result with the values sorted. Given `nums = [3, 1, 2]`, `sorted(nums)` returns `[1, 2, 3]`, but the original `nums` itself remains unchanged.
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.detail: In contrast, `list.sort()` modifies the list itself. This card serves as a supplementary explanation to help you understand how looping logic and looping tools work in actual code. When solving problems, clearly distinguish the loop’s starting value, the loop condition, the current value of the loop variable, the `update` line, and the `break` and `continue` conditions.

side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.title: "reversed" produces a result that is the reverse of the original sequence.
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.when_to_show: When reviewing reversed, list, order
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.body: `reversed` is a tool that allows you to read ordered values, such as lists or strings, in reverse. If you wrap it in a list—like `list(reversed([1, 2, 3]))`—you’ll get a result like `[3, 2, 1]`.
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.detail: `reversed` itself does not directly modify the original list. This card serves as a supplementary explanation to help you understand how loop flow and loop tools are executed in actual code. When solving problems, the loop’s starting value, condition, current value of the loop variable, `update` line, and `break` and `continue` conditions are displayed separately.

side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.title: `enumerate` takes both an index and a value
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.when_to_show: When reviewing enumerate, index, value
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.body: `enumerate` is a tool that returns both an index number and the actual value when iterating.
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.detail: If you write `for i, name in enumerate(names)`, `i` will hold numbers like 0, 1, 2, and `name` will hold the actual values from the list. You can also change the starting index by setting `start=1`. This card serves as a supplementary explanation to help you understand how looping structures and looping tools work in actual code.

side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.title: A ZIP file bundles multiple lists into a single location.
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.when_to_show: When reviewing zip, tuple, parallel iteration
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.body: `zip` groups values at the same positions across multiple lists and iterates over them. Given `names` and `scores`, `zip(names, scores)` pairs names with scores at the corresponding positions.
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.detail: It is important to note that this does not generate all possible combinations, but rather pairs values at the same positions. This card serves as a supplementary explanation to help you understand how looping flows and looping tools work in actual code. When solving problems, clearly distinguish the loop’s starting value, the loop condition, the current value of the loop variable, the update line, and the `break` and `continue` conditions.

side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.title: The loop tool starts by reading the current value.
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.when_to_show: When `while`, `enumerate`, `zip`, `sorted`, and `reversed` are used together
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.body: When combining iteration tools, the first thing to check is what values are assigned to the variables in the current iteration.
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.detail: `while` checks whether a condition is `True`; `enumerate` provides both an index and a value; and `zip` pairs values at corresponding positions. `sorted` and `reversed` can be used to change the order of the iteration. This card serves as a supplementary guide to help you understand how loop flow and loop constructs work in actual code.

side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.title: The `open` and `read` functions read the contents of a file as a string.
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.when_to_show: When looking at code that reads the contents of a file all at once
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.body: open() opens a file and read() brings the opened file's contents into Python as a string. First identify which file and mode are used, then follow the variable that receives the read result.
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.detail: After with open('memo.txt', 'r', encoding='utf-8') as f:, text = f.read() places the whole file contents into text as a string. Read the path, mode, encoding, and destination variable together. For a large file, reading everything at once may be expensive, so also check how the following code processes the content.

side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.title: "with" is a mechanism for safely opening and closing files.
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.when_to_show: When looking at the `with open(...) as f` structure
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.body: The `with` statement is a mechanism for safely using resources such as files.
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.detail: Within the `with open(...) as f:` block, you can read from or write to the file via `f`, and the file is automatically closed when the block ends. This reduces the likelihood of errors compared to code that explicitly uses `close`. When reading file-handling code, distinguish between what happens inside the `with` block and the fact that file usage has ended outside the block.

side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.title: "write" means to write, and "append" mode means to add to the end
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.when_to_show: When reviewing write, append, file mode
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.body: When opening a file, "w" mode is often used to mean "write," and "a" mode is often used to mean "append." The `write` function writes a string to a file.
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.detail: Be careful with "w" because it overwrites the existing content, while "a" appends new content to the end of the existing content. When reading code, you should first check whether the second argument of `open` is 'r', 'w', or 'a'. This card is intended as a supplementary explanation to help you understand file handling and exception handling through actual code flow, rather than just memorizing the terms.

side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.title: pathlib's `Path` treats paths as building blocks
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.when_to_show: When you see code like `Path('data') / 'file.txt'`,
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.body: pathlib.Path treats a file path as structured path parts instead of one manually assembled string. Path('data') / 'memo.txt' builds a path to memo.txt inside the data folder.
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.detail: A Path exposes name for the filename, suffix for the extension, stem for the name without the extension, and parent for the containing folder. This is clearer than manually slicing strings or joining platform-specific separators. When reading code, distinguish between building a Path and performing file work such as read_text().

side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.title: Path.read_text and write_text are convenient for handling small files
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.when_to_show: When reading from or writing to a file directly using a Path object
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.body: The `Path` object provides convenient methods such as `read_text` and `write_text`. `Path('memo.txt').read_text(encoding='utf-8')` reads the file’s contents as a string, and `write_text` writes a string to the file.
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.detail: For handling short text files, this can be more concise than using `with open`. However, in actual code, you must verify that the encoding and file path are correct. This card is intended as a supplementary explanation to help you understand file handling and exception handling not just by memorizing terms, but by following the actual code flow.

side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.title: The try/except block safely wraps code that might cause an error
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.when_to_show: When I see code that could fail, such as integer conversions or opening files
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.body: Place code that might raise an error in the `try` block, and place code to be executed when an error occurs in the `except` block.
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.detail: For example, since `int('x')` can raise a `ValueError`, wrapping it in a `try/except` block allows the program to set a default value or display a message instead of stopping immediately. When reading code, try to distinguish between the normal flow and the error flow. This card is a supplementary explanation designed to help you understand file handling and exception handling through actual code flow, rather than just memorizing the terms.

side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.title: The error type of `except` determines which failures can be caught
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.when_to_show: when you see a ValueError or a FileNotFoundError
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.body: The type of error following `except` determines which type of failure is handled. `ValueError` often occurs during value conversion, while `FileNotFoundError` often occurs when a file does not exist.
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.detail: Since not all errors are handled by the same `except` block, you must verify which errors can occur on which lines and whether the `except` block catches those errors. This card is a supplementary explanation designed to help you understand file handling and exception handling through actual code flow, rather than just memorizing the terms.

side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.title: Files and JSON are viewed in the order of reading, parsing, and using.
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.when_to_show: When looking at code that reads a JSON file and writes it to a dictionary
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.body: Code that handles JSON files typically follows this flow: it reads a string from the file, converts it to a Python dictionary or list using `json.loads` or `json.load`, and then retrieves values using keys or indices.
side_cards/python_foundation_level3_side.detail: Reading a file and parsing JSON are two distinct steps. When reviewing code, you must distinguish between the stage where the file contents are a string and the stage where they have been converted into Python data structures. This card serves as a supplementary explanation to help you understand the actual code flow, rather than just memorizing terms related to file handling and exception handling.

side_cards/python_foundation_level4_side.title: A class is a blueprint, and an object is the actual instance created from it.
side_cards/python_foundation_level4_side.when_to_show: When distinguishing between class definitions and object creation
side_cards/python_foundation_level4_side.body: A class can be thought of as a blueprint for creating values of the same type. Just because you define `class Dog:` doesn’t mean a dog is created right away.
side_cards/python_foundation_level4_side.detail: An actual object is created when you call the class name, such as `dog = Dog()`. When reading code, look at the class block to see what attributes and methods it defines, and then follow along to the line where the object is created to see where the actual value is generated. This card is not intended to help you memorize object-oriented concepts by rote, but rather to serve as a supplementary explanation for understanding how `class`, `object`, `self`, `__init__`, `attribute`, and `method` are interconnected in actual Python code.

side_cards/python_foundation_level4_side.title: `self` refers to the current object itself
side_cards/python_foundation_level4_side.when_to_show: When you see code like `self.name` inside a method
side_cards/python_foundation_level4_side.body: `self` refers to the current object on which the method is being executed. When you read `dog.name` or call `dog.speak()`, you can think of `self` inside the `speak` method as referring to the `dog` object.
side_cards/python_foundation_level4_side.detail: Therefore, `self.name` is an expression that reads the `name` attribute of the current object. Rather than memorizing `self` as if it were a separate piece of information, it’s important to understand it in the context of which object’s method is being called. This card is not intended to make object-oriented programming difficult to memorize, but rather to serve as a supplementary explanation for understanding how `class`, `object`, `self`, `__init__`, `attribute`, and `method` are connected in actual Python code.

side_cards/python_foundation_level4_side.title: __init__ is executed the first time an object is created.
side_cards/python_foundation_level4_side.when_to_show: When looking at the __init__ method inside a class
side_cards/python_foundation_level4_side.body: Calling Dog('Momo') normally lets __new__ create an instance and then __init__ initialize its state. __init__ is commonly called a constructor, but it does not itself create and return the instance.
side_cards/python_foundation_level4_side.detail: Follow arguments into parameters and then into self attributes.

side_cards/python_foundation_level4_side.title: An attribute is a label associated with an object.
side_cards/python_foundation_level4_side.when_to_show: When you see dot notation like `obj.name` or `obj.score`,
side_cards/python_foundation_level4_side.body: An attribute can be thought of as a label for a value held by an object.
side_cards/python_foundation_level4_side.detail: `student.name` is an expression that reads the `name` value held by the `student` object, and `student.score = 90` is an expression that creates or changes the `score` attribute. Unlike local variables inside a function, attributes remain attached to the object. When using dot notation, you must verify which attribute of which object you are reading or modifying.

side_cards/python_foundation_level4_side.title: A method is treated like a function attached to an object.
side_cards/python_foundation_level4_side.when_to_show: When you see code in the form of `obj.method()`
side_cards/python_foundation_level4_side.body: A method is a function defined within a class that operates on an object. Functions where the first parameter is `self`—such as `def speak(self):`—can be called by the object.
side_cards/python_foundation_level4_side.detail: When `dog.speak()` is executed, the `self` inside `speak` becomes `dog`. Methods can read or modify attributes and return calculation results. When reading code, first check which object `self` refers to within a method.

side_cards/python_foundation_level4_side.title: Objects created from the same class each have their own attributes.
side_cards/python_foundation_level4_side.when_to_show: When creating multiple objects of the same class
side_cards/python_foundation_level4_side.body: You can create multiple objects of the same class, but each object can have its own attributes. If you create `a = User('A')` and `b = User('B')`, `a.name` could be `A` and `b.name` could be `B`.
side_cards/python_foundation_level4_side.detail: Even though they are created from the same blueprint, their actual values are managed separately. When reading code, you must not get confused about which object’s attribute is being printed. This card is not intended to help you memorize object-oriented concepts by rote, but rather to serve as a supplementary explanation for understanding how `class`, `object`, `self`, `__init__`, `attribute`, and `method` are interconnected in actual Python code.

side_cards/python_foundation_level4_side.title: A class variable is a shared value associated with the class.
side_cards/python_foundation_level4_side.when_to_show: When looking at variables assigned directly within a class
side_cards/python_foundation_level4_side.body: A class variable is stored on the class and instances can share it through attribute lookup. An instance assignment can shadow it, and a mutable class variable such as a list can create unintended shared state.
side_cards/python_foundation_level4_side.detail: Distinguish common configuration from per-instance state.

side_cards/python_foundation_level4_side.title: Object code is read in the order of creation, storage, and invocation.
side_cards/python_foundation_level4_side.when_to_show: When you need to quickly grasp the overall flow of a class's code
side_cards/python_foundation_level4_side.body: Object-oriented code is easier to trace as class definition → object creation → attribute storage → method call. Read the blueprint first, then follow what values and behavior the actual object uses.
side_cards/python_foundation_level4_side.detail: Inside the class block, identify the attributes and methods it defines. At a line such as dog = Dog('Momo'), __init__ commonly sets the object's initial attributes. Later, dot expressions such as dog.name or dog.speak() show which object's data is read or which method is called.

side_cards/python_beginner_mixed_review_.title: Variable tracking involves comparing the initial value and the final value.
side_cards/python_beginner_mixed_review_.body: A variable is like a label, and assignment is the act of changing the value that label refers to. If `x = 1` is followed by `x = x + 2`, the value of `x` changes to 3.
side_cards/python_beginner_mixed_review_.detail: When reading code, don’t just look at the initial value and stop there; you must check to see if there are any lines where a new value is assigned to the same variable. In particular, the output changes depending on which line the `print` statement appears on. This card is not intended for memorizing basic grammar; rather, it is a review card designed to help you read short code in the actual order of execution.

side_cards/python_beginner_mixed_review_.title: "print" is used for screen output and is different from storing variables.
side_cards/python_beginner_mixed_review_.body: `print` is an operation that displays a value on the screen. Just because you use `print` on a value does not mean that value is automatically stored in a new variable.
side_cards/python_beginner_mixed_review_.detail: Conversely, even if you store a value in a variable, it may not appear on the screen unless you use `print`. When reading code, you must distinguish between the lines where values are calculated and the lines where they are actually printed to the screen. This card is not intended for memorizing basic grammar rules, but rather as a review tool for reading short code in its actual execution order.

side_cards/python_beginner_mixed_review_.title: The if/else statement executes only one branch depending on the result of the condition.
side_cards/python_beginner_mixed_review_.body: In an if/else structure, the system first evaluates whether the conditional expression is True or False. If the condition is True, the if block is executed; if it is False, the else block is executed.
side_cards/python_beginner_mixed_review_.detail: Not both blocks are executed every time. You can tell which lines are inside the if block and which are inside the else block by looking at the indentation. These cards are not intended for memorizing basic grammar rules, but rather as review cards for reading short code in its actual execution order.

side_cards/python_beginner_mixed_review_.title: For cumulative totals, view the total change as shown in the table.
side_cards/python_beginner_mixed_review_.when_to_show: In problems involving calculating totals or counts using a `for` loop,
side_cards/python_beginner_mixed_review_.body: In a loop, if you see a line like `total = total + n`, `total` changes with each iteration.
side_cards/python_beginner_mixed_review_.detail: You can avoid confusion by writing down the initial value of `total`, the value of `n` for this iteration, and the new value of `total` after the calculation, in that order. Summing, counting, string concatenation, and list appending can all be understood as cumulative loop patterns. This card is not intended for memorizing basic syntax separately, but rather as a review tool for reading short code in the actual order of execution.

side_cards/python_beginner_mixed_review_.title: In a list, the position and value are separate.
side_cards/python_beginner_mixed_review_.body: In a list, position and value are separate concepts. This card is a review card designed to have you read through a short problem in execution order after you’ve already learned about lists.
side_cards/python_beginner_mixed_review_.detail: A list contains multiple values in order, and `items[0]` refers to the first value. Here, 0 is not a value itself but a position number. `items[1]` does not refer to the number 1, but rather to the second value in the current list.

side_cards/python_beginner_mixed_review_.title: A dictionary uses a key to find a value.
side_cards/python_beginner_mixed_review_.body: A dictionary stores keys and values as pairs. This card is a review card designed to have you read short code snippets in the order they are executed after you’ve already reviewed the definition of a dictionary.
side_cards/python_beginner_mixed_review_.detail: data['name'] is an expression that reads the value associated with the key "name," and scores['kim'] is an expression that retrieves the value associated with the key "kim." Assigning a value to the same key does not create a new dictionary; instead, it updates the value associated with that key. Therefore, when solving problems, you should first write down the initial state of the dictionary, then track on the next line whether a key is added, whether the value of an existing key is changed, and what value is ultimately printed.

side_cards/python_beginner_mixed_review_.title: A function executes when it is called and returns a value using the `return` statement.
side_cards/python_beginner_mixed_review_.when_to_show: In problems that involve both `def` and function calls,
side_cards/python_beginner_mixed_review_.body: The `def` keyword is used to define a function, and the function body is executed when the function is called.
side_cards/python_beginner_mixed_review_.detail: When you call the function—as in `result = add(2, 3)`—the arguments are passed to the parameters, and the return value is stored in `result`. When solving function problems, distinguish between the definition line and the call line, and follow where the returned value goes. This card is not intended for memorizing basic grammar separately, but rather as a review card for reading short code in its actual execution order.

side_cards/python_beginner_mixed_review_.title: For mixed problems, proceed one line at a time.
side_cards/python_beginner_mixed_review_.body: Mixed problems may seem difficult, but you can solve them by looking at them line by line.
side_cards/python_beginner_mixed_review_.detail: Organize the order of execution—which comes first: variable assignment, conditional statements, loops, lists, dictionaries, or function calls. Rather than trying to deeply analyze every unfamiliar term, you’ll get closer to the correct answer by first determining whether the current line reads, modifies, or outputs a value. These cards are not intended for memorizing basic grammar separately, but rather as review cards for reading short code in its actual execution order.

side_cards/python_beginner_reading_notes.title: In the entrance exam, calculate the right side first and then attach it to the left side.
side_cards/python_beginner_reading_notes.when_to_show: When you see code like `x = x + 1`,
side_cards/python_beginner_reading_notes.body: When reading an assignment statement, calculate the expression on the right side first, rather than trying to memorize the name on the left.
side_cards/python_beginner_reading_notes.detail: For example, `x = x + 1` works by reading the existing value of `x`, adding 1 to it, and then assigning the result back to the variable `x`. So, if `x` was 2, after execution, `x` becomes 3. Beginners may find it strange that `x` appears on both sides simultaneously, but you can think of the `x` on the right as the previous value and the `x` on the left as the name where the new value will be stored.

side_cards/python_beginner_reading_notes.title: The "print" line determines the value displayed on the screen.
side_cards/python_beginner_reading_notes.body: In problems involving output results, you’re often asked what value appears on the screen at the end. Even if a value is stored in a variable, it won’t appear on the screen unless you use `print`.
side_cards/python_beginner_reading_notes.detail: Conversely, if a calculation is included inside a `print` statement, the result of that calculation appears immediately on the screen. `print(x + 1)` is not code that changes `x` itself; rather, it reads the value of `x`, adds 1, and displays the result. Always read storage and output separately.

side_cards/python_beginner_reading_notes.title: A data type determines how a value behaves.
side_cards/python_beginner_reading_notes.when_to_show: When reviewing type, str, int, bool
side_cards/python_beginner_reading_notes.body: In Python, the number 3 and the string '3' may look similar on the screen, but they behave differently. The number 3 is used in addition operations, while the string '3' can be concatenated like any other character.
side_cards/python_beginner_reading_notes.detail: True and False are boolean values frequently used in conditional statements. When reading code as a beginner, don’t just look at the appearance of a value; check whether it’s enclosed in quotes, whether it’s the result of a comparison, or whether it’s used in a numerical calculation. This sidebar isn’t meant as a hint to quickly spot problems, but rather as reading material designed to help beginners internalize the actual order in which they should read code.

side_cards/python_beginner_reading_notes.title: A conditional statement evaluates the result of the conditional expression first.
side_cards/python_beginner_reading_notes.body: When reading an `if` statement, don’t start with the indented lines; first determine whether the condition is `True` or `False`.
side_cards/python_beginner_reading_notes.detail: If the condition is `True`, the `if` block is executed; if it is `False`, the `else` block is executed if present. If there are `elif` clauses, they are evaluated in order from the top, and only the first block that evaluates to `True` is executed. If you assume that all blocks will be executed, it’s easy to get the output or variable results wrong.

side_cards/python_beginner_reading_notes.title: It's easier to understand loops by looking at a table that shows how values change with each iteration.
side_cards/python_beginner_reading_notes.body: A loop is a structure that executes a single line of code multiple times. In cumulative code like `total = total + n`, the value of `total` changes with each iteration.
side_cards/python_beginner_reading_notes.detail: When solving a problem, you can write down the loop counter, the value of `n`, and the value of `total` after each iteration in a table. With a `while` loop, you must pay particular attention to when the condition becomes `False`. If there is no update line like `i = i + 1`, the loop may never end.

side_cards/python_beginner_reading_notes.title: List indices start at 0.
side_cards/python_beginner_reading_notes.when_to_show: When you see expressions like items[0] and items[1]
side_cards/python_beginner_reading_notes.body: List indices start at 0. This card is not a review of the entire list, but rather a reading note intended to help beginners avoid common misunderstandings, particularly when reading indices.
side_cards/python_beginner_reading_notes.detail: People often refer to it as “the first one,” but in a Python list, the first value is at index 0. Therefore, `items[0]` is the first value, and `items[1]` is the second value. If you interpret `items[1]` as the number 1, or mistake the second position for the first, you’ll easily get the wrong answer.

side_cards/python_beginner_reading_notes.title: A dictionary looks up entries by key, not by location.
side_cards/python_beginner_reading_notes.when_to_show: When you see an expression like `data['name']`,
side_cards/python_beginner_reading_notes.body: Dictionaries are looked up by key, not by position. This card is a study note for beginners who confuse list indices with dictionary keys.
side_cards/python_beginner_reading_notes.detail: In a list, `items[0]` refers to the 0th position, but in a dictionary, `data['age']` refers to the key named “age.” Therefore, `data['score'] = 90` does not mean inserting 90 at the “score” position; rather, it stores the value 90 under the “score” key or updates the existing value. Attempting to access a nonexistent key directly using square brackets can cause an error, whereas using `get()` allows for safe handling with a default value when the key is missing.

side_cards/python_beginner_reading_notes.title: A function is not defined; it is executed when it is called.
side_cards/python_beginner_reading_notes.when_to_show: When reviewing function, def, call, return
side_cards/python_beginner_reading_notes.body: `def` is the code used to define a function, and the function body is executed when the function is called.
side_cards/python_beginner_reading_notes.detail: When `add(2, 3)` is called, 2 and 3 are passed as parameters, and the return value is sent back to the calling location. If `result = add(2, 3)`, the return value is stored in `result`. If there is only a function definition and no call, the `print` statement inside the function will not execute.

side_cards/python_beginner_reading_notes.title: The `return` statement returns the function's result and terminates the function.
side_cards/python_beginner_reading_notes.when_to_show: When there are multiple `return` statements in a function
side_cards/python_beginner_reading_notes.body: A `return` statement returns a value to the outside of the function. Once a `return` is executed, the rest of the function body is no longer executed.
side_cards/python_beginner_reading_notes.detail: If there is a `return` inside an `if` statement and the condition is `True`, the function may end at that `return`. Therefore, in function problems, you must identify which `return` is actually executed. `print` and `return` are different.

side_cards/python_beginner_reading_notes.title: Variables inside a function and variables outside a function are treated as separate scopes.
side_cards/python_beginner_reading_notes.when_to_show: When a variable with the same name appears within a function
side_cards/python_beginner_reading_notes.body: Variables inside a function and variables outside a function are distinguished by their scope.
side_cards/python_beginner_reading_notes.detail: This card is a light, easy-to-read note that explains scope primarily through the lens of execution flow, so that beginners encountering the concept for the first time don’t find it too difficult. Variables created inside a function are typically values used mainly while the function is executing. Even if a variable inside a function has the same name as an outer variable, you shouldn’t assume that an assignment inside the function will always change the outer value.

side_cards/python_beginner_reading_notes.title: String methods create new strings or lists.
side_cards/python_beginner_reading_notes.when_to_show: When looking at split, strip, and join
side_cards/python_beginner_reading_notes.body: String methods are frequently used to manipulate, split, or concatenate text.
side_cards/python_beginner_reading_notes.detail: `strip` removes leading and trailing whitespace or line breaks, `split` splits a string into a list, and `join` concatenates a list of strings into a single string. Don’t assume that the original string itself changes automatically; instead, check which variable stores the result. You must reassign it—like `text = text.strip()`—for the updated value to remain in `text`.

side_cards/python_beginner_reading_notes.title: A boolean value acts as the gatekeeper in a conditional statement.
side_cards/python_beginner_reading_notes.body: A boolean value is either True or False. The comparison expression `score >= 60` also produces a boolean value.
side_cards/python_beginner_reading_notes.detail: Code such as `if active:` executes the `if` block if the value of `active` is evaluated as True. In boolean problems, you must distinguish whether the word “True” is being printed or used as a condition. Although the boolean used in a condition may not be visible on the screen, it determines which blocks are executed.

side_cards/python_beginner_reading_notes.title: Error handling is a flow that wraps lines that may fail.
side_cards/python_beginner_reading_notes.body: Code that might fail is placed inside the `try` block.
side_cards/python_beginner_reading_notes.detail: Converting a string that is difficult to convert to a number—such as `int('x')`—can raise a `ValueError`, and if that error is caught by `except ValueError`, the `except` block is executed. Error handling isn’t a trick to get the right answer; it’s a mechanism that allows the program to continue along a different path rather than stopping immediately. Read the code separately for normal and failure cases.

side_cards/python_beginner_reading_notes.title: File operations are viewed as a sequence of open, read/write, and close operations.
side_cards/python_beginner_reading_notes.body: File operations follow a flow where you open a file, read from or write to it, and close it when you’re done. The `with open(...) as f:` construct helps you handle this process safely.
side_cards/python_beginner_reading_notes.detail: `read` reads the file’s contents as a string, and `write` writes a string to the file. Since screen output and file writing are different, you shouldn’t assume that `f.write('hi')` will print “hi” to the screen. This sidebar is not a hint for quickly debugging problems, but rather reading material designed to help beginners internalize the actual order in which code is read.

side_cards/python_beginner_reading_notes.title: Object code distinguishes between design specifications and actual values.
side_cards/python_beginner_reading_notes.body: A class is a blueprint, and an object is the actual instance created by instantiating the class. `self` refers to the current object on which the method is being executed.
side_cards/python_beginner_reading_notes.detail: `__init__` is a special method that initializes attributes when the object is first created. When reading code as a beginner, rather than trying to memorize object-oriented concepts in depth, simply follow the sequence: class definition, object creation, attribute storage, and method invocation. This sidebar is not a hint for quickly guessing the answer to a problem, but rather reading material designed to help beginners internalize the actual order in which they should read code.

side_cards/python_beginner_reading_notes.title: Solve mixed-type problems by breaking them down into a checklist.
side_cards/python_beginner_reading_notes.body: Mixed-type problems are difficult if you try to recall all the relevant grammar at once. First, identify the output line, then trace back to the variables or function calls required to produce that output.
side_cards/python_beginner_reading_notes.detail: Next, if there are conditional statements, select only the blocks that are actually executed; if there are loops, note how the values change with each iteration. For lists and dictionaries, check the final remaining values. Simply following this checklist will significantly reduce mistakes on beginner-level problems.

side_cards/python_function_scope_reading.title: `def` defines a function, and calling it starts its execution.
side_cards/python_function_scope_reading.body: The line `def add(a, b):` is code that declares the function. The function body does not execute immediately upon encountering that line. Actual execution begins when the function is called—for example, `add(2, 3)`—with parentheses following the function name.
side_cards/python_function_scope_reading.detail: A "def" line is not a line that executes a function; rather, it prepares the function so that it can be called later. Actual execution begins on the call line, where parentheses follow the function name, as in `add(2, 3)`. When reading code, distinguish between the definition and the call, and consider that the flow within the function restarts each time it is called.

side_cards/python_function_scope_reading.title: A parameter is the name of an input used within a function.
side_cards/python_function_scope_reading.when_to_show: When looking at where the function call arguments go
side_cards/python_function_scope_reading.body: In `def double(x):`, `x` is a parameter. When you call `double(4)`, the argument 4 is assigned to the parameter `x`. Inside the function, you can use 4 under the name `x`.
side_cards/python_function_scope_reading.detail: A "parameter" is the name given to an input value within a function, while an "argument" is the value actually passed when the function is called. In the case of `double(4)`, the value 4 is assigned to the parameter `x` and is used as `x` within the function body. If there are default values or keyword arguments, you should list the final values for each parameter in a table to ensure you don’t lose track of the flow.

side_cards/python_function_scope_reading.title: The `return` statement returns a value and terminates the function's execution.
side_cards/python_function_scope_reading.body: The `return` statement returns the function’s result to the calling location. When `return` is executed, the function’s execution ends. Therefore, even if there is code with the same indentation level below `return`, it may not be executed.
side_cards/python_function_scope_reading.detail: A `return` statement returns a value created within a function to the point where it was called and terminates the function’s execution at that moment. Since the line following the `return` statement may not be executed, its position is important. Unlike `print`, it should be understood as passing a value to be used in subsequent calculations or assignments, rather than a value displayed on the screen.

side_cards/python_function_scope_reading.title: "print" and "return" serve different purposes.
side_cards/python_function_scope_reading.when_to_show: When You Confuse `print` and `return` Inside a Function
side_cards/python_function_scope_reading.body: `print` and `return` serve different purposes. This card helps you distinguish between screen output and function results within a function’s scope. A `print` statement inside a function displays a value on the screen.
side_cards/python_function_scope_reading.detail: When reading a function, you must keep `print` and `return` separate. Write `print` in the output field, and write `return` in the field for the value returned to the caller. Even if only `print` is executed within a function, the call result may be `None`. On a line like `result = func()`, check the value displayed on the screen and the value stored in `result` separately.

side_cards/python_function_scope_reading.title: Variables within a function are evaluated first during the function's execution.
side_cards/python_function_scope_reading.when_to_show: When reviewing local variable, scope, function
side_cards/python_function_scope_reading.body: Variables inside a function are tracked first within the function’s execution. Rather than providing a deep theoretical explanation of scope, this card is a “Function Scope Reading Card” that tells you which lines to read and in what order when dealing with real-world problems.
side_cards/python_function_scope_reading.detail: Variables inside a function are first tracked in the inner scope of the function. Even if there is a variable with the same name outside the function, you should not assume that an assignment inside the function immediately changes the value of the outer variable. It is safest to clearly distinguish between the value of the outer variable before the call, the value passed as a parameter, changes to the local variables inside the function, and the value that remains in the outer scope after the return statement.

side_cards/python_function_scope_reading.title: Variables with the same name are treated differently depending on whether they are inner or outer variables.
side_cards/python_function_scope_reading.body: There may be an `x = 10` outside the function and an `x = 3` inside it. In this case, it’s easy to make a mistake by assuming that the `x` inside the function and the `x` outside are always the same. The `x` that is newly assigned inside the function is read first as the value used in the function’s internal flow.
side_cards/python_function_scope_reading.detail: If variables with the same name exist both inside and outside a function, they can behave as if they were different variables. Even if you execute `x = 3` inside a function, the outer `x` may remain unchanged. When reading code, check which scope the current line is in, where the name was defined, and whether the output is the inner value or the outer value.

side_cards/python_function_scope_reading.title: The result of a function call can be stored in a variable.
side_cards/python_function_scope_reading.when_to_show: When looking at the form `result = func(...)`,
side_cards/python_function_scope_reading.body: `result = add(2, 3)` means that the value returned by the `add` function is stored in `result`. The value calculated inside the function is returned, and that return value becomes the right-hand side of the assignment statement.
side_cards/python_function_scope_reading.detail: The result of a function call can be used as the value on the right-hand side of an assignment statement. In `result = add(2, 3)`, the return value of `add` is stored in `result`. Even if the variable names inside and outside the function are different, the flow is connected via the `return` statement. Distinguish whether the result of a call is discarded, stored in a variable, or passed to another function.

side_cards/python_function_scope_reading.title: If there is no `return` statement, the result of the call may be `None`.
side_cards/python_function_scope_reading.body: If a Python function ends without encountering a `return` statement, it usually returns `None`. Even if you use `print` inside the function, the return value may be `None` if there is no `return` statement. If you run `print(result)` after `result = hello()`, the output from inside the function and the output of `result` may appear separately.
side_cards/python_function_scope_reading.detail: Functions that end without a `return` statement typically return `None` as the result of the call. Even if a `print` statement is executed inside a function and displays a value on the screen, the value stored in `result = func()` may be `None`. When reading code, distinguish between what a function displays and what it returns, and note that `None` can behave like `False` in conditional statements.

side_cards/python_function_scope_reading.title: A conditional `return` statement can terminate a function early
side_cards/python_function_scope_reading.when_to_show: When reviewing early return, if, return
side_cards/python_function_scope_reading.body: If an `if` condition inside a function evaluates to `True` and the `return` statement is executed, the function terminates immediately. Subsequent `return` statements or assignments may not be executed.
side_cards/python_function_scope_reading.detail: A `return` statement without a condition can terminate a function prematurely. If the `if` condition evaluates to `True` and the function encounters a `return` statement, any subsequent assignments or other `return` statements may not be executed. In a function with multiple `return` statements, the conditions are evaluated from top to bottom based on their actual values, and the function must follow the first return path that is executed.

side_cards/python_function_scope_reading.title: If you pass a list to a function, changes made within the function may be retained.
side_cards/python_function_scope_reading.when_to_show: When a list is appended within a function
side_cards/python_function_scope_reading.body: If you pass a list to a function and then call `items.append('a')` within the function, the same list object is modified, so the change may be visible from outside the function as well.
side_cards/python_function_scope_reading.detail: If you pass a list to a function and then perform operations that modify its contents—such as `append` or `pop`—the changes may still be visible from outside the function even after it has finished executing. The behavior of directly modifying the list object differs from the behavior of creating a new list and returning it. You must distinguish between modifying the value and returning a new value.

side_cards/python_function_scope_reading.title: Assigning a value to a numeric variable inside a function does not change its value outside the function.
side_cards/python_function_scope_reading.when_to_show: When changing a numeric parameter inside a function
side_cards/python_function_scope_reading.body: Even if you execute `n = n + 1` inside a function, the outer variable `x` is not automatically updated. `n` is the parameter name used inside the function, and `x` is the outer variable. For a function to pass a new value to the outside, it must return the value (e.g., `return n`), and the outside must reassign it (e.g., `x = add_one(x)`).
side_cards/python_function_scope_reading.detail: For values such as numbers, even if you set `n = n + 1` inside a function, the outer variable `x` is not automatically updated. Parameters inside a function are tracked by their inner names first; to change the outer value, you usually need to use `return` to return a new value and then store it again. Writing the values before and after the call separately helps reduce confusion.

side_cards/python_function_scope_reading.title: Nested functions require the inner `def` to be called as well.
side_cards/python_function_scope_reading.when_to_show: When reviewing nested function, def, call
side_cards/python_function_scope_reading.body: Even if there is another `def` inside a function, the inner function must be called in order to execute. When the outer function is called, the inner function definition may be set up, but unless there is a call such as `inner()`, the body of the inner function will not execute.
side_cards/python_function_scope_reading.detail: In nested functions, the inner `def` statement merely prepares the function; its body is executed only when it is called separately. Just because the outer function is executed does not mean the inner function is automatically executed. When reading code, you should identify the outer and inner calls separately and also check whether the inner function accesses outer variables.

side_cards/python_function_scope_reading.title: "global" indicates that the outer variable will be modified directly.
side_cards/python_function_scope_reading.body: The `global x` keyword indicates that the function will use the outer `x` variable rather than creating a new local variable named `x` within the function.
side_cards/python_function_scope_reading.detail: The `global` keyword indicates that the function will directly access the outer variable rather than creating a new local variable. Therefore, when a function containing `global` is called, the value of the outer variable may change. Generally, returning a value using `return` is safer, so `global` is considered a warning sign that makes it difficult to trace the flow of the program.

side_cards/python_function_scope_reading.title: The default argument is used when no argument is provided.
side_cards/python_function_scope_reading.when_to_show: When you see code like `def greet(name='Guest')`,
side_cards/python_function_scope_reading.body: If a function parameter has a default value, you can omit the argument when calling the function. If you call `greet()` from `def greet(name='Guest')`, `name` becomes `Guest`; if you call `greet('Mina')`, `name` becomes `Mina`. Default values are important for determining what values are actually passed to parameters when reading a function call.
side_cards/python_function_scope_reading.detail: The default value is the value assigned to a parameter when the argument is omitted during a function call. Even though `greet()` and `greet('Mina')` call the same function, the final value of the parameter differs. When reading code, it is helpful to clearly distinguish between the actual value provided, the default value used when the argument is omitted, and the value specified using a keyword for each function call.

side_cards/python_function_scope_reading.title: Key-value arguments pass values by name.
side_cards/python_function_scope_reading.body: Key-value arguments are a way of passing arguments by parameter name rather than by position. As in `greet(age=10, name='Mina')`, even if the order changes, the value is assigned to the corresponding parameter as long as the name matches.
side_cards/python_function_scope_reading.detail: Keyword arguments pass values based on parameter names, not position. As in `func(age=10, name='kim')`, even if the order changes, the values are assigned to the corresponding parameters as long as the names match. You must map the keyword arguments in the function call to the parameter list in the function definition, and when default values are provided, you must determine which values have been omitted.

side_cards/python_function_scope_reading.title: The function scope problem is read in four steps
side_cards/python_function_scope_reading.body: For function problems, first check where the `def` statement is located, then find the line where the function is actually called. Second, write down how the arguments are passed to the parameters. Third, follow the local variables and the `return` statement inside the function.
side_cards/python_function_scope_reading.detail: The function scope problem can be broken down into four steps for a systematic approach. First, write down the initial values outside the function and locate the actual call line. Next, describe how the arguments are passed to the parameters, and trace the local variables and the return statement within the function. Finally, check what remains in the outer variables and in the console output after the return statement.

side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.title: The `print` statement only counts the lines that are actually displayed on the screen.
side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.body: `print` is an operation that displays a value on the screen. Even if a value is stored in a variable, it will not appear on the screen unless you use `print`.
side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.detail: Conversely, if there are multiple `print` statements, the output will span multiple lines. `print(x + 1)` is not code that changes the value of `x`; rather, it reads the value of `x` and displays the result of the calculation. When working on output problems, first check how many times `print` is executed and what the values inside each `print` statement are.

side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.title: print: Storing expressions and variables are different
side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.when_to_show: When you get confused between `print(x + 1)` and `x = x + 1`
side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.body: print(x + 1) displays the result of the calculation but does not assign a new value to x. x = x + 1 calculates the expression on the right and then assigns the result back to x on the left.
side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.detail: Although the two lines look similar, they produce different results. Beginners might mistakenly assume that if they see 3 on the screen, x has also changed to 3. When reading code, start by distinguishing between screen output and variable assignment.

side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.title: The value received as input is initially a string.
side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.when_to_show: When reviewing input, str, type conversion
side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.body: Even if the user enters a value that looks like a number using `input()`, it is initially a string.
side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.detail: Therefore, if you want to perform `age + 1` after `age = input()`, you need to convert it using something like `int(age)`. Although '3' and 3 look similar on the screen, they behave differently. In input-related problems, you must first check whether the value received via `input()` is still a string or has already been converted to an `int` or `float`.

side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.title: Input validation comes before conversion
side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.body: If we assume that users always enter valid numbers, the program could easily crash. `int(text)` succeeds only when `text` is in numerical format.
side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.detail: Therefore, in real-world apps, we first check if the input is an empty string or handle conversion failures using `try/except`. At the beginner level, it’s more important to understand the concept that input values are strings and require conversion before numerical calculations than to focus on perfect validation. This card isn’t meant to provide the answer to a problem right away; rather, it’s reading material designed to help beginners repeatedly practice how to read Python code.

side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.title: int, float, and str change how values behave
side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.when_to_show: When reviewing int, float, str, type
side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.body: int('3') converts the string '3' into the integer 3. float('3.5') converts it into a value suitable for floating-point calculations.
side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.detail: str(3) converts the number 3 into a string that can be concatenated like text. Conversion functions do more than just change the appearance; they alter how the value behaves in subsequent operations. You should check the data type before and after a calculation.

side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.title: Even if it looks like a number, if it contains quotation marks, it is a string.
side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.when_to_show: When distinguishing between string addition and numeric addition
side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.body: '2' + '3' is not 5, but '23'. If you use quotes, Python treats it as a string rather than a number.
side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.detail: Conversely, 2 + 3 is numerical addition, so it equals 5. Since both may appear to be numbers on the screen, be sure to check your code for quotation marks when solving problems. This habit alone will significantly reduce many beginner mistakes.

side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.title: A comparison expression returns either True or False.
side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.body: "score >= 60" is not code that directly outputs a score; rather, it is a comparison expression that returns either True or False. This boolean value determines which block of code will be executed in the if statement.
side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.detail: While `print(score >= 60)` may display True or False on the screen, `if score >= 60:` does not display anything on the screen; it simply branches the flow of execution. You must distinguish the role of the comparison expression when reading the code. This card is not intended to provide the answer to a problem directly; rather, it is reading material designed to help beginners repeatedly practice how to read Python code.

side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.title: "if active:" is code that uses the value of "active" as a condition.
side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.body: A statement can function as a conditional even without a comparison operator, as in `if active:`. If `active` evaluates to `True`, the `if` block is executed; if it evaluates to `False`, it is skipped.
side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.detail: In beginner-level problems, you should first identify where `active` is defined and what value it has been assigned. Don’t assume a value is `True` just because the variable name sounds plausible; instead, follow the actual value that was assigned to it. This card is not intended to reveal the correct answer to a problem immediately; rather, it is a reading exercise designed to help beginners repeatedly practice how to read Python code.

side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.title: The if/elif/else statements are evaluated one by one from the top down.
side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.body: The `if, elif, else` structure evaluates conditions from top to bottom. Once the first block that evaluates to `True` is executed, the remaining `elif` and `else` blocks are not executed.
side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.detail: Therefore, even though `score >= 60` is `True` when `score` is 85, if the `score >= 80` condition appears earlier in the code, the execution flows to the `80` condition. In problems with multiple conditions, you must always check the order of the conditions. This card is not intended to provide the answer to a problem immediately; rather, it is a reading resource designed to help beginners repeatedly practice reading Python code.

side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.title: Indentation indicates which lines do not meet the condition.
side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.body: Python uses indentation instead of curly braces to delimit code blocks. Lines indented under an `if` statement are executed only when the condition is true.
side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.detail: Lines that are no longer indented are outside the conditional block and can be executed in the subsequent flow regardless of the condition’s outcome. In output exercises, the reason there are more or fewer `print` statements than expected is usually because you missed an indentation boundary. This card is not intended to provide the correct answer immediately, but rather to serve as reading material that helps beginners repeatedly practice how to read Python code.

side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.title: A `for` loop iterates through a list of values, processing them one by one.
side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.when_to_show: When looking at the code "for n in numbers,"
side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.body: "for n in [1, 2, 3]" means that n takes the values 1, 2, and 3 in sequence. The same block of code is executed in each iteration, but the value of n changes.
side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.detail: For the output problem, simply write down what n is in each iteration. For objects that can hold multiple values—such as lists, strings, and `range`—the `for` loop retrieves those values one by one and passes them to the body of the loop. This card is not intended to provide the immediate answer to a problem; rather, it is a reading exercise designed to help beginners repeatedly practice reading Python code.

side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.title: For cumulative variables, the initial value before the loop is important.
side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.when_to_show: When a cumulative total appears after "total = 0"
side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.body: `total = 0` is the initial value used to start the accumulation. When `total = total + n` is executed inside the loop, the current `n` is added to the previous `total` and the result is stored back in `total`.
side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.detail: The final result varies depending on whether the initial value is 0 or 1, an empty string, or an empty list. For accumulation problems, we examine the initial value before the loop, the changes during the loop, and the output value after the loop. This card is not intended to provide the answer to the problem immediately, but rather serves as reading material to help beginners repeatedly practice reading Python code.

side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.title: When using a `while` loop, you need to consider both the condition and the update together.
side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.body: A `while` loop repeats as long as the condition is `True`. Therefore, you must check whether there is a line of code within the loop that updates the condition.
side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.detail: If there is no update—such as `i = i + 1`—the condition may remain `True`, causing the loop to never end. When analyzing a `while` problem, read it in the following order: the initial value of `i`, the condition check, the execution of the body, and the condition check again after the update. This card is not intended to provide the answer to a problem immediately, but rather serves as reading material to help beginners repeatedly practice reading Python code.

side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.title: "break" and "continue" change the flow of a loop
side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.body: `break` terminates the entire loop. `continue` skips only the remainder of the current iteration and moves on to the next one.
side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.detail: Although these two keywords may seem similar, they produce significantly different results. When solving a problem, mark the point where you encounter a `break` as the exit from the loop, and when you encounter a `continue`, check whether the `print` or `append` statements below it are executed in that iteration. This card is not intended to provide the immediate answer to a problem; rather, it is a reading exercise designed to help beginners repeatedly practice reading Python code.

side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.title: Lists remember the order of their values.
side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.body: A list contains multiple values in order. The first value has index 0, and the second value has index 1.
side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.detail: `items[1]` does not refer to the number 1; rather, it is an expression that retrieves the second value. When working with lists, you must not confuse the values themselves with their index numbers. Since the indices may change after using `append` or `insert`, you should reevaluate the list after making changes.

side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.title: `append` adds a value to the end of a list
side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.body: `items.append(x)` adds `x` to the end of the `items` list. It’s better to think of `append` as an operation that modifies the list itself, rather than a function that returns a new list.
side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.detail: That’s why if you run `print(items)` after `append`, you’ll see the added value. Using `append` inside a loop is a common pattern for creating a result list. When used with a conditional statement, it collects only the values that satisfy the condition.

side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.title: len counts the number of values, but it is different from index
side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.body: `len(items)` returns the number of elements in a list. `items[0]` retrieves the first element.
side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.detail: Both are related to lists, but they serve different purposes. For a list with a length of 3, the last index is 2, not 3. Beginners often make mistakes by using the result of `len` directly as an index.

side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.title: A dictionary looks up a value based on a key.
side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.when_to_show: When you see an expression like `data['name']`,
side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.body: A dictionary looks up a value based on a key. This card is designed to reinforce your understanding of how to read keys in actual data code, within the broader concept of dictionaries.
side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.detail: For example, data where multiple items are grouped by labels—such as API responses, JSON, configuration settings, and student grade sheets—is often represented as a dictionary. data['name'] reads the value associated with the "name" key, while scores.get('kim') retrieves the value if the "kim" key exists and handles the case safely if it does not. If you reassign a value to the same key, that key’s value changes, so the final value may differ from the initial one.

side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.title: `get` safely handles keys that do not exist
side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.body: dict.get returns None or a chosen default instead of raising for a missing key. It fits an accumulator such as counts.get(ch, 0), where missing means zero, but it should not hide a required key.
side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.detail: Define whether absence is valid and what the default means.

side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.title: "keys," "values," and "items" are different ways of looking at a dictionary
side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.when_to_show: When reviewing dict, keys, values, items
side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.body: "keys" refers to the list of keys, "values" refers to the list of values, and "items" is used when referring to key-value pairs.
side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.detail: The statement `for key, value in data.items():` iterates through each pair, assigning the key and value to separate variables. When solving dictionary iteration problems, you must first determine what exactly is being iterated over. The meaning of the code changes depending on whether you’re iterating only over keys, only over values, or over both.

side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.title: `split` splits a string into a list
side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.body: `split` is a method that splits a string into multiple parts and creates a list.
side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.detail: `text.split(",")` splits the string at commas, and if you omit the delimiter, as in `text.split()`, it splits the string at whitespace characters. Since the result is a list rather than a single string, you can access elements using an index (e.g., `parts[0]`) or iterate over them using a `for` loop (e.g., `for part in parts:`). The most important point to note is the change in data type before and after the `split` operation.

side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.title: `strip` removes leading and trailing spaces
side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.body: `strip` removes leading and trailing whitespace or line breaks from a string. When reading a line from a file, a line break may be appended at the end, and user input may contain leading or trailing whitespace.
side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.detail: `text.strip()` creates a new, trimmed string. To apply the changes to the original variable, you must reassign it, like `text = text.strip()`. Always check where the result of a string method is assigned.

side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.title: The `join` function concatenates a list of strings into a single string.
side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.body: `join` is a method that combines multiple strings into a single string. Its syntax is not `list.join(...)`, but rather `separator_string.join(list_of_strings)`.
side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.detail: For example, `"-".join(["a", "b", "c"])` produces `"a-b-c"`. The separator string is inserted between each element, and the result is a single string, not a list. A common mistake made by beginners is thinking of `join` as an operation that modifies a list, like `append`.

side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.title: A function consists of an input, a processing step, and an output.
side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.body: Functions typically take input, process it internally, and return a result. A “parameter” is the name used for an input value within a function, while an “argument” is the actual value passed when the function is called.
side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.detail: The “return” statement sends the result of the processing back to the caller. When working on function problems, first locate the call line, map which arguments correspond to which parameters, and then trace the return value. This card is not intended to provide the answer to a problem immediately; rather, it is a reading guide designed to help beginners repeatedly practice reading Python code.

side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.title: Separating `return` and `print` makes functions easier to understand
side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.body: Separating `return` and `print` makes functions easier to understand.
side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.detail: This card is a beginner-level reading practice card designed to help you train yourself to identify the correct answer when you encounter `print` and `return` together within the same function while solving actual problems. `print` displays a value on the screen, while `return` returns a value to the caller. A function that only has `print` and no `return` may display a value on the screen, but the result of the call may be `None`.

side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.title: Scope is a way of distinguishing between names inside and outside a function.
side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.when_to_show: When there are variables with the same name inside and outside a function
side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.body: Scope is a way to distinguish between names inside and outside a function.
side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.detail: This card takes the concept a step further than the “local variable” card; it helps you practice determining which scope’s name to use when the same name appears in multiple locations. Just because you set `x = 3` inside a function doesn’t mean the outer `x` is always affected. Names created within a function are typically looked up first within the function’s internal scope, and to pass a value to the outside, you must check if there is a `return` statement.

side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.title: File processing is different from screen output.
side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.when_to_show: When You Confuse `write` and `print` in Files
side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.body: f.write('hi') writes "hi" to a file. This does not mean that "hi" will appear on the screen.
side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.detail: To display it on the screen, you need to use print('hi'). In file-related problems, you must distinguish between the values stored in the file and those printed to the screen. `read` retrieves the contents of a file as a string, and `write` writes a string to a file.

side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.title: The try/except statement separates the normal flow from the failure flow.
side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.body: Code preceded by `try` is executed first. If it succeeds, the `except` block is not executed.
side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.detail: If it fails and the error type matches the `except` clause, the `except` block is executed. `int('7')` succeeds, but `int('x')` may raise a `ValueError`. When working on exception handling problems, you should analyze the code by separating the two flow paths: what values remain when everything works normally, and what default values are assigned when an error occurs.

side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.title: Class code distinguishes between design diagrams and actual objects.
side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.body: Executing a class statement creates a class object. Calling Dog() normally creates an instance through __new__ and initializes it through __init__; self refers to the instance receiving a method call.
side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.detail: Separate class definition, instance creation, attribute assignment, and method calls.

side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.title: Debugging is the process of comparing expected values with actual values.
side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.body: Debugging isn’t about scolding yourself for writing incorrect code; it’s the process of finding where the actual values differ from what you expected.
side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.detail: Beginners can solve many problems simply by inserting `print` statements to check variable values. Inside loops, observe how values change with each iteration; inside functions, check the parameters and return values. This card isn’t meant to give you the answer right away; rather, it’s a reading guide designed to help beginners repeatedly practice reading Python code.

side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.title: Beginner Code Reading Starts with a Checklist
side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.body: When looking at a mixed problem, first find the output line. Next, trace back through the variables and function calls required for the output.
side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.detail: If there are conditional statements, select only the blocks that are actually executed; if there are loops, note how the values change with each iteration. For lists and dictionaries, check the final remaining values. Just by following this order, code you’ve never seen before becomes much less complicated.

side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.title: Link to external sources using links and summaries rather than copying the content.
side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.when_to_show: When reviewing external resource, license, reading
