side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.body: While good educational websites and official documentation can be helpful for learning, copying long passages of content directly into the app can lead to copyright and quality control issues.
side_cards/python_side_density_reading_p.detail: A safe approach is to write the internal explanations yourself and link external materials to cards that include the title, source, link, difficulty level, related concepts, and reasons why they’re worth reading. This way, learners gain access to more reading material, and the app can maintain the quality of its own explanations. These cards are not meant to provide immediate answers to problems; rather, they serve as reading material to help beginners repeatedly practice reading Python code.

side_cards/python_core_gaps_side_cards_v.title: min, abs, and round make numbers easier to read
side_cards/python_core_gaps_side_cards_v.when_to_show: When finding the minimum value in a list of numbers or reading the difference or the rounded result
side_cards/python_core_gaps_side_cards_v.body: min selects the smallest value, abs returns an absolute value, and round returns a rounded value.
side_cards/python_core_gaps_side_cards_v.detail: They do not mutate the input, but min([]) raises ValueError and binary floating-point rounding may differ from an intuitive decimal rule. Check input type, emptiness, and how the result is used.

side_cards/python_core_gaps_side_cards_v.title: `any` and `isinstance` are tools for checking conditions.
side_cards/python_core_gaps_side_cards_v.when_to_show: When checking whether any of the conditions in the list is true or verifying the type of a value
side_cards/python_core_gaps_side_cards_v.body: `any` and `isinstance` are commonly used tools for checking conditions. `any` evaluates the entire expression to `True` if any one of several conditions is `True`.
side_cards/python_core_gaps_side_cards_v.detail: For example, `any(x > 10 for x in nums)` checks whether there is at least one value greater than 10 in `nums`. `isinstance(value, int)` checks whether `value` is of the `int` data type. When reading code, look first at the loop condition inside `any` and determine which condition, if any, needs to be satisfied.

side_cards/python_core_gaps_side_cards_v.title: `startswith`, `endswith`, and `find` check the position and format of a string
side_cards/python_core_gaps_side_cards_v.when_to_show: When checking file names, prefixes, suffixes, and locations
side_cards/python_core_gaps_side_cards_v.body: `startswith`, `endswith`, and `find` are tools for checking the structure and position of a string.
side_cards/python_core_gaps_side_cards_v.detail: `startswith` returns `True` or `False` depending on whether a string begins with a specific character, and `endswith` returns `True` or `False` depending on whether it ends with a specific character. `find` returns the position where the target string first appears as a number; if it is not found, it returns -1. When reading code, note that `startswith` and `endswith` are often used directly in conditional statements, while `find` is frequently used to determine positions for slicing or branching decisions.

side_cards/python_core_gaps_side_cards_v.title: An f-string embeds a variable's value within a string
side_cards/python_core_gaps_side_cards_v.when_to_show: When outputting a string that contains variable values
side_cards/python_core_gaps_side_cards_v.body: An f-string is a syntax that naturally embeds variable values into a string.
side_cards/python_core_gaps_side_cards_v.detail: When you use curly braces ({}) within a string prefixed with an "f"—such as {name} or {count}—the current value of the variable or the result of a simple calculation is inserted in that position. When reading code, it’s easier to distinguish between characters that remain as-is within the quotes and parts that are evaluated within the curly braces. For example, `f"{user}, {score} points"` reads the current values of `user` and `score` to construct a single string.

side_cards/python_core_gaps_side_cards_v.title: `list.pop` removes a value from the list while retrieving it.
side_cards/python_core_gaps_side_cards_v.when_to_show: When retrieving the last value or a value at a specific position from a list
side_cards/python_core_gaps_side_cards_v.body: list.pop returns and removes the item at an index, using the last item when no index is supplied. An empty list or out-of-range index raises IndexError.
side_cards/python_core_gaps_side_cards_v.detail: Track the list before the call, the returned item, and the list afterward.

side_cards/python_core_gaps_side_cards_v.title: `setdefault` and `dict.pop` modify the state of the dictionary
side_cards/python_core_gaps_side_cards_v.when_to_show: When setting a default value in a dictionary or removing a key
side_cards/python_core_gaps_side_cards_v.body: Both `setdefault` and `dict.pop` are tools that can modify the state of a dictionary. `setdefault(key, default_value)` sets the default value if the key does not exist and returns that value.
side_cards/python_core_gaps_side_cards_v.detail: If the key already exists, it does not set the new default value but simply returns the existing value. This is why it’s often seen in the “create if it doesn’t exist, use the existing one if it does” pattern. `dict.pop(key)` removes the value associated with that key from the dictionary.

side_cards/python_core_gaps_side_cards_v.title: Distinguish between discard, intersection, difference, and set comprehension
side_cards/python_core_gaps_side_cards_v.when_to_show: When safely removing elements from a set or identifying similarities and differences
side_cards/python_core_gaps_side_cards_v.body: A set is a collection of unique values. While a list prioritizes order and position, a set focuses on which values are included and on removing duplicates.
side_cards/python_core_gaps_side_cards_v.detail: `discard` is a safe removal tool that removes a value without raising an error even if the value is absent. `intersection` finds the common values between two sets, while `difference` finds values present in one set but not in the other. A set comprehension is a syntax for creating a new set using loops and conditions, similar to a list comprehension.

side_cards/python_core_gaps_side_cards_v.title: `readline` and `readlines` read files line by line.
side_cards/python_core_gaps_side_cards_v.when_to_show: When looking at code that reads the first line or multiple lines from a file,
side_cards/python_core_gaps_side_cards_v.body: You’ll often encounter `readline` and `readlines` when creating a workflow to read a file line by line.
side_cards/python_core_gaps_side_cards_v.detail: While `read()` fetches the entire file as a single large string, `readline()` reads only one line from the current position and moves on to the next line. This makes them a natural choice for creating a “read one line, check it, and store only the necessary values” workflow within a loop. Since `readlines()` retrieves multiple lines as a list, it’s convenient for quickly reviewing configuration files or sample data that don’t contain many lines.

side_cards/python_core_gaps_side_cards_v.title: "global" indicates that the variable outside the function will be modified directly.
side_cards/python_core_gaps_side_cards_v.when_to_show: When you see code that modifies an outer variable from within a function
side_cards/python_core_gaps_side_cards_v.body: The `global` keyword indicates that you intend to directly modify a variable outside the function. At the beginner level, it’s more important to read code carefully than to use `global` frequently.
side_cards/python_core_gaps_side_cards_v.detail: If you write something like `count = count + 1` inside a function, Python typically treats `count` as a local variable within that function. However, if `global count` is present, it means the function intends to directly modify the outer `count`. When reading code, as soon as you see `global`, you should assume that the value of the outer variable may change even after the function has finished executing.

side_cards/python_foundation_micro_gaps_.title: "max" and "all" produce a single result based on multiple values.
side_cards/python_foundation_micro_gaps_.body: max and all reduce an iterable to one result. max returns the largest item but raises ValueError for an empty iterable; all tests whether every item is truthy and returns True for an empty iterable. Distinguish an item result from a Boolean result and consider empty input.
side_cards/python_foundation_micro_gaps_.when_to_show: This is demonstrated in the beginner-level built-in function card that covers `max()`, `all()`, maximum values, and whether all conditions are met.

side_cards/python_foundation_micro_gaps_.title: `extend` and `insert` are methods that directly modify a list.
side_cards/python_foundation_micro_gaps_.body: Both `extend()` and `insert()` are methods that directly modify the state of a list. `extend(other)` iterates through the elements in `other` one by one and appends them to the end of the list. Therefore, `items.extend([3, 4])` does not insert a single list named `[3, 4]`, but rather adds 3 and 4 individually.
side_cards/python_foundation_micro_gaps_.when_to_show: This is demonstrated in problems involving adding multiple values to a list or inserting values in the middle of a list.
side_cards/python_foundation_micro_gaps_.detail: `extend` and `insert` are methods that directly modify a list. `extend([3, 4])` does not add an entire list; instead, it appends 3 and 4 to the end of the list, respectively. `insert(index, value)` inserts a value before the specified position, pushing the subsequent elements to the right. You must specify the list before the call, the value to be added, and the list after the call.

side_cards/python_foundation_micro_gaps_.title: raise, TypeError, and KeyError are signals that reveal failures rather than hiding them
side_cards/python_foundation_micro_gaps_.body: `raise` is a statement that causes the code to throw an exception directly. It explicitly signals a failure—such as `raise ValueError(...)`—when a value is incorrect or when continuing would cause a more serious problem. A `TypeError` often occurs when a value’s type or usage is incorrect.
side_cards/python_foundation_micro_gaps_.when_to_show: This is shown on the card that asks about exception types, direct errors, dict key errors, and data type errors.
side_cards/python_foundation_micro_gaps_.detail: `raise` is a statement that explicitly signals a failure in the code, and the error type indicates the cause of the problem. `TypeError` typically occurs due to data type or usage issues, `KeyError` occurs when attempting to access a key that doesn’t exist in a dictionary, and `ValueError` often results from a failed value conversion. Rather than hiding errors, these should be viewed as signals that clearly indicate where and why the program stopped.

side_cards/python_foundation_micro_gaps_.title: A traceback starts with the last line of the error and reads back from the line of code immediately above it.
side_cards/python_foundation_micro_gaps_.body: A traceback is a log that shows the path through which Python encountered an error. It might look intimidating at first, but as a beginner, you just need to follow a specific order when reading it. First, look at the last line.
side_cards/python_foundation_micro_gaps_.when_to_show: This is shown on a card that asks about error logs, tracebacks, and the debugging process.
side_cards/python_foundation_micro_gaps_.detail: A traceback is a log that shows the path where an error occurred. Even if it’s long, start by looking at the error type and message on the last line, then check the filename, line number, and actual code line immediately above it. If it’s a KeyError, check for a missing key; if it’s a TypeError, check the data type; if it’s a ValueError, check the conversion value—and narrow down the issue by printing the actual values.

side_cards/python_foundation_micro_gaps_.title: assert and pytest help you develop the habit of comparing expected values with actual values
side_cards/python_foundation_micro_gaps_.body: assert is useful for internal assumptions and test expectations, while pytest collects tests that follow its discovery rules. Python optimization can remove assert statements, so never rely on them for required user-input validation or production behavior. Passing tests guarantee only the cases and properties that were written.
side_cards/python_foundation_micro_gaps_.when_to_show: This is shown on a card that asks about assert, pytest, expected/actual, regression testing, and verification routines.

side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.title: Accessibility UI considers the keyboard, screen readers, and semantic structure together
side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.body: When reviewing accessibility UI code, we don’t just look at the visual appearance; we also verify whether users can navigate using a keyboard, whether screen readers can interpret the content, and whether status changes are effectively communicated to the user.
side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.when_to_show: Let's take a look at accessibility, keyboard navigation, screen readers, semantic HTML, and UI state in the cards.
side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.detail: Accessibility UI is a criterion for determining whether users can actually interact with and understand the interface, rather than just how it looks on screen. We evaluate keyboard navigation, focus indicators, meaningful tags, screen reader guidance, and error message links together. In learning apps, a lack of accessibility can disrupt the problem-solving process itself. Therefore, we prioritize checkability and guidance over visual effects.

side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.title: Analysis and personal information are interpreted in terms of data minimization and the consent process.
side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.body: Analytics code logs data to better understand user behavior, but you must first determine what information is permissible to store. In the context of privacy, this involves considering consent, data minimization, anonymous identifiers, aggregated metrics, and the ability to delete data or opt out.
side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.when_to_show: We'll cover these topics together in the card that addresses learning records, event analysis, privacy protection, opt-in/opt-out, and anonymous IDs.
side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.detail: Analytics code can help improve learning, but you must first determine what data is permissible to store. Focus on the purpose of data collection, minimum data collection, anonymization, consent and withdrawal, and the possibility of deletion rather than event names. For security, personal notes and sensitive inputs should be kept separate from analytics events. It is also advisable to handle necessary metrics, such as accuracy rates, at the aggregate level to minimize the risk of personal identification.

side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.title: i18n reads the string keys and the locale fallback flow
side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.body: The i18n code uses a structure that separates screen text into keys and translation data, rather than hard-coding it directly into the code. “Locale” refers to the language and regional format selected by the user, while “fallback” is the process of safely reverting to the default language when a translation is unavailable.
side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.when_to_show: We'll cover language switching, translation dictionaries, message keys, locales, and fallback languages together in this card.
side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.detail: The i18n process involves separating on-screen text from the code and managing it using keys and translation data. It covers locale selection, fallback languages, handling missing translations, and verifying date and number formats. This structure is crucial even for apps primarily in Korean, in case English descriptions need to be added later. It also takes into account how button lengths and the meanings of technical terms vary by language.

side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.title: The learning UX should lead to review, habit formation, and the next action.
side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.body: Learning UX design isn’t just about displaying scores; it’s a flow that guides users on what to do next. When terms like “streak,” “daily goal,” “review queue,” and “weak concept” come up, we examine how learning motivation and review timing are linked. A good learning app doesn’t scold users for missed questions but instead offers a path to try again.
side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.when_to_show: Let's take a look at the cards that cover the review queue, study streak, goal adjustments, weak concepts, and recommended next cards.
side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.detail: Learning UX shouldn’t end with simply displaying a score; it should lead to the next review action. Features such as streaks, daily goals, review queues, and weak concepts help create a habit loop for users. When reading code, consider the combination of progress tracking, recommendation criteria, reward messages, and retry paths.

side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.title: Mobile UX is evaluated based on small screens, finger gestures, and reading flow.
side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.body: Mobile UX design isn’t just about scaling down a desktop screen. You need to check whether elements are large enough to tap with a finger, whether key buttons are accessible with one hand, and whether code blocks remain intact on small screens.
side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.when_to_show: Let's take a look at the cards covering mobile screens, touch targets, responsive layouts, and code block widths.
side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.detail: Mobile UX isn’t simply a matter of scaling down a desktop screen; it’s about maintaining the learning flow while adapting to small screens and finger-based input. Check touch sizes, button spacing, the horizontal width of code blocks, scrolling, and state preservation after screen rotation. If the reading flow is interrupted, it can lead to users abandoning the learning process. In particular, code examples must be checked for both horizontal scrolling and line breaks.

side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.title: PWAs and offline workflows are determined by cache, installation, and update status
side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.body: PWA code not only makes web pages look like apps but also includes a structure that allows them to function to some extent even when offline. Service workers and caches help ensure fast execution, but if outdated files remain, new versions may not be reflected.
side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.when_to_show: We'll cover these topics together in the cards on PWA installation, service workers, cache busting, offline-first, and handling synchronization conflicts.
side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.detail: The PWA and offline workflow are structured so that service workers, caches, versions, update banners, and offline notifications work together. While caching improves speed, it can leave outdated files behind, so version indicators and refresh prompts are crucial. You must also check for synchronization conflicts with stored data.

side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.title: A recovery design is a structure that allows operations to resume after a failure.
side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.body: Recovery design does not assume that errors will never occur; rather, it is an approach that allows users to resume their tasks in the event of a failure. “Fallback” refers to an alternative path, “retry” means to try again, and “safe default” refers to a default value that is not risky when the actual value is unknown.
side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.when_to_show: We'll cover these topics—fallback, retry, partial failure, safe default, and error recovery—together on the corresponding card.
side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.detail: Recovery design is an architecture that does not assume failure will never occur, but rather enables users to resume their operations after a failure. It distinguishes between fallback, retry, safe default, error state, and recovery action. When reading code, check whether it hides failures, explains them, or routes users to a retry or alternative path.

side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.title: Data governance examines the source, license, and reuse conditions separately.
side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.body: In data governance, it is more important to document the conditions under which data can be used than to simply obtain the data. Being “publicly available” is not the same as being “commercially reusable,” and the ability to modify the data and the requirement to attribute the source must also be considered separately.
side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.when_to_show: Let's take a look at the cards covering copyright, public data, source attribution, open licenses, and derived data.
side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.detail: The core of data governance lies not in acquiring data, but in documenting the conditions under which it can be used. Consider the following criteria separately: whether the data is public, whether it can be reused, whether the source must be cited, whether it can be modified, and what exclusion criteria apply. In educational apps or submitted materials, citing sources and licenses builds credibility. While using data from unknown sources may be convenient, it can increase the risk of legal issues later on when the data is incorporated into a service.

side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.title: The card creation pipeline is divided into the drafting, review, and deployment stages.
side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.body: The card creation pipeline is structured to divide the process of adding a new issue into the stages of creation, review, validation, and deployment. “Required fields” are the minimum requirements to ensure the card functions correctly in the app, while “duplicate checks” prevent similar issues or descriptions from being duplicated.
side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.when_to_show: We'll cover this together in the card that covers card creation, field validation, duplicate checks, the review workflow, and the publish step.
side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.detail: The card creation pipeline consists of the following stages: creation, validation of required fields, duplicate check, human review, and version freezing. As more new cards are added, the generation scripts and validators must serve as quality gates. Traceable steps are necessary to make it easier to identify the cause of errors later on. You should also document which cards were changed in each version.

side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.title: AI tool code distinguishes between training, inference, evaluation, and resource usage
side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.body: When reading AI tool code, you should break it down into the stages of training a model and running a pre-trained model. Terms like “supervised learning,” “LoRA,” “quantization,” “checkpoint,” and “inference” indicate that data, models, and hardware resources are interconnected.
side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.when_to_show: Let's take a look at the cards covering AI training methods, torch/cuda, attention masks, checkpoints, quantization, and inference.
side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.detail: When reviewing the code for an AI tool, you should analyze the sections for training, inference, evaluation, and resource usage separately. Data is input, passes through the tokenizer and tensor transformations, is transferred to the device, and then the model generates the results. GPU, VRAM, batch size, checkpoints, and quantization are directly linked to executability and cost.

side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.title: OCR and document extraction are part of the image-to-PDF-to-text conversion workflow.
side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.body: OCR and document extraction code is a process that converts documents or images visible to humans into text that a program can read. PIL and OpenCV are more focused on opening and preprocessing images, while pytesseract and EasyOCR are more focused on recognizing text within images.
side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.when_to_show: Let's take a look at the cards covering image reading, OCR, PDF text extraction, OpenCV, PyMuPDF, and pdfplumber.
side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.detail: OCR and document extraction are processes that convert images or PDFs into text that a program can handle. Check the input format, preprocessing, extraction engine, failure page logs, and output format in that order. The approach may vary depending on whether the PDF is text-based or a scanned image. For documents containing a mix of tables and images, page-by-page quality logs are also required.

side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.title: Asynchrony and concurrency are structures that determine how to divide up tasks that involve waiting.
side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.body: Asynchronous code is a structure that allows other tasks to proceed while waiting, rather than pausing to process long-running tasks sequentially. `async` and `await` are indicators of asynchronous flow, while `gather` is a pattern for waiting for multiple tasks simultaneously.
side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.when_to_show: We'll cover this together in the card that compares async/await, asyncio.gather, semaphores, workers, and threads/processes/async.
side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.detail: Asynchrony and concurrency are frameworks for determining how to divide and limit waiting tasks. `async`, `await`, and `gather` are flow mechanisms that handle waiting times concurrently, while semaphores and rate limits prevent too many tasks from running simultaneously. It is important to distinguish between accelerating computations and reducing network wait times.

side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.title: Authentication and authorization are discussed in terms of identity verification, tokens, and request headers.
side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.body: Authentication verifies identity; authorization limits allowed actions. Inspect token or session storage, validation, expiration, and failure responses. CORS and preflight are browser cross-origin request policies, not substitutes for identity or permission checks.
side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.when_to_show: We'll cover these topics together in the cards that cover OAuth, Bearer tokens, authorization headers, CORS, and the login flow.

side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.title: Architecture code focuses first on boundaries, responsibilities, and data flow
side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.body: When it comes to architectural code, it’s more important to look at how files and modules share responsibilities than to focus on a single line of code. The service layer groups functional flows, the domain model represents core data, and DTOs define the format of data passing between layers.
side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.when_to_show: We'll look at these together in the cards covering service layer, DTO, interface, boundary, dependency injection, and architecture diagram.
side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.detail: Architectural code focuses first on the responsibilities of each layer and the flow of data, rather than on individual lines of code. It examines where requests enter the system, how they are transformed into DTOs or domain models, and where validation, storage, and display are separated. The service layer and boundaries serve as mechanisms to minimize the scope of impact from changes.

side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.title: CSV and data cleaning are understood in terms of rows, columns, missing values, and transformation flows
side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.body: The CSV and pandas code reads table data as rows and columns and organizes it into the required format. DictReader uses header names as keys, allowing each row to be treated like a dictionary. When you encounter terms like `read_csv`, `sep`, `TSV`, or `delimiter`, you need to check what delimiter is used to separate the file.
side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.when_to_show: We'll cover this together in the card that covers CSV/TSV, pandas `read_csv`, missing values, rows/columns, and rolling means.
side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.detail: When working with CSV files and data cleaning, you should review the file format, delimiters, headers, rows and columns, missing values, type conversions, and storage results in that order. While tools like DictReader and pandas make it easier to handle tabular data, errors often occur with column names and the handling of NaN values. You must verify the data structure before performing any calculations.

side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.title: File operations consider the path, backups, temporary files, and atomic saves together
side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.body: File operation code must consider not only opening and writing files, but also the path from which it is executed, whether existing files can be overwritten, and how to recover in case of failure. Confusing absolute and relative paths can result in modifying files in the wrong location.
side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.when_to_show: We'll cover this together in the cards that deal with paths, folder creation, backup files, temporary files, atomic writes, and safe patches.
side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.detail: When working with files, you must consider the following sequence: path, backup, temporary files, atomic saves, verification, and cleanup. A safe patching script must not corrupt the original file if it fails. It is important to get into the habit of verifying that the script uses relative paths, overwrites existing files, and has a recovery mechanism for intermediate failures. After saving, use `diff` and verification results to confirm that only the intended files have been modified.

side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.title: Refactoring is the process of changing the structure of a program to make it easier to read while preserving its functionality.
side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.body: Refactoring is the process of making the structure of code easier to read and modify without changing its behavior. Duplicate code increases the number of places that need to be modified, and poor naming hides the code’s intent.
side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.when_to_show: We'll cover these topics together in the cards that address refactoring, removing duplication, naming conventions, separating configuration, backward compatibility, and patch risk.
side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.detail: Refactoring is the process of making code easier to read and modify while preserving its functionality. We’ll look at removing duplication, naming conventions, separating configuration, using smaller functions, and backward compatibility. Maintainability is a criterion that asks whether code that’s currently running will remain safe after the next modification. Therefore, patches that change the structure without verifying the results are risky.

side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.title: System concepts are understood by comparing the differences in roles, such as sensors, processes, and ontologies.
side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.body: The System Concepts card goes beyond Python syntax to cover the background knowledge needed to understand real-world systems. Sensors observe values, actuators generate actions, and controllers make decisions based on inputs. Noise, drift, and synchronization illustrate the reality that data is not always clean or received simultaneously.
side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.when_to_show: Let's look at them together on the comparison cards for sensors/actuators/controllers, noise/drift/sync, OWL/SHACL/SPARQL, and threads/processes.
side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.detail: When learning system concepts, it’s better to understand them by comparing the roles each element plays within the system rather than simply memorizing the terms. Terms such as “thread,” “process,” “async,” and “ontology” are also best understood in terms of their position and role.

side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.title: Other runtime product patterns attempt to connect features to user flows
side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.body: The "Other Runtime Product Patterns" card is a supplementary card designed to group together runtime product features—such as Notes, Search, Progress, Save, Performance, and UI Feedback—that are not broken down into separate sub-cards.
side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.when_to_show: View user notes, search filters, saved settings, progress backups, performance metrics, and dashboard cards all in one place.
side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.detail: A runtime product pattern is a card that connects the flow of a user opening an app, entering values, experiencing state changes, viewing results, and continuing from there. Since it serves as a fallback for product features that are not broken down into separate detail cards, it allows you to review input, state changes, saving, recovery, display, and validation criteria all at once.

side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.title: Notes and bookmarks are features that allow learners to mark where they left off.
side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.body: The note and bookmark features are runtime functions that allow users to revisit important cards or confusing concepts later. When terms such as “bookmark,” “favorite,” “user note,” “note editor,” and “auto-save note” appear, they should be viewed not as simple save buttons, but as mechanisms that help users retain what they’ve learned.
side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.when_to_show: You can view runtime product features, user status, search and filters, notes, progress, performance, and UI feedback all together on a single card.
side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.detail: Notes and bookmarks are features that allow users to return to important cards or concepts they’re unsure about. Check the save key, card ID linking, auto-save timing, the distinction between deleted and empty notes, and restoration after refreshing. Since personal notes can be sensitive, it’s safer to separate them from analytics events. If linked to search and filter functions, review the entire process of retrieving information as well.

side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.title: As the number of cards increases, search, filter, and sort features help you find a learning path.
side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.body: Search, filtering, and sorting are features that help users quickly find the learning items they need as the number of cards increases.
side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.when_to_show: You can view runtime product features, user status, search and filters, notes, progress, performance, and UI feedback all together on a single card.
side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.detail: Search, filter, and sort are features that help users find the learning paths they need as the number of cards increases. Check the following: search term normalization, tag and level filters, AND/OR conditions, sort criteria, handling of empty results, and display of current conditions. When conditions change, the page layout and scroll position may also adjust accordingly. Prompts displayed when no results are found are also important for maintaining the learning flow.

side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.title: Progress, Scores, and Dashboards Should Guide Learners Toward Their Next Steps
side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.body: A progress tracker and dashboard are ineffective if they merely show how much a user has reviewed. When terms like “progress tracking,” “mastery score,” “wrong answer log,” “mistake note,” and “export progress” appear, you’re looking at a system that links that data to the next review action.
side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.when_to_show: You can view runtime product features, user status, search and filters, notes, progress, performance, and UI feedback all together on a single card.
side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.detail: Progress, Scores, and the Dashboard are features that aggregate original learning records and translate them into the next review action. They categorize data into the number of completed items, accuracy rates, weak concepts, recent incorrect answers, and cards indicating the need for review. Rather than simply displaying a lot of numbers, it’s important to provide a flow that tells users exactly what they need to review right now. The export feature must also specify the scope of the individual’s learning history.

side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.title: Saving and restoring state keeps the user's workflow uninterrupted.
side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.body: Runtime saving and state restoration are features that allow users to continue where they left off even after refreshing or reopening the app. When terms such as `localStorage`, `auto save`, `debounce`, `state restore`, `settings`, and `user data` come up, examine how the screen state is linked to the saved data.
side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.when_to_show: You can view runtime product features, user status, search and filters, notes, progress, performance, and UI feedback all together on a single card.
side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.detail: Saving and restoring state is a feature that allows users to continue their learning progress even after reopening the app. We’ll look at localStorage, JSON parsing, default values, version changes, migration, fallback, and debounce together. Even if something goes wrong, the app must revert to a safe default, and it must distinguish between settings changed by the user and the default values.

side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.title: Large list performance is evaluated by considering rendering, pagination, and feedback together
side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.body: If there are too many cards, the app may slow down—even if the features work as intended—which can disrupt the learning flow. Whenever terms like pagination, virtual list, large list, rendering, loading indicator, or performance budget come up, check how much content is being displayed on the screen at any given time.
side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.when_to_show: You can view runtime product features, user status, search and filters, notes, progress, performance, and UI feedback all together on a single card.
side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.detail: When evaluating the performance of large lists, it is important to distinguish between the total number of data items and the number of items actually rendered on the screen. Pagination and virtual lists are methods for reducing the rendering cost of long lists. When used in conjunction with search and filters, you should also check the cache, loading indicators, and mobile scroll responsiveness. Performance improvements aim not only for speed but also for a seamless user experience.

side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.title: UI flow and feedback help users understand their current status.
side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.body: UI flow and feedback are features that help users understand what is happening when they press a button. When terms such as “loading state,” “empty state,” “error state,” “event handler,” “click,” “feedback,” and “user action” come up, examine how the screen state responds to user actions.
side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.when_to_show: You can view runtime product features, user status, search and filters, notes, progress, performance, and UI feedback all together on a single card.
side_cards/python_zero_visible_support_s.detail: UI flow and feedback are read as a single, continuous sequence linking user actions, state changes, and screen displays. Button clicks or changes in input lead to states such as “loading,” “empty,” “error,” or “success.” A good UI lets users know what they’re waiting for and what they can do next if something goes wrong.

side_cards/python_dev_environment_practi.title: The terminal is a window for entering commands
side_cards/python_dev_environment_practi.body: A terminal is a window through which you send text-based commands to a computer. PowerShell, CMD, and Bash differ in appearance and some of their commands, but they all execute commands and operate based on the current folder.
side_cards/python_dev_environment_practi.detail: Beginners should first check which folder they are running commands from. Even the same command can target different files depending on the location. Checking the path displayed in the command prompt, the `cd` or `Set-Location` commands, and the file path can help reduce many execution errors. Checking your current location before running a command is essential.

side_cards/python_dev_environment_practi.title: Current folder and path
side_cards/python_dev_environment_practi.body: The current folder is the base directory from which the command is executed. An error indicating that a file cannot be found may occur not because the file actually does not exist, but because the current folder is different. Therefore, check the path before executing the command.
side_cards/python_dev_environment_practi.detail: In PowerShell, you use `Set-Location` to change directories. Relative paths are interpreted relative to the current directory, while absolute paths specify the full location starting from the drive or root. If you cannot find a validation script or JSON file, you should first verify that the current directory is the project root. It is especially important to check the location before running the script.

side_cards/python_dev_environment_practi.title: What are Ubuntu and WSL?
side_cards/python_dev_environment_practi.body: Ubuntu is a Linux distribution, and WSL is a feature that allows you to run a Linux environment within Windows. Although it is distinct from Python itself, you’ll often come across it when reading documentation on server and AI development.
side_cards/python_dev_environment_practi.detail: Learning Python itself is different from learning Ubuntu. However, since documentation for servers, AI tools, CUDA, and deployment is often written with Linux in mind, familiarity with Ubuntu or WSL makes it easier to read development documentation. On Windows, PowerShell is frequently used, while on Ubuntu or WSL, Bash and the `apt` command are commonly used.

side_cards/python_dev_environment_practi.title: sudo runs with administrator privileges
side_cards/python_dev_environment_practi.body: In Linux, `sudo` means to run a command with administrative privileges. While it may be necessary for tasks that affect the entire system, it is not a one-size-fits-all solution that should be used with every command.
side_cards/python_dev_environment_practi.detail: Tasks that affect the entire computer, such as installing packages or configuring the system, may require `sudo`. Conversely, if you force a solution to a Python package issue in a project folder using `sudo`, it can cause file ownership or permissions to become corrupted. When an error occurs, you should first check whether the task requires elevated privileges.

side_cards/python_dev_environment_practi.title: apt and pip are used for different types of installations.
side_cards/python_dev_environment_practi.body: apt installs Ubuntu system packages, while pip installs Python packages. Although both look like installation commands, they differ in what they install and their scope. In a virtual environment, check the pip installation as well.
side_cards/python_dev_environment_practi.detail: System tools such as `git` and `build-essential` are often installed using `apt`. Python libraries such as `requests`, `numpy`, and `pandas` are installed using `pip`. In projects that use virtual environments, Python packages are typically installed using the command `python -m pip` to ensure they are compatible with the current environment.

side_cards/python_dev_environment_practi.title: A virtual environment is a project-specific Python environment
side_cards/python_dev_environment_practi.body: A virtual environment separates package installation locations and reduces project version conflicts. Activation is a PATH convenience, not a requirement; the environment interpreter can be called directly. Record dependency versions and supported Python, then run tests to reproduce the setup more closely.

side_cards/python_dev_environment_practi.title: requirements.txt is a list of dependencies
side_cards/python_dev_environment_practi.body: requirements.txt lists package requirements for pip; it is not automatically a complete environment lock. Consider pinning, Python and OS constraints, and transitive dependencies. Verify the installation by running the program or tests.

side_cards/python_dev_environment_practi.title: Basic Git Workflow: Check → Commit → Push → Upload
side_cards/python_dev_environment_practi.body: Git is a tool for tracking changes to code. Typically, you use `status` to check the current status, `add` to stage changes, `commit` to record them, and `push` to upload them to a remote repository like GitHub.
side_cards/python_dev_environment_practi.detail: `git add` is not yet a final commit; it is the step where you select the files to include in this commit. `git commit` creates a local commit, and `git push` sends it to the remote repository. For beginners, it’s important to get into the habit of frequently checking `status` to see which files have been modified and what to commit.

side_cards/python_dev_environment_practi.title: "clone" and "pull" retrieve code
side_cards/python_dev_environment_practi.body: clone creates a new local repository from a remote. pull fetches remote changes and integrates them into the current branch, so it is not simply overwriting files with 'the latest version' and may conflict. Check the current branch and uncommitted work first.

side_cards/python_dev_environment_practi.title: CUDA is a gateway to NVIDIA GPUs
side_cards/python_dev_environment_practi.body: nvidia-smi reports GPU and driver state, while torch.cuda.is_available() tests whether the selected PyTorch environment can use CUDA. A system CUDA toolkit is not always required because a PyTorch build may include runtime components. Also inspect tensor/model devices and VRAM.

side_cards/python_import_debug_beginner_.title: The `import` statement locates a module by its name.
side_cards/python_import_debug_beginner_.body: The `import` statement does not search for files just anywhere. Python looks for module names in specific locations, such as the current execution location, the project folder, and the locations of installed packages.
side_cards/python_import_debug_beginner_.detail: Beginners should first check “which folder they are running Python from” and “whether the file or package they are trying to import is visible from that location.” Import errors are often caused by location issues rather than syntax. Since the result of an import can vary depending on where the file is executed—even if it’s the same file—it’s important to get into the habit of running Python from the project root.

side_cards/python_import_debug_beginner_.title: Order of Checks for ModuleNotFoundError
side_cards/python_import_debug_beginner_.body: A `ModuleNotFoundError` means that Python could not find the module with that name.
side_cards/python_import_debug_beginner_.detail: Common causes include the module not being installed, a different virtual environment, an incorrect execution path, or a typo in the module name. First, check for typos, and then verify whether it was installed in the current virtual environment. If it’s a module within the project, check the current folder and the import path.

side_cards/python_import_debug_beginner_.title: The installation environment and the runtime environment may differ.
side_cards/python_import_debug_beginner_.body: If you run `pip install` but the import fails, you should suspect that the Python version used for installation is different from the one you're running.
side_cards/python_import_debug_beginner_.detail: It's a good idea to check whether you're using the same interpreter by running `python -m pip`. You may have installed it without starting the virtual environment, or you may have installed it using pip from a different Python installation. Therefore, for beginners, it’s safer to get into the habit of using `python -m pip install` instead of just `pip install`.

side_cards/python_import_debug_beginner_.title: My file name might obscure the library
side_cards/python_import_debug_beginner_.body: If you create files such as `requests.py` or `json.py` within your project, your files may be loaded before the actual libraries, which can cause import errors. Rename the files and check the cache folder as well.
side_cards/python_import_debug_beginner_.detail: It’s easiest to think of this phenomenon as “shadowing.” If you encounter a strange error after running `import requests`, you should check whether there’s a file or folder with the same name in the current directory. In particular, if you create a file named `requests.py` and then run `import requests`, the system may load your file first instead of the external package, so it’s safer to avoid using filenames that match the library name.

side_cards/python_import_debug_beginner_.title: A package is a folder that groups modules together
side_cards/python_import_debug_beginner_.body: A module is typically a single .py file, while a package is a folder that contains multiple modules. The __init__.py file is often used as a marker to indicate that the folder should be treated as a Python package.
side_cards/python_import_debug_beginner_.detail: Although Python often works without an __init__.py file these days, it’s easier for beginners to understand if you include one to clearly define the package structure. In particular, when importing modules from within a folder—such as app/helpers.py—it makes the project structure easier to read by indicating that the app folder is a single unit.

side_cards/python_import_debug_beginner_.title: sys.path and PYTHONPATH are for final verification
side_cards/python_import_debug_beginner_.body: `sys.path` is a list of paths that Python checks when importing modules. `PYTHONPATH` is an environment variable that adds paths to that list; beginners should only check it as a last resort and do so with caution.
side_cards/python_import_debug_beginner_.detail: For beginners, rather than immediately modifying `sys.path` or `PYTHONPATH`, it’s safer to first check whether the script is running from the project root, whether you’re in the correct virtual environment, and whether there are any file name conflicts. Forcing a path addition can make it difficult to reproduce the issue on another computer later. Even if it seems like a temporary fix, it can mask underlying issues with the project structure, so it should be used only as a last resort.

side_cards/python_mutable_default_beginn.title: Default arguments are initialized once when a function is created.
side_cards/python_mutable_default_beginn.body: Python's default arguments are not values that are created anew each time a function is called. They are initialized once when the function is defined and can be reused in subsequent calls.
side_cards/python_mutable_default_beginn.detail: Therefore, you should be especially careful when reading the default values of lists and dictionaries. Values that don’t change, such as numbers or strings, rarely cause major problems. However, if you use a value whose contents can change—such as a list or a dict—as a default argument, changes made in a previous call may carry over to the next call.

side_cards/python_mutable_default_beginn.title: The default value of a list can be shared
side_cards/python_mutable_default_beginn.body: If you pass a list directly as the default argument, it may appear as though the same list is being reused when the function is called multiple times.
side_cards/python_mutable_default_beginn.detail: Therefore, if you assume that a new empty list is created each time the function is called, you may misinterpret the results. Beginners often assume, “Since the function was called again, it will start with an empty list.” However, if the default `list` is reused, the values appended during the first call remain in the result of the second call, leading to unexpected output. This issue becomes a harder-to-find bug in projects with multiple functions intertwined than in code that is short.

side_cards/python_mutable_default_beginn.title: Pass "None" as an argument and create a new list inside the function
side_cards/python_mutable_default_beginn.body: If you need to change the default value, set the default argument to `None` and use a pattern where you create a new list or dictionary inside the function.
side_cards/python_mutable_default_beginn.detail: This approach helps reduce the problem of values being shared surreptitiously between calls. If you start with `def f(items=None):` and then handle it with `if items is None: items = []`, you can create a new list each time the function is called, if necessary. This helps reduce the problem of values from previous calls being mixed into subsequent calls.

side_cards/python_mutable_default_beginn.title: Changing a value within a function can affect the subsequent flow of the program.
side_cards/python_mutable_default_beginn.body: Operations within a function that modify existing objects—such as `list.append`—can affect the state outside the function or the results of subsequent calls.
side_cards/python_mutable_default_beginn.detail: Therefore, you should check not only the function’s return value but also whether the object has been modified. This kind of change can be called a side effect. Beginners tend to focus only on the return value, but in reality, they also need to check whether the original list has been modified within the function.

side_cards/python_oop_gap_beginner_side_.title: Classes are useful for grouping related data and behavior together.
side_cards/python_oop_gap_beginner_side_.body: Classes are not something you should use indiscriminately. They are best used as a single design unit when data of the same type and the actions that handle that data are repeated.
side_cards/python_oop_gap_beginner_side_.detail: Therefore, it is important to have criteria for determining whether to group only the data or to include the actions as well. For example, if a `Card` has properties such as `title`, `level`, and `answer`, and you also need to check whether an answer is correct, grouping them into a class makes the code easier to read. Conversely, if you’re simply calculating a single value once, a function alone may be sufficient.

side_cards/python_oop_gap_beginner_side_.title: Distinguishing Between Instance Variables and Class Variables
side_cards/python_oop_gap_beginner_side_.body: An instance variable is a value held by each individual object, while a class variable is defined at the class level and can be used as a value shared by multiple objects.
side_cards/python_oop_gap_beginner_side_.detail: It is important to distinguish between the two to avoid confusing object-specific values with shared values. Beginners should first treat values attached to `self`—such as `self.name`—as instance variables. Conversely, values defined directly within a class may be default settings or shared values referenced by all objects, so you must be careful about whether they are shared when modifying them.

side_cards/python_oop_gap_beginner_side_.title: Inheritance is a relationship in which a child inherits features from its parent.
side_cards/python_oop_gap_beginner_side_.body: Inheritance is a structure in which a child class inherits and uses the attributes and methods of a parent class.
side_cards/python_oop_gap_beginner_side_.detail: Common functionality is placed in the parent class, while the child class can modify only the parts that differ. As a beginner, you should start by understanding the process of inheriting functionality from the parent class. For example, if the `Animal` class has a `speak` method and `Dog` inherits from `Animal`, then `Dog` objects can also use `speak`.

side_cards/python_oop_gap_beginner_side_.title: "override" and "super" are used to modify or extend parent functionality
side_cards/python_oop_gap_beginner_side_.body: "Override" refers to redefining a method in a child class that has the same name as one in the parent class. "super()" is used when you want to use the parent class's implementation.
side_cards/python_oop_gap_beginner_side_.detail: These two concepts often appear together in an inheritance hierarchy when a child class modifies or extends the functionality of a parent class. If a child class wants to completely rewrite a parent class’s functionality, it can recreate a method with the same name. When you want to add only certain parts while retaining the parent’s initialization or common processing, you’ll see code like `super().__init__`.

side_cards/python_oop_gap_beginner_side_.title: dataclass makes it easy to create classes that group data together
side_cards/python_oop_gap_beginner_side_.body: @dataclass is a tool that reduces repetitive code—such as __init__—in data-centric classes. Simply defining the fields makes it easier to create objects.
side_cards/python_oop_gap_beginner_side_.detail: Therefore, it is well-suited for models that hold values, such as cards, settings, and progress states. A structure that holds values such as `title`, `level`, and `answer`—like `Card`—can be a good fit for `dataclass`. It’s important to understand that `dataclass` is not a syntax that replaces all aspects of OOP, but rather a convenience feature designed to make classes used for storing data concise and easy to read.

side_cards/python_oop_gap_beginner_side_.title: A class isn't always the right answer
side_cards/python_oop_gap_beginner_side_.body: While classes are great for organizing structure, there’s no need to turn every simple calculation or one-time task into a class. In fact, functions or dictionaries and lists may be easier to read for simple tasks.
side_cards/python_oop_gap_beginner_side_.detail: Beginners should first see if they can solve the problem using functions, dictionaries, or lists, and consider using a class only when the same data structure and related behavior recur. Using classes too early can increase the number of files and the complexity of filenames, which can actually make the code harder to read. Therefore, classes shouldn’t be used just because they look cool; instead, they should be viewed as a tool to be used when there’s a need to organize recurring structures.

side_cards/python_exception_traceback_be.title: Check the traceback starting from the last line.
side_cards/python_exception_traceback_be.body: A traceback shows the flow of the program from top to bottom where the error occurred.
side_cards/python_exception_traceback_be.detail: Beginners should first check the error type and message on the last line, and then work their way back up through the file and line numbers. The last line usually displays the error type—such as `ValueError` or `TypeError`—along with a human-readable message. Then, by following the `File` and `line` information at the top, you can narrow down where the problem originated—in which file and on which line.

side_cards/python_exception_traceback_be.title: "File" and "line" are clues for finding the location to correct.
side_cards/python_exception_traceback_be.body: A lower traceback frame is a strong clue to where the exception was detected, but that line is not guaranteed to be the root cause.
side_cards/python_exception_traceback_be.detail: Read the final exception type and message, then move upward through your code to find where the bad input originated.

side_cards/python_exception_traceback_be.title: `raise` intentionally raises an error
side_cards/python_exception_traceback_be.body: `raise` is a syntax that directly throws an exception when it detects problematic input or a problematic state.
side_cards/python_exception_traceback_be.detail: Instead of silently proceeding, it halts the execution flow and reveals the cause, leaving a clue for debugging. For example, if a score is negative, it may be safer to raise a `ValueError` to indicate that the input is invalid rather than continuing with the calculation. `raise` is not a syntax that annoys users; it is a mechanism that prevents the code from proceeding in an incorrect state.

side_cards/python_exception_traceback_be.title: "Finally" is often used in cleanup tasks.
side_cards/python_exception_traceback_be.body: finally runs cleanup during normal completion, handled exceptions, and ordinary control transfers such as return. It cannot guarantee execution after every forced process termination.
side_cards/python_exception_traceback_be.detail: A resource-specific context manager such as with is often simpler for files.

side_cards/python_exception_traceback_be.title: The "except" clause should be as specific as possible.
side_cards/python_exception_traceback_be.body: A specific except handles only failures the code expects and can recover from. A bare except also catches KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit, hiding stops and bugs.
side_cards/python_exception_traceback_be.detail: If recovery is impossible, preserve the traceback by re-raising after any necessary logging.

side_cards/python_exception_traceback_be.title: If you silently suppress errors, debugging becomes more difficult.
side_cards/python_exception_traceback_be.body: If you do nothing inside the `except` block or return a meaningless value, you may miss the actual cause. You need to log the reason for the failure or reproduce it so that you can track down the same problem later.
side_cards/python_exception_traceback_be.detail: Beginners often assume a problem is solved simply because the error is no longer displayed on the screen. However, if you move on without documenting the cause, it becomes difficult to trace the issue later when data is missing or results appear abnormal. You need to consider logging, error messages, and strategies for handling recurrence together.

side_cards/python_file_exists_mkdir_begi.title: Path.exists() first checks whether a file or folder exists
side_cards/python_file_exists_mkdir_begi.body: Path.exists() returns True or False to indicate whether the specified path actually exists. Checking this before reading a file makes it easier to narrow down the cause of a FileNotFoundError.
side_cards/python_file_exists_mkdir_begi.detail: The `exists()` function checks whether a file or folder exists. Therefore, it’s a good habit to also use `is_file()` to verify that it’s a file, or `is_dir()` to verify that it’s a folder. Beginners should first verify that the path is correct and that the location is relative to the current working directory.

side_cards/python_file_exists_mkdir_begi.title: is_file() and is_dir() distinguish between files and folders
side_cards/python_file_exists_mkdir_begi.body: Even if `exists()` returns `True`, you still need to check separately whether it is a file or a folder.
side_cards/python_file_exists_mkdir_begi.detail: `is_file()` is used to check if an item is a file, and `is_dir()` is used to check if it is a folder; this allows you to distinguish between reading a file and listing the contents of a folder. For example, even if a path named "data" exists, if "data" is a folder, you cannot read it directly using `read_text()`. Conversely, when creating an output folder, you must verify that it is a folder and not a file.

side_cards/python_file_exists_mkdir_begi.title: mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True) creates the necessary folders
side_cards/python_file_exists_mkdir_begi.body: mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True) creates missing parent directories and continues when the same directory already exists. It still fails if the path is a regular file or permissions are insufficient.
side_cards/python_file_exists_mkdir_begi.detail: It does not suppress every error.

side_cards/python_file_exists_mkdir_begi.title: Before writing a file, prepare the parent folder.
side_cards/python_file_exists_mkdir_begi.body: The "parent" in a file path refers to the folder where the file will be placed. Calling `path.parent.mkdir(...)` before `write_text()` can help reduce save failures.
side_cards/python_file_exists_mkdir_begi.detail: For example, to write to `output/result.txt`, the `output` folder must exist first. `path.parent` points to the `output` folder, not to `result.txt` itself. That’s why storage pipelines often follow the sequence of creating the parent folder first and then writing the file.

side_cards/python_json_error_encoding_be.title: A JSONDecodeError indicates that the JSON syntax could not be parsed.
side_cards/python_json_error_encoding_be.body: A JSONDecodeError is an error that occurs when `json.loads()` or `json.load()` cannot parse the JSON syntax. First, check the placement of commas, quotation marks, and curly braces.
side_cards/python_json_error_encoding_be.detail: JSON looks similar to a Python dictionary, but its syntax is stricter. String keys must be enclosed in double quotes, and commas are required between items. The line, column, and character information in error messages provides clues to pinpoint the location of the problem.

side_cards/python_json_error_encoding_be.title: utf-8-sig is useful when reading UTF-8 files that contain a BOM
side_cards/python_json_error_encoding_be.body: A UTF-8 BOM may appear as U+FEFF at the start of decoded text. In JSON it can cause a BOM-related JSONDecodeError; in CSV it may attach to the first header.
side_cards/python_json_error_encoding_be.detail: Use utf-8-sig when the source bytes are UTF-8 with a BOM rather than as a generic fix for every decoding error.

side_cards/python_json_error_encoding_be.title: "ensure_ascii=False" is often used to save Korean characters as-is.
side_cards/python_json_error_encoding_be.body: If you use `ensure_ascii=False` with `json.dumps()`, Korean characters are saved as human-readable text rather than being converted to the `\uXXXX` format. This is useful when checking Korean configuration files or logs.
side_cards/python_json_error_encoding_be.detail: By default, non-ASCII characters may be stored in Unicode escape format. While the data itself is not incorrect, it makes it difficult for humans to open and review the file. When saving flashcards or Korean description data, it is recommended to use both `ensure_ascii=False` and `encoding='utf-8'`.

side_cards/python_json_error_encoding_be.title: Ensure that JSON is stored in a readable format and verified for safety
side_cards/python_json_error_encoding_be.body: When saving JSON, the combination of `ensure_ascii=False`, `indent=2`, and `encoding='utf-8'` is often used. When reading JSON, you should check for both `JSONDecodeError` and encoding issues.
side_cards/python_json_error_encoding_be.detail: `indent=2` makes the structure easier for humans to read, `ensure_ascii=False` displays Korean characters as-is, and `encoding='utf-8'` specifies the file encoding. Conversely, if garbled text or parsing errors occur during reading, the system checks the JSON syntax, file encoding, and the presence of a BOM in that order.

side_cards/python_csv_writer_dictreader_.title: csv.writer writes rows in list form to a CSV file
side_cards/python_csv_writer_dictreader_.body: `csv.writer` takes a row as an ordered set of values—such as a list or tuple—and writes it to a CSV file.
side_cards/python_csv_writer_dictreader_.detail: `writerow()` is a method for writing a single row, and it eliminates the need to manually handle commas between values. If you concatenate a CSV directly as a string, it can be confusing to handle commas, quotes, and line breaks. Using `csv.writer` allows you to safely write each value one character at a time.

side_cards/python_csv_writer_dictreader_.title: csv.DictWriter uses the keys of the dictionary as column names.
side_cards/python_csv_writer_dictreader_.body: csv.DictWriter is used to save dictionary data as a CSV file. fieldnames specifies the column names and their order, and writeheader() writes the header row.
side_cards/python_csv_writer_dictreader_.detail: If the row data is a dictionary, you can save it using `writerow(row)`. In this case, the dictionary keys must match the field names for the values to be written to the correct columns. When saving multiple rows, first write the column names using `writeheader()`, and then write each row using `writerow()`.

side_cards/python_csv_writer_dictreader_.title: The results from `DictReader` can be read like a dictionary, row by row.
side_cards/python_csv_writer_dictreader_.body: csv.DictReader reads each row as a dictionary, using the CSV headers as keys. Using `list(reader)` allows you to collect multiple rows into a list.
side_cards/python_csv_writer_dictreader_.detail: When reading a CSV file and then filtering or transforming the data, it’s common to collect the rows into a list for processing. While `rows = list(reader)` loads all rows into memory—which is convenient for training with small files—it’s also important to get into the habit of processing large files one row at a time using `for row in reader`.

side_cards/python_csv_writer_dictreader_.title: Typos in CSV column names are a common cause of KeyErrors.
side_cards/python_csv_writer_dictreader_.body: Inspect reader.fieldnames and explicitly validate required columns at startup. row.get('score') can be useful for an optional column, but it can silently turn a missing required score into None.
side_cards/python_csv_writer_dictreader_.detail: If headers are normalized, preserve the original names and document the rule.

side_cards/python_requests_api_beginner_.title: When checking an API response, check the `status_code` and `text` first.
side_cards/python_requests_api_beginner_.body: The status and a limited body preview help diagnose HTTP failures or HTML returned instead of JSON.
side_cards/python_requests_api_beginner_.detail: A 2xx status means HTTP-level success, not semantically valid data, and bodies may contain secrets or personal data, so do not log them indiscriminately. Validate the response schema as well.

side_cards/python_requests_api_beginner_.title: Timeouts and RequestExceptions are safeguards designed to minimize downtime.
side_cards/python_requests_api_beginner_.body: A Requests timeout limits connect or no-progress read waits; it is not necessarily a deadline for the whole download.
side_cards/python_requests_api_beginner_.detail: RequestException is the common base for Timeout, ConnectionError, and HTTPError from raise_for_status(). Retrying also requires limits, backoff, and duplicate-execution safety.

side_cards/python_requests_api_beginner_.title: `raise_for_status()` raises an exception for an invalid HTTP status.
side_cards/python_requests_api_beginner_.body: response.raise_for_status() raises an HTTPError when a failure status code—such as 404 or 500—is received, ensuring that the issue is not hidden. This allows you to quickly detect failed API calls.
side_cards/python_requests_api_beginner_.detail: An API call is not always successful just because a response object has been returned. A 404 page or a 500 error response can also be returned as a response object. Using `raise_for_status()` prevents the code from proceeding as if it were successful and allows you to handle the failure state as an exception.

side_cards/python_requests_api_beginner_.title: `params` safely appends the URL query, and `response.json()` converts the JSON response into a dictionary or list.
side_cards/python_requests_api_beginner_.body: params helps encode a GET query and response.json() parses the body as JSON.
side_cards/python_requests_api_beginner_.detail: A successful status can still contain invalid JSON, and valid JSON can lack required fields, so handle HTTP status, decoding, and schema validation separately.

side_cards/python_pandas_beginner_side_c.title: Use `pd.read_csv()` to read a spreadsheet file into a DataFrame, and use `head()` to view the first few rows.
side_cards/python_pandas_beginner_side_c.body: In pandas, `pd.read_csv()` reads a CSV file into a DataFrame. `df.head()` is used to quickly check the first few rows to see if the data was read correctly.
side_cards/python_pandas_beginner_side_c.detail: Immediately after reading a file, it’s a good idea to check whether the rows and columns are as expected, rather than processing the entire dataset right away. By looking at `df.head()`, `df.shape`, and `df.columns` together, you can quickly check the file structure and easily identify issues such as incorrect delimiters or column names early on. For beginners, it’s safest to first check the first five rows and the column names before moving on to filtering or calculations.

side_cards/python_pandas_beginner_side_c.title: df['column_name'] selects a column, and the condition filters the rows
side_cards/python_pandas_beginner_side_c.body: In pandas, `df['score']` selects the single `score` column. If you write it as `df[df['score'] >= 80]`, it keeps only the rows that satisfy the condition, so you must first verify that the column name is correct.
side_cards/python_pandas_beginner_side_c.detail: The part that confuses beginners the most is the difference between column selection and row filtering. df['score'] is an expression that retrieves a column, while df['score'] >= 80 creates a True/False condition. When that condition is placed inside df[...], rows are filtered.

side_cards/python_pandas_beginner_side_c.title: df.to_csv(..., index=False) removes unnecessary index columns
side_cards/python_pandas_beginner_side_c.body: index=False omits DataFrame row labels from the CSV. That avoids an unnecessary column for a disposable RangeIndex, but a meaningful identifier stored in the index must not be discarded.
side_cards/python_pandas_beginner_side_c.detail: Confirm its meaning and read the output back to verify the columns.

side_cards/python_pandas_beginner_side_c.title: NaN is a missing value and is handled using isna, fillna, or dropna.
side_cards/python_pandas_beginner_side_c.body: NaN or NA is a pandas missing-value marker and may not be the same as an empty string. After counting missing entries with isna().sum(), choose deletion or imputation based on data meaning.
side_cards/python_pandas_beginner_side_c.detail: A zero score and an unrecorded score are different, so record the rule and affected rows.

side_cards/python_datetime_beginner_side.title: date.today() and strftime() create dates and convert them to strings
side_cards/python_datetime_beginner_side.body: date.today() uses the system's local date, and strftime formats a date as text. Fixed-width YYYYMMDD names sort well within one timezone, but servers in different timezones can produce different dates.

side_cards/python_datetime_beginner_side.title: strptime() parses a date string into a date object
side_cards/python_datetime_beginner_side.body: datetime.strptime() is a function that converts a date string, such as '2026-06-03', into an actual date and time object according to a specified format.
side_cards/python_datetime_beginner_side.detail: To perform the calculation, the text must first be interpreted as a date. Even though a string representing a date may look like a date, it is simply text. To sort dates, calculate the difference between dates, or filter by date range, you must convert it to a `datetime` object using `strptime()`.

side_cards/python_datetime_beginner_side.title: `timedelta` represents a date difference, such as "a few days ago" or "a few days from now."
side_cards/python_datetime_beginner_side.body: `timedelta(days=7)` represents a period of 7 days, and by adding or subtracting this value from a date, you can safely calculate dates a certain number of days before or after that date.
side_cards/python_datetime_beginner_side.detail: It is also frequently used in filters for recent records. Use `timedelta` for tasks that require calculating date differences, such as organizing backup files, filtering data from the last 7 days, or calculating expiration dates. It’s safer to perform calculations using date objects rather than subtracting date strings directly.

side_cards/python_datetime_beginner_side.title: Distinguishing between UTC and KST helps reduce the problem of dates being off by a day.
side_cards/python_datetime_beginner_side.body: Since the server time may be in UTC while users see KST, clearly distinguishing time zones can help minimize issues where dates are off by a day.
side_cards/python_datetime_beginner_side.detail: Also, specify the recording standard, and distinguish between the storage standard and the display standard. For services or learning records based on Korean standards, the date in KST may be important. In Python, you can create a fixed KST offset using `timezone(timedelta(hours=9))`, and you must clearly specify the reference time when saving records.

side_cards/python_regex_beginner_side_ca.title: re.search() returns `match` if it finds a pattern, and `None` if it doesn't.
side_cards/python_regex_beginner_side_ca.body: re.search() is a function that searches for a pattern throughout an entire string. Simply put, it looks for a specific substring within a long sentence and returns `None` if it doesn't find one.
side_cards/python_regex_beginner_side_ca.detail: Therefore, to be safe, you must always check for a match before calling `group()`. Beginners should read the code separately for the cases where a match is found and where it is not. Beginners to regular expressions often encounter an `AttributeError` when they try to access the result of `re.search()` directly with `.group()`.

side_cards/python_regex_beginner_side_ca.title: `re.findall()` collects all matches into a list, and the parentheses are capture groups that extract only a subset of them.
side_cards/python_regex_beginner_side_ca.body: re.findall() finds all values that match a pattern and returns them as a list. Simply put, it’s a function used to collect recurring elements—such as numbers, dates, or IDs—from a sentence all at once.
side_cards/python_regex_beginner_side_ca.detail: If there are multiple search results, you should think of using findall() before search(). I usually use `re.search()` when looking for a single occurrence and `re.findall()` when looking for all occurrences. For example, `findall` is convenient when extracting multiple numbers, dates, or IDs from a log.

side_cards/python_regex_beginner_side_ca.title: If you write regular expression patterns as raw strings, such as r'\d+', it helps avoid confusion with backslashes.
side_cards/python_regex_beginner_side_ca.body: Backslashes appear frequently in regular expressions, such as \d, \w, and \s. Simply put, \d stands for a digit, \w stands for a word character, and \s stands for a whitespace character.
