side_cards/python_regex_beginner_side_ca.detail: In Python, using raw strings like r'\d+' allows you to read these patterns more safely and with less confusion. Backslashes also have special meanings in regular Python strings. Since backslashes have special meanings in regular expressions as well, beginners often get very confused when writing patterns as regular strings.

side_cards/python_regex_beginner_side_ca.title: re.match() only checks the starting position, while re.sub() finds the pattern and replaces it
side_cards/python_regex_beginner_side_ca.body: re.match() searches only at the start, while re.sub() replaces matched text. A successful match can leave trailing characters, so re.fullmatch() is clearer for validating an entire input.
side_cards/python_regex_beginner_side_ca.detail: Test that a masking pattern covers all sensitive variants.

side_cards/python_argparse_cli_beginner_.title: The Differences Between CLI, sys.argv, and argparse
side_cards/python_argparse_cli_beginner_.body: CLI stands for Command Line Interface, which is a method of running programs by passing commands and arguments together in a terminal.
side_cards/python_argparse_cli_beginner_.detail: `sys.argv` provides the simplest list of arguments, while `argparse` allows you to handle named options and help messages more safely. Beginners tend to simply double-click a Python file or run it using the "Run" button. However, real automation tools are often executed in the terminal using a command like `python tool.py --input data.csv --output result.json`.

side_cards/python_argparse_cli_beginner_.title: argparse options, types, and default values
side_cards/python_argparse_cli_beginner_.body: argparse type=int reports string-conversion failures as usage errors, but it does not validate business rules such as a positive range. A default only defines omission behavior; it does not make every value safe.
side_cards/python_argparse_cli_beginner_.detail: Validate required options, ranges, files, and conflicting choices separately.

side_cards/python_argparse_cli_beginner_.title: parse_args and main guard
side_cards/python_argparse_cli_beginner_.body: parse_args() is the step where argparse reads terminal arguments and converts them into an args object.
side_cards/python_argparse_cli_beginner_.detail: The main guard ensures that main() runs only when the file is executed directly, and prevents it from running automatically when the file is imported from another file. In argparse code, you typically create a parser, register options using `add_argument()`, and then read the actual input with `args = parser.parse_args()`. You can then retrieve values by name, such as `args.input` and `args.output`.

side_cards/python_argparse_cli_beginner_.title: The Basic Workflow of a Small CLI Tool
side_cards/python_argparse_cli_beginner_.body: A small CLI tool is easier to understand if you break it down into the following steps: parsing arguments, validating input, performing the actual processing, and saving the results.
side_cards/python_argparse_cli_beginner_.detail: By breaking it down this way, you can integrate previously learned concepts—such as CSV, JSON, regular expressions, and date handling—into a single executable tool. At first, it’s easy to write all the code as one long block in a single file, but if you want to turn it into a tool, it’s better to break it down into separate functions. For example, you could have `parse_args()` read user input, `validate_input()` check if a file exists, `process()` handle the actual data, and `save_result()` save the results.

side_cards/python_pathlib_argparse_file_.title: Linking argparse Values to Path Objects
side_cards/python_pathlib_argparse_file_.body: File paths received via `argparse` are initially strings. By converting this value into a `Path` object—such as `Path(args.input)`—you can more easily work with path information, such as the filename, extension, parent folder, and whether the file exists.
side_cards/python_pathlib_argparse_file_.detail: CLI tools are typically run like this: python tool.py --input data.txt --output out/result.txt. In this case, args.input and args.output are passed as strings. While you can use them as strings, converting them to Path objects allows you to naturally use functions such as `input_path.exists()`, `input_path.suffix`, and `output_path.parent`. As a beginner, it’s a good idea to get into the habit of treating paths not just as simple strings, but as objects for working with the file system.

side_cards/python_pathlib_argparse_file_.title: Checking Input Using `exists` and `suffix`
side_cards/python_pathlib_argparse_file_.body: exists() reports only that a path exists at check time and is also true for a directory. For file input, use is_file() and still handle read errors. suffix is only a hint for choosing a parser; it does not prove that the content is valid JSON or CSV.
examples: if not input_path.exists(): raise SystemExit('File not found')
if input_path.suffix != '.txt': raise SystemExit('Only .txt files are allowed')

side_cards/python_pathlib_argparse_file_.title: read_text, write_text, mkdir flow
side_cards/python_pathlib_argparse_file_.body: read_text and write_text load or write a whole text file, so consider memory for large files. mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True) can prepare parents but still fails for a conflicting file or insufficient permissions. Define encoding and overwrite policy explicitly.

side_cards/python_pathlib_argparse_file_.title: Basic Workflow of the CLI for Processing Actual Files
side_cards/python_pathlib_argparse_file_.body: The actual file-processing CLI is easier to understand if broken down into the following steps: parsing arguments, converting paths, validating input, reading files, processing them, creating an output folder, and saving the results. This step brings together the argparse, pathlib, regex, CSV, and JSON concepts we learned earlier.
side_cards/python_pathlib_argparse_file_.detail: At first, it’s easy to write all the code in a single file. However, if you plan to use it repeatedly as a tool, it’s better to break the code into separate sections. `parse_args()` reads the command-line arguments, `Path(args.input)` creates a path object, and `exists()` checks for the input. Next, you can retrieve data using `read_text()` or by reading CSV/JSON files, perform the necessary processing, and then save the results using `write_text()` or by saving to a CSV file. Once you get the hang of this structure, you can turn small automation scripts into actual tools.
examples: parse_args() -> Path conversion -> exists() -> read_text() -> write_text()

side_cards/python_json_csv_cli_practice_.title: Grouping Handlers by File Extension
side_cards/python_json_csv_cli_practice_.body: Dispatching on suffix makes JSON and CSV loader flow clear. Use suffix.lower() if uppercase extensions are accepted, and handle each parser's exceptions because an extension does not validate content. Report the supported extensions for unknown input.

side_cards/python_json_csv_cli_practice_.title: Reading and Writing JSON
side_cards/python_json_csv_cli_practice_.body: You can read a string from a JSON file using `read_text()` and convert it to Python data using `json.loads()`. Conversely, when saving the result, you can convert Python data to a JSON string using `json.dumps()`.
side_cards/python_json_csv_cli_practice_.detail: It’s easy to understand the JSON processing flow as a process that moves back and forth between strings and Python data. `input_path.read_text(encoding='utf-8')` reads the file contents as a string, and `json.loads(text)` converts that string into a dictionary or list. To save the processed results, use `json.dumps(data, ensure_ascii=False, indent=2)` to create a human-readable JSON string, then save it using `write_text()`. If the data contains Korean characters, using `ensure_ascii=False` makes the output easier to read.

side_cards/python_json_csv_cli_practice_.title: CSV DictReader and DictWriter
side_cards/python_json_csv_cli_practice_.body: csv.DictReader allows you to read CSV rows as a dictionary organized by column names. csv.DictWriter is used to save a list of dictionaries back to CSV, and you use `fieldnames` to specify the column names and their order.
side_cards/python_json_csv_cli_practice_.detail: If the first line of a CSV file is a header, beginners will find it easier to read the file using `DictReader`. This is because each row can be accessed by its column name, such as `row['name']`. When saving, use `DictWriter` and specify the column names in `fieldnames`. `writeheader()` writes the header row, and `writerows(rows)` saves multiple rows. It’s also a good idea to learn how to use `newline=''` and `encoding='utf-8'` together to handle CSV files safely.

side_cards/python_json_csv_cli_practice_.title: Creating a Data Summary
side_cards/python_json_csv_cli_practice_.body: File-processing CLIs often generate summary results—such as the number of rows, a list of columns, a list of keys, and the number of errors—rather than simply copying the original data. If you store the summary in a dictionary, it’s easy to use for both saving as JSON and displaying on the screen.
side_cards/python_json_csv_cli_practice_.detail: For example, if you’ve read a CSV file, you can store the number of rows and a list of columns in a `summary` dictionary. If the JSON is a list, you can count the number of items; if it’s a dictionary, you can create a list of keys. A summary created this way is easy to save using `json.dumps()` and can be easily expanded into logs or reports later. The key point is to separate reading, processing, and saving—rather than mixing them all into a single line—by using a function like `make_summary()`.

side_cards/python_file_cli_error_recover.title: Understanding JSONDecodeError
side_cards/python_file_cli_error_recover.body: A `JSONDecodeError` is an error that occurs when a JSON string is syntactically incorrect. Simply put, it means that the JSON is not formatted according to the rules—such as the use of curly braces, quotes, and commas—and therefore cannot be converted into Python data.
side_cards/python_file_cli_error_recover.detail: When you read a JSON file using `read_text()`, it is still a string. If there is a syntax error during the process of converting this string into a dictionary or list using `json.loads()`, a `json.JSONDecodeError` will occur. In CLI tools, it’s better to replace this error with a simple message like “Please check the JSON format” rather than displaying the traceback as-is. This is a common failure that occurs especially when accepting user-generated JSON files as input.
examples: except json.JSONDecodeError: raise SystemExit('JSON format error')

side_cards/python_file_cli_error_recover.title: Checking for "file not found" and "file exists"
side_cards/python_file_cli_error_recover.body: An exists() precheck enables a friendly message, but the file can disappear immediately afterward. Use is_file() for file-only input and handle FileNotFoundError and PermissionError from the actual read. Showing the working directory and resolved path helps diagnose mistakes.
examples: if not input_path.exists(): raise SystemExit('Input file does not exist')
except FileNotFoundError: raise SystemExit('Please check the file path')

side_cards/python_file_cli_error_recover.title: Handling CSV Column KeyErrors
side_cards/python_file_cli_error_recover.body: A row read using `csv.DictReader` behaves like a dictionary that uses column names as keys. If you try to access a column name that does not exist in the CSV—such as `row['score']`—a `KeyError` may occur.
side_cards/python_file_cli_error_recover.detail: Column names may vary from one CSV file to another. While the code expects a column named "score," the actual file may contain different names such as "Score," "score," or "value." In this case, attempting to read `row['score']` directly will result in a `KeyError`. You can make error messages clearer by checking the list of columns using `reader.fieldnames` or by first verifying whether the required columns exist. In the data processing CLI, verifying column names is a crucial part of input validation.
examples: if 'score' is not in reader.fieldnames: raise SystemExit('No 'score' column')

side_cards/python_file_cli_error_recover.title: Basic Workflow for CLI Error Recovery
side_cards/python_file_cli_error_recover.body: Error handling in a file-processing CLI should be divided into three parts: input validation, specific exception handling, and clear error messages. The key is to clearly inform users of issues they can resolve themselves, rather than hiding all errors.
side_cards/python_file_cli_error_recover.detail: A good CLI tool isn’t one that never fails, but one that clearly explains the cause of a failure when it does occur. If a file is missing, it should tell you to check the path; if the JSON syntax is invalid, it should tell you to check the JSON format; and if a CSV column is missing, it should simply tell you the name of the required column. In such cases, it’s safer to handle errors by raising specific exceptions—such as `FileNotFoundError`, `JSONDecodeError`, or `KeyError`—rather than using a generic `bare except` block to catch all errors. Finally, you can use `SystemExit` to display a short, clear message to the user.
examples: except json.JSONDecodeError: raise SystemExit('JSON format error')
except KeyError as e: raise SystemExit(f'The required column is missing: {e}')

side_cards/python_logging_verbose_cli_si.title: Basic Understanding of Logging Levels
side_cards/python_logging_verbose_cli_si.body: Logging can be categorized into levels such as DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, and ERROR. Beginners will find it easier to get started if they understand that INFO refers to general progress, DEBUG refers to detailed internal checks, and ERROR refers to failure conditions.
side_cards/python_logging_verbose_cli_si.detail: "print" is simple, but all messages appear to have the same level of importance. "logging" allows you to assign levels to messages, enabling a more systematic view of the execution status. For example, a message indicating that a file has started to be read is typically classified as INFO; values that developers need to check, such as the `input_path` or the number of rows, are classified as DEBUG; and unhandled failures are classified as ERROR. By changing the level setting, you can configure the system to display only the messages you need.

side_cards/python_logging_verbose_cli_si.title: The Role of the `verbose` Option
side_cards/python_logging_verbose_cli_si.body: --verbose is an option you enable when you want to see detailed execution information that is normally hidden. In argparse, if you set it to action='store_true', it returns True or False depending on whether input is provided.
side_cards/python_logging_verbose_cli_si.detail: If a CLI tool is always verbose, users may miss important messages. Therefore, it is common to display only INFO-level logs during normal execution, and to show DEBUG-level logs as well when the --verbose flag is added to indicate a problem. You can create the flag using `parser.add_argument('--verbose', action='store_true')` and then choose between `logging.DEBUG` or `logging.INFO` based on the value of `args.verbose`.
examples: level = logging.DEBUG if args.verbose else logging.INFO

side_cards/python_logging_verbose_cli_si.title: Distinguishing Between `print` and `logging`
side_cards/python_logging_verbose_cli_si.body: `print` is useful for simply displaying results, while `logging` is good for recording the execution process and error-tracking messages. As a small script grows into a CLI tool, the benefits of `logging` become more significant.
side_cards/python_logging_verbose_cli_si.detail: At first, simply using `print('Done')` might be enough. However, once you start reading input, processing data, saving results, and handling errors, it can become confusing to distinguish between messages that indicate the result and those intended for debugging. By using `logging`, you can categorize messages as follows: `INFO` for progress, `DEBUG` for internal checks, and `ERROR` for failures. Think of this as the first step in separating the output visible to users from the messages that developers use for tracing.

side_cards/python_logging_verbose_cli_si.title: Where to place debug logs
side_cards/python_logging_verbose_cli_si.body: Useful DEBUG logs record paths, formats, counts, and branches that narrow a failure. Never log API keys, tokens, personal data, or full sensitive responses—even in --verbose mode. Prefer structured fields and keep diagnostics separate from user output.

side_cards/python_env_secret_config_side.title: Basic Understanding of Environment Variables
side_cards/python_env_secret_config_side.body: Environment variables are a way to pass configuration values to a program from outside the code. This makes it easier to manage configurations, as the same code can be run with different values in the development, testing, and production environments.
side_cards/python_env_secret_config_side.detail: For example, values such as the API address, execution mode, and log level are easier to change if they are read as environment variables rather than hard-coded. In Python, you can retrieve these values using the syntax `os.environ.get('NAME')`. For settings that require a default value, you can use `os.environ.get('APP_MODE', 'dev')`, and for values that are strictly required, you can configure the script to terminate with a `SystemExit` if they are missing.

side_cards/python_env_secret_config_side.title: Handling API Keys and Secrets
side_cards/python_env_secret_config_side.body: As a general rule, values such as API keys, tokens, and passwords should not be hard-coded. If these values are leaked through GitHub, screenshots, or shared files, it could lead to financial or authorization issues.
side_cards/python_env_secret_config_side.detail: Keep secret values separate from the code and read them from environment variables, server secret storage, or local .env files. Especially for public repositories or portfolio projects, never include actual keys; it’s safer to include only examples in the README, such as `OPENAI_API_KEY=your_key_here`. It’s also important to make it a habit to pause the program with a clear message before sending any requests if the required key is missing at startup.
examples: if not api_key: raise SystemExit('Set OPENAI_API_KEY')

side_cards/python_env_secret_config_side.title: .env and load_dotenv Workflow
side_cards/python_env_secret_config_side.body: load_dotenv() makes .env values available like environment variables and, by default, does not override an existing variable of the same name. It is a local convenience file, not a secret store, so also protect file permissions and exclude it from Git. Prefer platform secret settings in deployment.

side_cards/python_env_secret_config_side.title: .env and .gitignore
side_cards/python_env_secret_config_side.body: .gitignore reduces the chance of newly committing an untracked .env. It does not remove a tracked file or erase old commits. Revoke and rotate an exposed key immediately, then handle repository history separately if required.

side_cards/python_requirements_dependenc.title: The Basics of requirements.txt
side_cards/python_requirements_dependenc.body: requirements.txt is a file that lists the external packages required for a project. It tells you which packages need to be installed when running the same project on another computer.
side_cards/python_requirements_dependenc.detail: Small code projects that use only the Python standard library may not require a `requirements.txt` file. However, if you use packages that need to be installed separately—such as requests, pandas, or python-dotenv—you should include a list of them. This allows anyone who receives the project on a new computer or server to quickly install the necessary packages. Think of requirements.txt not as code itself, but as a file that describes the runtime environment.

side_cards/python_requirements_dependenc.title: pip install -r flow
side_cards/python_requirements_dependenc.body: "python -m pip install -r requirements.txt" is a command that installs all the packages listed in `requirements.txt` at once. It is typically run after activating a virtual environment.
side_cards/python_requirements_dependenc.detail: -r means to read the requirements file. Using the `python -m pip` syntax makes it easier to run the pip associated with the currently active Python environment. This helps reduce confusion—especially on Windows, where multiple Python installations may be present or when using venv—where pip might be installed in the wrong environment. After installing a package, you can import and use it in your code.

side_cards/python_requirements_dependenc.title: Version Locking and pip freeze
side_cards/python_requirements_dependenc.body: Exact pins reduce variation but do not by themselves fix Python, the operating system, or every transitive dependency. pip freeze can include packages installed by accident. Review direct and transitive requirements and use a suitable lock or hashes plus runtime documentation when stronger reproduction is needed.

side_cards/python_requirements_dependenc.title: Reproducible Runtime Environment
side_cards/python_requirements_dependenc.body: A virtual environment plus requirements is a basic dependency-isolation workflow. Activation is optional because the environment interpreter can be called directly. Document supported Python and OS constraints, pinning policy, and a real verification command for stronger reproducibility.

side_cards/python_readme_setup_troublesh.title: Basic Structure of the README
side_cards/python_readme_setup_troublesh.body: The README is the first guide to a project. It should allow first-time users to understand what the project does, what preparations are needed, and how to install, run, and verify that it works properly.
side_cards/python_readme_setup_troublesh.detail: For a README aimed at beginners, a step-by-step guide is more important than a fancy explanation. It’s a good idea to include sections such as Project Introduction, Prerequisites, Setup, Environment Variables, Run, Verify, and Troubleshooting. Even for personal projects, it’s important to get into the habit of writing down commands you’ve actually tested, so that you can run them again later.

side_cards/python_readme_setup_troublesh.title: How to Write Installation Instructions
side_cards/python_readme_setup_troublesh.body: The "Setup" section explains the steps a new user should follow when first receiving the project. Typical steps include cloning the project, navigating to the correct folder, creating a venv, activating it, and installing the requirements.
side_cards/python_readme_setup_troublesh.detail: Commands should be listed in the order they are actually executed. For example, after running `git clone`, use `cd` to enter the project folder, then create a virtual environment with `python -m venv .venv` and activate it. Next, install the required packages using `python -m pip install -r requirements.txt`. If the commands differ between Windows and macOS/Linux, it’s a good idea to list them separately.

side_cards/python_readme_setup_troublesh.title: .env.example Guide
side_cards/python_readme_setup_troublesh.body: .env.example is a sample file that lists the necessary environment variable names without revealing the actual secret values. The README can instruct users to copy this file to create a .env file.
side_cards/python_readme_setup_troublesh.detail: Since the actual .env file may contain sensitive information such as API keys, it’s safer not to commit it to Git. Instead, use placeholders in the `.env.example` file, such as `OPENAI_API_KEY=your_key_here`. This way, others can see the names of the necessary variables and add their own values only to their local `.env` file. This approach balances security with ease of use.

side_cards/python_readme_setup_troublesh.title: Troubleshooting: Writing
side_cards/python_readme_setup_troublesh.body: For ModuleNotFoundError, check the interpreter, venv, and installation, then import spelling, launch location, and local name shadowing. For a port conflict, identify the owning process before stopping it or choose another port. For environment errors, verify the name, load timing, and deployment setting; include the exact message and a safe diagnostic command.
examples: Address already in use → use another port

side_cards/python_unlinked_core_gap_side.title: Reading the Validation Flow
side_cards/python_unlinked_core_gap_side.body: Validation is the process of verifying whether code or data meets the expected conditions.
side_cards/python_unlinked_core_gap_side.detail: Validation code is typically read in the following order: input verification, rule checking, collection of failed items, and output of results. Its role is not simply to check for errors, but to catch conditions in advance—such as missing fields, incorrect data types, duplicate IDs, and out-of-range values—that could cause the app to malfunction later on. In educational apps, it is crucial for automatically verifying quality criteria such as the number of cards, JSON structure, inclusion of correct answers, and side card connections.
examples: Check that the card JSON contains all of the following: id, question, choices, and answer.
If the "answer" is not found in the "choices," it is treated as a validation failure.

side_cards/python_unlinked_core_gap_side.title: Understanding the Debugging Flow
side_cards/python_unlinked_core_gap_side.body: Debugging is the process of narrowing down the reasons why code behaves differently than expected.
side_cards/python_unlinked_core_gap_side.detail: When debugging, rather than fixing the issue immediately based solely on the symptoms, check the following in order: the conditions under which the error occurs, the error message, any suspicious input values, and finally, the point where the program last behaved normally. For a traceback, start by looking at the error type and message on the last line, then trace back up the file name and line numbers. It’s a good idea to use `print` or `logging` to check intermediate values, and after making a fix, leave a small verification command to ensure the same problem doesn’t occur again.
examples: If a KeyError occurs, first check to see if you tried to access a key that doesn't exist.
If a value seems unusual, check both the data type and the actual value using `print(type(x), x)`.

side_cards/python_unlinked_core_gap_side.title: Reading JSON Data Streams
side_cards/python_unlinked_core_gap_side.body: Separate raw JSON text from the dictionary or list produced by json.loads/json.load. Check encoding, BOMs, JSONDecodeError, required keys, and nested types. ensure_ascii=False controls non-ASCII escaping; it does not repair bad encoding, so specify file encoding separately.
examples: `json.loads(text)` converts a JSON string into a Python dictionary or list.
json.dumps(data, ensure_ascii=False) is often used to save data without garbling Korean characters.

side_cards/python_unlinked_core_gap_side.title: Reading the Pipeline Flow
side_cards/python_unlinked_core_gap_side.body: A pipeline is a workflow consisting of multiple processing steps linked together in a specific order.
side_cards/python_unlinked_core_gap_side.detail: It’s easier to understand pipeline code if you break it down into stages: receiving input, preprocessing, transforming, validating, and saving the results. Each stage takes the output from the previous stage as its input. Therefore, you need to check the filenames, intermediate outputs, restart points in case of failure, and logs together. In batch processing, it is also important to determine whether items that have already been processed are skipped and whether only failed items can be rerun.
examples: Data is processed in the following order: collection → refinement → validation → storage.
If you save the intermediate JSONL file, it will be easy to resume from that step in case of a failure.

side_cards/python_unlinked_core_gap_side.title: Understanding the API Call Flow
side_cards/python_unlinked_core_gap_side.body: Read an API call as URL, method, headers, query/body, timeout, status, and then response schema. Load secrets from protected settings and never log them. Retry only eligible transient failures with backoff, a limit, and an idempotency check.
examples: Set a timeout as shown in `requests.get(url, params=params, timeout=10)`.
After calling `response.raise_for_status()`, read the data using `response.json()`.

side_cards/python_unlinked_core_gap_side.title: Reading the Database Code Flow
side_cards/python_unlinked_core_gap_side.body: Database code deals with the structure for storing and retrieving data.
side_cards/python_unlinked_core_gap_side.detail: Database-related code should be read in the following order: connection setup, table structure, queries, and result handling. CRUD stands for Create, Read, Update, and Delete, and most data storage functions combine these four operations. When writing SQL directly, concatenating input values as strings can be risky, so you must verify parameter binding. In the app architecture, the repository layer serves to centralize database access.
examples: SELECT retrieves data, and INSERT adds new data.
The Repository pattern wraps database queries so that the app code doesn't have to worry as much about how data is stored.

side_cards/python_unlinked_core_gap_side.title: Reading Schemas and Data Structures
side_cards/python_unlinked_core_gap_side.body: A schema is a set of rules that define which fields and data types the data must have.
side_cards/python_unlinked_core_gap_side.detail: By looking at the schema, you can first understand the structure of the data. You can determine which fields are required, whether they are strings or numbers, whether they are lists or dictionaries, and whether there are any value ranges. JSON objects, API responses, and database tables can all be analyzed from a schema perspective. When the schema is clear, it’s easier to automate validation, and even as the dataset grows, you can quickly identify missing values, typos, and type errors.
examples: A lesson card requires fields such as id, question, choices, and answer.
You can define data types such as `score` (a number) and `tags` (a list of strings).

side_cards/python_unlinked_core_gap_side.title: Performance Bottlenecks in Reading
side_cards/python_unlinked_core_gap_side.body: Performance is a measure of how fast and reliably code runs.
side_cards/python_unlinked_core_gap_side.detail: Performance issues typically arise from the number of iterations, the number of file or network calls, redundant calculations, and how large datasets are processed. First, time each step to identify which ones are slow, and check whether the same data is being read repeatedly or the same API is being called over and over. Caching is a method of reusing the same results to reduce both processing time and costs. In batch processing, you must also consider the number of items to process at once and the cost of retrying in case of failure.
examples: Reading the same file repeatedly within a loop can slow things down.
Caching frequently used API responses can reduce the number of calls and lower costs.

side_cards/python_unlinked_secondary_gap.title: Learning to Read UX Flows
side_cards/python_unlinked_secondary_gap.body: Learning UX refers to the screen flow and feedback structure designed to help users continue their learning.
side_cards/python_unlinked_secondary_gap.detail: UX code for learning isn’t just about creating visually appealing screens; it’s about creating a flow that lets users know what they’ve learned, what they got wrong, and what they need to do next. Features like “progress,” “review,” “mistake note,” “bookmark,” and “streak” all display the user’s learning status or encourage review. When reading the code, consider state management, display conditions, and the user’s next action together.
examples: Collect the questions you got wrong in a "mistake note" so you can review them later.
The "progress" value shows the number of cards solved today and the number of cards remaining.

side_cards/python_unlinked_secondary_gap.title: Understanding the Checkpoint and Resume Workflow
side_cards/python_unlinked_secondary_gap.body: A checkpoint should record completed IDs, input version, output location, and validation state. File existence alone can mistake a partial output for success, so use atomic writes or a completion marker. On resume, verify duplicates, omissions, and changed inputs.
examples: If the process fails after processing 60 out of 100, it restarts from the 61st.
If an output file already exists, the same items are not processed again.

side_cards/python_unlinked_secondary_gap.title: Understanding the GPU·Torch·Training Workflow
side_cards/python_unlinked_secondary_gap.body: The model and tensors must use the same device. Training uses loss.backward() and optimizer.step(); inference uses model.eval() to change dropout and batch-normalization behavior and no_grad() or inference_mode() to disable gradient recording. These settings serve different purposes, so check both.
examples: Use `torch.cuda.is_available()` to check whether CUDA is available.
Verify that `model.to(device)` and `tensor.to(device)` point to the same device.

side_cards/python_unlinked_secondary_gap.title: Understanding the Security·Settings·Secret Workflow
side_cards/python_unlinked_secondary_gap.body: Keep secrets out of code, logs, and clients by injecting them through protected environment or platform secret settings. A local .env is a convenience file, and .gitignore does not protect an already tracked secret. Rotate exposed values and review least privilege, retention, and personal-data transfers.
examples: Read the secret using `os.environ.get('API_KEY')` and do not hardcode it in the code.
Add the .env file to .gitignore so that it isn't pushed to the repository.

side_cards/python_unlinked_secondary_gap.title: Understanding the Retry, Timeout, and Resilience Workflow
side_cards/python_unlinked_secondary_gap.body: A timeout prevents indefinite waits, while a retry repeats eligible transient failures. Use a maximum, exponential backoff, and jitter. Do not automatically retry a side-effecting request such as POST unless idempotency is guaranteed, and stop immediately for authentication or validation failures.
examples: If a request fails, it will retry up to three times and log the failure.
Set a limit, such as `timeout=10`, to prevent the system from getting stuck waiting for unresponsive requests.

side_cards/python_unlinked_secondary_gap.title: Understanding the RAG, Search, and LLM Trends
side_cards/python_unlinked_secondary_gap.body: RAG is a method that searches for relevant information and appends it to the LLM's input before answering a question.
side_cards/python_unlinked_secondary_gap.detail: The RAG code should be read in the following order: question analysis, query generation, document retrieval, candidate ranking, context construction, and LLM invocation. Since poor search quality can lead to unreliable LLM responses, you must verify what sources were used and why they were selected. Embeddings are used to find documents with similar meanings, while keyword search is advantageous for finding materials that contain exact words.
examples: First, search for any cards or documents related to the question, and then send them to the LLM along with the question.
If there are insufficient search results, it indicates that further verification is needed rather than providing an answer.

side_cards/python_unlinked_secondary_gap.title: Understanding FastAPI and Server Workflow
side_cards/python_unlinked_secondary_gap.body: The FastAPI code demonstrates a server workflow that receives HTTP requests, processes them using functions, and returns responses.
side_cards/python_unlinked_secondary_gap.detail: FastAPI code is easiest to understand when read in the following order: route decorator, path, request parameter, and response model. A line like `@app.get('/items')` maps a specific URL request to the function that will handle it. Since server code receives external input, validation, exception handling, and status codes are also important. During development, run the code using Uvicorn, and in production, be sure to check environment variables and log settings as well.
examples: @app.get('/health') is often used as an API to check the server's status.
Check how the query parameters and JSON body are passed as function arguments.

side_cards/python_unlinked_secondary_gap.title: Reading the Input and Output Flow of a Function
side_cards/python_unlinked_secondary_gap.body: Function code can be viewed as a small sequence of steps that takes input, processes it, and returns a result.
side_cards/python_unlinked_secondary_gap.detail: When reading a function, break it down into its parameters, internal processing, and return value. For functions that involve I/O—such as those handling files, user input, or API responses—you must distinguish between values coming in from the outside and values going out, such as screen output, file saves, and return values. A good function has a single, clear responsibility, and its inputs and outputs are predictable. The easier a function is to test, the easier it is to debug.
examples: def clean_text(text): return text.strip() cleans up the input string and returns it.
It's easier to test the code if you separate the functions that read files from those that calculate data.

side_cards/python_unlinked_tertiary_gap_.title: Understanding the File·pathlib·encoding Workflow
side_cards/python_unlinked_tertiary_gap_.body: Path makes path composition and inspection convenient and portable, but it does not make a path secure. Check the working directory, existence and kind, permissions, encoding, overwrite policy, and read/write exceptions.
examples: Construct the path as follows: Path('data') / 'input.txt'.
Use `read_text(encoding='utf-8')` to safely read Korean text.

side_cards/python_unlinked_tertiary_gap_.title: Understanding the Object-Method-Class Flow
side_cards/python_unlinked_tertiary_gap_.body: Class code is read as a way to see what data and behaviors an object possesses.
side_cards/python_unlinked_tertiary_gap_.detail: An object is an actual entity created based on a class. A method is an action that an object can perform, and `self` refers to the object itself. When reading class code, check what state is stored in the constructor and whether methods read or modify that state. In particular, methods that modify internal state—such as those for lists or dictionaries—can have side effects, so you must also observe the changes before and after they are called.
examples: Distinguish between methods that simply return a value and those that directly modify the object's state.

side_cards/python_unlinked_tertiary_gap_.title: Understanding the Packaging and Dependency Flow
side_cards/python_unlinked_tertiary_gap_.body: venv and requirements are basic tools for isolation and installation requirements. Strong reproduction may also require Python and OS constraints, direct and transitive pins, a lock or hashes, and a verification command. The environment interpreter can be invoked directly without activation.
examples: Create a project-specific virtual environment using `python -m venv .venv`.
Install the required packages using `python -m pip install -r requirements.txt`.

side_cards/python_unlinked_tertiary_gap_.title: Understanding the Metadata, Deduplication, and Integrity Workflow
side_cards/python_unlinked_tertiary_gap_.body: In data processing, the reliability of the results is verified through deduplication, joins, and integrity checks.
side_cards/python_unlinked_tertiary_gap_.detail: Metadata is information that describes the data itself. For example, values such as source, creation date, file name, and ID can be considered metadata. Deduplication is the process of removing duplicates to ensure that the same item is not included multiple times. Joins and SQL are used to link multiple tables, but if the keys are incorrect, rows may be lost or duplicated. Therefore, after processing, you must verify the count, check for missing rows, identify duplicates, and ensure key integrity.
examples: Remove duplicate rows based on the `item_id`.
Check whether the number of rows has suddenly increased or decreased after the join.

side_cards/python_unlinked_tertiary_gap_.title: Understanding the PWA, Cache, and LocalStorage Workflow
side_cards/python_unlinked_tertiary_gap_.body: PWAs manage state and cache so that web apps function seamlessly even when offline or during subsequent visits.
side_cards/python_unlinked_tertiary_gap_.detail: PWA-related code is often structured to store app files in the cache and save the user’s progress in a storage mechanism such as localStorage. The cache is a mechanism for quickly loading app resources or for use while offline, while localStorage is used to store small amounts of state, such as user preferences or learning progress. When reading the code, be sure to check the timing of storage and retrieval, as well as the conditions for updates.
examples: Store the ID of the last study card in localStorage.
A service worker caches the app files so they load quickly when the user returns to the site.

side_cards/python_unlinked_tertiary_gap_.title: Understanding Automation, Workflow, and Git Workflows
side_cards/python_unlinked_tertiary_gap_.body: Automation moves repeated work into scripts or CI. A Git flow commonly covers change, verification, staging, commit, and push; a tag is optional when a release checkpoint is needed. Separate mutations from checks and ensure a failed quality gate blocks publication.
examples: The code must pass validation before it can be committed.
We use GitHub Actions to automatically run tests to verify that quality standards are met.

side_cards/python_unlinked_tertiary_gap_.title: Understanding the Architecture·Documentation Workflow
side_cards/python_unlinked_tertiary_gap_.body: The architecture document serves as a roadmap that describes the project's components and the separation of responsibilities.
side_cards/python_unlinked_tertiary_gap_.detail: When reviewing the architecture, check which modules are responsible for what and which layers the data passes through. Documentation doesn’t just describe how to use the system; it can also explain why a particular structure was chosen and guide you on which files to review first. In a service-oriented architecture, roles are divided into components such as the UI, API, storage, and batch jobs, so connecting the inputs and outputs of each part reveals the overall flow.
examples: Check the README for instructions on how to run the program and the main folder structure.
We will examine how the UI layer and the data layer are connected through certain functions.

side_cards/python_unlinked_tertiary_gap_.title: Reading Float, Numeric, and NaN Flows
side_cards/python_unlinked_tertiary_gap_.body: A float is a binary approximation, so decimal comparison and rounding need care. pandas NaN or NA marks missing data, is not simply an empty string, and may compare differently from ordinary numbers. Check conversion errors, missing-data policy, dtype, tolerances, and expected range.
examples: float('3.14') converts a string into a decimal number.
NaN values may need to be handled differently than regular numerical comparisons.

side_cards/python_unlinked_quaternary_ga.title: Understanding GitHub Pages, URLs, and Version History
side_cards/python_unlinked_quaternary_ga.body: During the deployment process, the system verifies that the URLs for the local server and GitHub Pages, as well as the app version string, match.
side_cards/python_unlinked_quaternary_ga.detail: For static web apps deployed via GitHub Pages, the files visible locally may differ from those visible at the actual public URL. Therefore, you should first verify them on the local_server, and after pushing, verify again that the `index.html`, `app.js`, and JSON files at the GitHub Pages URL are up to date. Version strings, such as `app_data_version`, serve as a reference for determining whether the cache is displaying outdated files.
examples: On your local machine, first check the URL http://127.0.0.1:5173/.
After deployment, check the `APP_DATA_VERSION` in `app.js` on GitHub Pages.

side_cards/python_unlinked_quaternary_ga.title: Reading the Evidence·Lineage·Provenance Flow
side_cards/python_unlinked_quaternary_ga.body: Evidence supports a decision; provenance and lineage trace a source through transformations. Filenames and line numbers are convenient but can drift after edits, so also record stable source IDs, a version or hash, extraction time, and transformations. Verify that each citation actually supports its claim.
examples: Include the source filename and line number next to your answer.
Record the steps taken from the raw data to the processed results.

side_cards/python_unlinked_quaternary_ga.title: Understanding the Batch·Shard·Memory Flow
side_cards/python_unlinked_quaternary_ga.body: Divide large tasks into batches and shards, and process them while monitoring memory usage.
side_cards/python_unlinked_quaternary_ga.detail: A "batch" is a unit that groups multiple items for processing, while a "shard" is a large dataset divided into multiple pieces. Reading a `large_file` all at once can cause memory issues, so it needs to be processed line by line or in small batches. Concurrency is a method of executing multiple tasks simultaneously, but increasing it too much can lead to failures and memory shortages before any speed gains are realized.
examples: Large JSONL files are processed by reading them one line at a time.
The files are split into parts such as shard_001 and shard_002 for parallel processing.

side_cards/python_unlinked_quaternary_ga.title: Understanding the Environment·main·checklist Workflow
side_cards/python_unlinked_quaternary_ga.body: The execution environment, the `main` entry point, and the checklist are the basic steps for running the script reliably.
side_cards/python_unlinked_quaternary_ga.detail: The environment refers to the conditions under which the code runs. The same code may behave differently depending on the Python version, installed packages, current directory, and environment variables. `main` is the point where the script actually begins, and the checklist summarizes the conditions that should be verified before and after execution. If a `parse_error` occurs, you should first determine whether the issue is due to a syntax error or a problem with the input file format.
examples: The execution flow begins below if __name__ == '__main__':.
Before execution, it checks whether the current folder and the input file exist.

side_cards/python_unlinked_quaternary_ga.title: Understanding the Count·Filter·Aggregation Flow
side_cards/python_unlinked_quaternary_ga.body: Many data summarization processes involve filtering the data, counting the number of records, and aggregating the results by group.
side_cards/python_unlinked_quaternary_ga.detail: Filtering is the process of retaining only the necessary items, while counting is the process of determining the number of items that meet a given condition. Aggregation involves grouping multiple values to produce summary statistics such as totals, averages, and distributions. If there are classification values such as “level,” you can calculate the count or percentage for each level. When reading code, you should check the order to determine whether the filter conditions come first or the aggregation comes first.
examples: Count the number of cards that are at the beginner level.
Use a counter to count the number of cards per file.

side_cards/python_unlinked_quaternary_ga.title: Understanding Rollback, Separation, and UI Flow
side_cards/python_unlinked_quaternary_ga.body: Keep UI changes and logic changes separate, and manage them so that they can be rolled back if a problem arises.
side_cards/python_unlinked_quaternary_ga.detail: Separation is a design approach that divides roles. For example, CSS is responsible for the visual appearance of the screen, while JavaScript logic handles data processing and user interaction. UI changes have a significant visual impact, but when they are mixed with logic errors, it becomes difficult to pinpoint the source of the problem. Rollback is the process of reverting a problematic change to its previous state. Breaking commits into smaller units makes rollbacks easier.
examples: Whenever possible, separate CSS changes and JSON data changes into separate commits.
If a problem arises, check the most recent commit to narrow down the scope of the changes.
